2166: The Food Inspector of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi visited the shop of the respondent and took a sample of curd for the purpose of testing whether there was any adulteration. Each part of the sample contained a small quantity of charas, which was kept in a separate bottle and sealed by the Food Inspector. One of the bottles containing the sample of the curd was handed over to the respondent who gave a certificate on October 23, 1961, in which he noted that the sample of curb had become highly decomposed and no analysis of it was possible. The respondent applied to the Director of the Central Food Laboratory under section 13(2) of the , for obtaining a certificate from the Director of Central Food Laboratory as regards the percentage of the contents of the curb in the sample. The Director of the Food Laboratory refused to grant such certificate on the ground that the sample was not sent for examination by the Director of CFL. The respondent filed an appeal before the Sessions Judge against this order of acquittal. The Sessions Judge dismissed the appeal but the High Court confirmed the order of acquittal passed by the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 13(2)(a) of the Act confers a right on the accused vendor to have the sample sent for examination to the Director, Central Food Laboratory. If the Director is satisfied that the report of the Public Analyst has been obtained by the prosecution as contemplated by section 13(1), he can send the sample for examination to a laboratory other than the Director of Food Adulteration. [119 B] (ii) Sub section (2) of section 13 of the Act gives a right to the accused vendor of his choice to get the sample analysed by the Director, CFL if he so desires. But the Director of a Central Food Laboratory cannot be said to have been given a right to obtain a certificate from him as required by sub section (2). [119 D E] (iii) The Director of a central Food Laboratory cannot claim to be a person aggrieved by the decision of the Director of an Central Food Laboratory because he is not a person aggrieved. [120 F] (iv) The Director is not a mere post office or a banker. He is merely a creature of the statute.

2907: The respondent, a member of a scheduled tribe, was awarded a contract for the supply of stone to the appellant. He refused to accept the tender and accepted the same. The Divisional Forest Officer, after considering the offer made by the respondent, rejected the tender on the ground that the amount offered was not payable under the provisions of the Assam Forest Regulation, 1891. The respondent 's appeal against the order of the Divisional Forest Officer was dismissed. In an appeal filed by the respondent before the High Court, the High Court held that the amount claimed was not recoverable under the provisions Of the Assam Forest Act, 1917. The State appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High Court. HELD : (i) The amount claimed is not recoverable under any law for the time being in force as if it were an arrear of land revenue. [312 D] (ii) The rule does not give rise to any liability to pay a sum of money. It only gives rise to a liability to pay money. [313 E] (iii) The Rule does not give any right to the respondent to recover the amount alleged to be due from him. It merely provides for the recovery of the amount which he may claim as a matter of right. [314 F]

2023: The assessee was a resident of India in the year 1950. He was assessed to income tax for the said two years. In respect of his income, he claimed that he was entitled to exemption under International Law as he had not received any income from the sale of his property during the accounting year. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim and assessed him to income tax. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not liable to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, in respect of income which accrued or arose to him up to the date of merger. The Tribunal allowed the appeals of the assessee and dismissed the assessee 's objections. The High Court held that under the International Law, the assessee was exempt from taxation under the International law. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee enjoyed immunity from taxation under International Law in respect of his incomes which accrued or arisen to him up 26th January 1950, and that as the assessee ceased to be a sovereign from January 26, 1950, his income, even though he was a ruling chief, he was exempted from taxation under section 4(1)(c) of the Income tax Act. HELD : (i) The assessee was not entitled to exemption because he did not receive any income from his sale of property during the relevant accounting year. [272 D] (ii) The assessee could not claim exemption under International law in respect of the assessment for the year 1950 51 on the ground that under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. income tax was charged on the assessee ' s income from his business during the accounting period. [273 C] (iii) The assessee continued to be a ruling chief until the merger of India with India. [274 E]

2511: The appellant was charged with offences under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code read with section 135 of the New Act and sections 23(IA) and 23B of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. He pleaded that he had been wrongly convicted by the trial court but was acquitted on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that a Central Excise Officer under section 21(2) of the , could not be said to be an officer in charge of a police station within the meaning of those words in section 25 of the Evidence Act. HELD : (i) Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act is not applicable to the case of the appellant. It applies only to cases where a person has been found guilty of an offence punishable under section 120 B of the Indian Indian Penal Code or section 135 of a new Act. [616 D] (ii) A Customs Inspector exercising powers under the Act cannot be said to have been a police officer within the meaning Of section 25 of that Act. [609 F] (iii) There is no provision in the Act which makes him a police officer for the purposes of section 25 of Evidence Act. The word 'officer ' in section 25 does not include a Customs Officer. [605 C] (iv) The provisions of section 25 are not intended to make any distinction between officers who are empowered to investigate offences committed by persons other than those specified therein. [607 E] (v) The provisions contained in section 25 are intended to enable the officers mentioned therein to exercise the powers conferred on them by the Act. [590 G H; 591A] (vi) The provisions in section 25 do not contemplate that a Customs Officer can also be a police officer. [591C] (vii) The provisions relating to investigation under section 25 of an act are not intended merely to assist the police officers in investigating offences. They are meant to facilitate the investigation of such offences as well as to prevent the mischief involved in the investigation of offences. [593D] (viii) The provisions regarding investigation under section 26 of the Act are not intended either to enable the police officers to investigate offences under the Act or to use their power to investigate offences. The assessee claimed deduction of Rs.26986 being interest paid to barring of the said amount. The Tribunal also held that the portion of the loan was not intended to meet the income and therefore did not come under section 57 (iii) of Act 1922. On reference, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal before this Court it was contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the assessee was entitled to claim deduction of interest paid to the extent of Rs. 10,276 as interest paid to her. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 12(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is not applicable to the facts of the case. [547E] 2.1 The expression "any expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of earning income" in section 12(2)(i) means any expenditure laid out wholly and exclusivelyfor the purpose of the business or profession. The Legislature is competent to enact a law with retrospective effect so long as the law is not inconsistent with the provisions
5892: The petitioners in these two writ petitions, who were candidates for admission to MBBS/BDS Course in the three medical colleges of the State of Bihar, applied for allotment of seats in the said courses. They were allotted seats in the first year MBBS course and the second year MBBS course. The petitioners in the other two writ petitions were not given any seat in the first batch of MBBS/BD Courses. In the first batch, the petitioners were allotted seats for the first year of MBBS/ BDS course. The petitioner Amanjit Singh Gill was allotted a seat in the second year of MBBS course. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the allotment of seats on the ground that the allocation of seats in one batch was contrary to the guidelines issued by the Central Government under section 10(1) of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act'). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the guidelines issued under section 10 of the Act had no statutory force and that the guidelines framed by the Central Board of Secondary Education did not have the force of law. The petitioners challenged the High Court 's decision in the present appeals. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The guidelines issued by Central Board of secondary education are binding on all the medical colleges in the country. [908C D] 2. The guidelines do not provide for any reservation of seats in any particular medical college or institution. It is only for the purpose of filling up the vacant seats in the medical colleges. The guidelines merely indicate that the Central Board has been empowered to make rules for the purpose. [909E F] 3. The guidelines cannot be construed as laying down any principle which would govern the allocation of vacant seats in any medical college or institutions. [910F] 4. The guidelines are not binding on the Central Board. 748: The respondent was employed in the factory of the appellant as a 'workman ' and claimed that he had been employed in the said factory since 1948. He alleged that he had not been paid overtime wages due to him from April 1, 1949, to September 30, 1954, under section 59 of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948 (Bom. 79 of 1948) and that he had also been paid overtime for the period prior to May 19, 1953, when he had worked as a 'Wageman'. The appellant contested the claim on the ground that the respondent had not been given a holiday within the three days prior to or the three days subsequent to the said date, and that the claim made by him was barred by limitation. Held, that the respondent was entitled to overtime wages under section 59, of the Bombay shops and Establishments Act 1948, and that his claim must be deemed to have been abandoned by him. The claim for overtime wages is a claim for compensation against the employer who has failed to pay the wages due to the workman under section 59. Section 70 of the Bombay Shop and Establishments Act is not applicable to claims for overtime wages. The claim made by the respondent was not a claim for payment of overtime wages but a claim for damages for wrongful dismissal. The claim was not a right for recovery of wages under section 60 of the Bombay Labour Code, 1948, but a claim based upon a right to get overtime wages.
2406: The appellants, who were the owners of the land in dispute, executed two mortgage deeds in 1928 in favour of one Laxmanrao and his son, who had become occupancy tenants of this plot. In 1940, the proprietary rights of the appellants were transferred by sale to the predecessors in title of the appellants. In 1942, the proprietary right of the appellants was purchased by one Vinayakrao, who died on September 30, 1944. In 1943, the proprietary interest of the appellants came to vest in the respondent in respect of this plot in the hands of the respondent. On October 1, 1946, the respondent sold the entire land to the appellants. The appellants filed a suit for possession against the respondent on the ground that they had become ex proprietor occupancy tenant of this plot under section 12(1) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had become an occupancy tenant of the plot in the year 1895. The respondent appealed to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. The appellants then filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent became an occupancy tenant under section 12 (1) of Act and that she could not be dispossessed from the plot without the consent of the respondent and that the appellants were entitled to recover possession from the respondent. The appellants thereafter filed two appeals before this Court. The question for consideration was whether the respondent was entitled to claim actual possession from the appellants. Held: (i) The respondent was not entitled to claim possession from the appellant as he had no right to obtain possession from the mortgagors. The respondent had acquired the status of occupancy tenant under the provisions of the Act and the appellants were not entitled to take advantage of the provisions of section 12(2). The respondent had no right or title to the land in question. The respondent was, therefore, not entitled to the possession of the land from the appellants as it was not the case of the respondent that she had become an ex estate occupancy tenant of that land. The respondent could not claim actual possession of the property from the appellants because the respondent had no such right. The respondent did not acquire any right to the land from any other person. The respondent, therefore, was not entitled,to the protection of section 12 of the Act

1257: The appellant was convicted under section 307, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The condition of acute emaciation in which Bimla Devi was found on 5th June, 1956, was not due to any calculated starvation but it was on account of prolonged illness, the nature of which was not known to the accused till Dr. It follows therefore that a person committed an offence under section 308, Indian Penal code. [701 D E] (2) The first condition is that the act must be an act capable of causing death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death. If the act is so intensely excruciating that the person would not have been able to maintain himself or herself out from her lust, it may be possible for the offender to escape from the punishment provided by law. But if he commits the act with the intention of causing bodily injury or knowing it to be likely that he would thereby cause death, and there is no reasonable explanation for the same, then the act will fall within the ambit of section 304, Part I, Indian PenalCode. [702 F H; 703 A B] (3) The second condition is that there must be some preconcert in the mind of the accused and the accused must have acted in the right direction of the victim. The third condition is that he must have caused the injury intended to be inflicted. This condition has to be satisfied before the accused can be convicted. [704 C D]

3786: The appellant was appointed as a Subordinate Judge in 1935. He joined the erstwhile State of Manipur as a junior clerk in 1935. In December 1962 he was served with a notice for compulsory retirement under Fundamental Rule 56 of the Indian Railway Establishment Code, Vol. I. The appellant did not earn good reports from superior officers. On his attaining the age of 55 years he was served on October 30, 1963 with a notice to retire from service with effect from January 1, 1964. The appellant challenged the order of compulsory retirement by a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) Fundamental Rule 56 at the material time contained no reservation of any powers in the appointing authority to retire an officer who had completed years qualifying service; (ii) the impugned order of compulsory ret irement was null and void because the Fundamental Rule 56 was not applicable to the case; (iii) the impugned orders were invalid because they were passed without giving him reasonable opportunity of showing cause against them; (iv) the impugned action was mala fide and colourable exercise of power; (v) the impugned decision was arbitrary and violative of article 14 of the Constitution; (vi) the impugned notification dated March 31, 1965 was issued in violation of the principles of natural justice; (vii) the impugned notice was bad because the impugned order was made after the Government of India had taken over the administration of the State of Manipur and therefore the impugned order could not be sustained; (viii) the impugned proceedings were vitiated by non application of mind; (ix) the impugned notifications were invalid because the impugned orders of compulsory retirement were passed without affording the appellant an opportunity of being heard; (x) the impugned notices were bad because they were issued without giving the appellant an opportu nity of hearing; (xi) the impugned Notification was issued in contravention of the principles laid down in Tara Singh etc. vs State of Rajashtan and ors.(1) and (xii) the impugned Government order was also bad because the Government had not given the appellant an adequate opportunity of being considered. 891: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain properties in Ahmedabad. He died on November 11, 1947. His widow, one of his daughters, was the sole surviving heir. The assessee claimed that the income from these properties should be assessed as an " association of persons" and not as an "individual". The Income tax Officer issued notices to the legal heirs of the deceased, and after considering the explanation offered by the assessee, passed orders for assessment of the income of the deceased. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire estate of the deceased was inherited by the three widows and that the income of each of them ought to have been assessed separately in the hands of the three widows by reason of the provisions in section 9(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal held that the income could be assessed in the status of an association of persons under section 9(1)(a) of the Act. On reference, the High Court answered the question against the department. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the entire property of the deceased should be assessed in its hands in the status as an association of person. [947E] (ii) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide whether the three widows were entitled to the income of their respective shares in the assets of the deceased or whether they were liable to be assessed in their hands in the capacity of an association. [948F] (iii) The Tribunal has rightly held that the three widows are entitled to the share of the income from the properties of the deceased in their hands. [949A]

1135: The respondent Sabha is a statutory body constituted under the Madhya Pradesh Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 1958. It has been carrying on mining operations in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellants are the owners of coal mines sold for export by rail or sold otherwise than for export by railway within the territorial limits of the Independent Mining Board for the area in question. The respondent Sabha has now taken the place of the said Mining Board and has issued notices against them calling upon them to pay the tax due for the different periods mentioned in the notices. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the notices. On March 12, 1959, the High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that the appellants ' claims were barred by res judicata by reason of the earlier decision of this Court in the case of the Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. The appellants have come up to this Court by special leave. The appellants contended that the impugned notices were illegal as they did not give any notice to the appellants to pay the amount of tax demanded from them. Held, that the appellants had no locus standi to challenge the validity of these notices. The High Court was right in holding that the notices were valid. The appellants had no vested right to claim the benefit of the provisions of section 51 of the Act. The appellants could not be heard to say that they were entitled to the benefit of section 51 because the liability to pay tax was not an existing one. The appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 51. The appellants having failed to make out their case, the appeals must fail.

6051: The assessee was a co operative society constituted under the Cooperative Societies ACt. The assessee was an agriculturist and a member of the society. For rendering the services of ginning and pressing cotton, the assessee charged the members a certain amount by way of ginning charges. 6421: The appellants, who were working as Assistant Engineers in the Bihar Engineering Service Class II, were promoted to the cadre of Executive Engineers by a resolution dated February 18, 1977. The said resolution was passed by the Bihar Government in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the Bihar State Re servation of 'Public Services Act, 1976 (hereinafter called the Act). By an order dated February 18. 1977, the Bihar Public Service Commission (in short the Commission ) constituted under the Act, inter alia, for the purpose of recruiting the Assistant Engineers in Public Works Department. The Commission submitted its report on March 31, 1978 and recommended that the cadre of District Engineers be merged with the equivalent/parallel cadre of Executive Engineer of Public Works Department, with effect from April 1, 1978. The Commission also recommended that the posts of Superintendent Engineers be re merited and the combined cadre of Executive engineers be re merced with the posts of Assistant Engineers. The Commission, however, did not recommend any promotion to the post of Executive Engineer. The State Government, therefore, issued a notification dated May 27, 1979, revising the cadre of the District Engineers. In the notification, it was stated that the cadre would consist of the cadre of Assistant Engineers and the cadre of executive engineer would consist of Assistant Engineers, who would be appointed by direct recruitment. The appellants challenged the above mentioned notification before the Patna High Court which dismissed their writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The State of Bihar is a party to the litigation. It has been impleaded as a respondent in the writ petition. [880C] 2. Under the 1939 Rules, Assistant Engineers are eligible for promotion to the posts of Executive Engineers. By merg erating the cadres, the chances of promotion of the Assistant Engineers are likely to be adversely affected and as such cannot be prejudiced. The merger of the District Engineer cadre with the ingredu ction of Executive Engineers of Public Works Depart ment is thus contrary to the 1939 Rules and as such can never be sustained. [883E F] 3. The State has taken a policy decision to merge the cadre of officers into the services of the State. The State cannot change the policy
6116: The appellant, a mortgagor of the mort gagee property, filed a suit for redemption on 28.12.1913, contending that he had been put in possession of the mortgaged property on 1.11.19 13 and that he was entitled to redeem the same on or before the 1st of November, 1973. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the sale deed contained an acknowledgment of the right of the mortgagor to redeem the mortgage property. On appeal, the High Court held that the sale by the mortgagee in favour of the appellant was not a valid one as it did not state that the mortgagor 's right of redemption was extinguished. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The recitals in the document do not serve as an acknowledgement. It merely states that what stands transferred to the purchaser is not only the fight of the mortgagee for recovering the principal amounts and interest according to the mortgage deed (which, as earlier stated, still remained outstanding), but also "the rights and inter est" regarding the redemption of the mortgaged land. If the recitals are read as a whole, they clearly show that the mortgagor had acknowledged his right of redemption to be subsisting on the date of the sale deed. [614 D E] (2) The recital in the document does not serve as a mere narration of the previous mortgage that had been created on the property. The recitals do not serve any such purpose. The recital in this document does not appear to have been intended to convey any title to the mortgagor. The recital does not even refer to the fact that the mortgagor has already sold all his mortgagee rights along with the original mortgage consideration and interest which according to the terms of the said document has accrued and is payable to the instant vendor. [615 F H; 616 A B] (3) The recital that the mortgagor was put in possession on 1. 11.19 13 cannot be construed as an admission of the right claimed by the mortgagor. [617 C D]

The Company also made an application for reference of the dispute to the Industrial Court. The Industrial Court held that the Company was in a very sound financial position and could easily bear the burden of payment of gratuity to the extent of Rs. 50,000/ or even more. On appeal, the High Court set aside the award holding that the Company had failed to prove that it was in a position to bear the burden. The object of the provision for gratuity is to provide relief to the workman from being forced to accept employment when he finds himself unemployed and to enable him to do so. 6141: The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, is engaged in the manufacture of Ossein and Gelatine. It has been granted an application for registration to establish an undertaking for the manufacture of Oceanic Oil. The application was rejected by the C.G. on 20th September, 1988. The appeal against that order was also dismissed on 20th November, 1988. In the writ petition filed by the appellant, the High Court held that the order dated 20th September 1988 was vitiated as it merely set out the bald conclusion of the officer concerned. The High Court further held that the C.C. had not given any reasons in support of its conclusions. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated 20.9.1988 is not a reasoned or well considered order. [766F] 2.1. The order does not disclose any reason for rejecting the application made by the appellant. The order merely states "the representative of Modis had presented certain documents at the personal hearing but copies thereof had not been supplied to the appellant despite a grievance made by it the very next day. This coupled with the change in personnel referred to above, has resulted in the denial of natural justice to the petitioner. [767A B] 2.2. The order is not a speaking order. [776E F] 3.1. An order which contains no reasoning whatsoever cannot be said to have been passed in accordance with law. [777B] 4.1. A quasi judicial authority must act fairly without any bias. It would be subversive of good administration if it acts in a manner which does not disclose a fair minded deal. [774D E] 4.2. If the order is arbitrary, unreasoned or based on extraneous considerations, it would be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [773F] 4.3. The order can be set aside only when the non-observance of principles of natural justice and the same principle applies to administrative orders affecting individuals. [775H; 778A B] 4.4. The order may cause prejudice to the person who has been prejudiced by the order.
199: The Mysore Income tax Act, 1950, was enacted by the Central Legislature in 1948 and came into force on April 1, 1950. Section 3 of the Act provided that the income tax and super tax shall be levied and collected in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act. Section 4 empowered the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. Section 5 provided that the rules so made shall be laid before each House of Parliament. The Mysore Income Tax Act, 1950 was passed by the Central legislature and came into operation on April 1. 1950. Section 6 provided that the Central Government may make rules for regulating the levy and collection of the tax under the Indian Income Tax Act. Section 7 provided that the Rules would come into force from April 1, 1951. Section 8 provided that the provisions of Chapter V of the Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to the assessment and collection of income tax and Super tax. Section 9 provided that the Income tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner or the Appellate Tribunal or the High Court shall have power to require any person who has not been assessed to income tax or super tax to furnish a return of his income or to give information respecting the matters specified in section 10. Section 11 provided that the tax payable by an assessee under the Indian Incometax Act shall be assessed and paid in accordance with such rules as may be made under the Act. The Mysore General Sales Tax Act, 1957, was passed by Parliament and came into effect on April 1., 1950. The Mysore Act was repealed by the Mysore General Sales tax Act, 1957.
