4800: The appellant was appointed as a Manager of the Sugar Mill in the State of Uttar Pradesh. On account of certain disputes between the appellant and the Sugar Mill, the Central Government issued an order dated July 30, 1978 under Rule 125A of the Defence of India Rules (hereinafter referred to as the Rules) directing that the management of the Sugar Mills shall be taken over by the Central Government on the date of the order. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Central Government had no power to take over the management of an undertaking which was not engaged in production, generation, supply, distribution or provision of water, transport, fuel, light, electricity or other power or any other thing or service which is notified by the Government as essential to the life of the community because the Mill was closed with intent of not reopening the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power conferred upon the Central Government under rule 125A of Order No. 125A can be exercised only if there is a notification under section 3(2) of the Act notifying the undertaking. [535C] 1.2 The power conferred on the Central Government by section 3(3)(a) of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 is a power to take possession of the property of the undertaking. It is not necessary for the Central Government to issue a notification under Section 3(2). The power conferred by section 3 (3)(b) is a power exercisable by the Central government when it has reason to believe that the property of an undertaking is being used for the purpose of manufacturing or producing articles or things or for the purpose aforesaid. [536E F] 1.3 The power conferred under section 3 (2) is a discretionary power. It is a power coupled with a duty. It is an extraordinary power. It must be exercised with due regard to public interest. [537F] 1.4 The power conferred is a power incidental to the exercise of the power conferred. It is inherent in the power itself. It is the duty of the court to see whether the exercise of such power is justified. [538G H] 2.1 The Central Government cannot delegate its power
4302: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the sole proprietor of a certain property. In the year 1948, the deceased executed a will bequeathing his estate to his wife and two sons. The deceased died on February 11, 1950 leaving a large and extensive estate. On his death his son Aloke Mitra, the accountable person filed a return of estate duty valuing the estate of deceased at Rs. 3,75,235. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty did not accept this part of the return and included shares in the circumstances of the case constituted property which passed on the death of the deceased. The Assistant Collector of Estate Duty held that the share scrips belonged to the deceased as he had no interest or title to the shares. He accordingly included the value of these shares in the principal value of the estate passing on his death. The Appellate Tribunal upheld the view taken by the Assistant Controller of Estates but the High Court refused to answer questions other than those which were raised before it. The question whether the shares were benami properties or not was answered against the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the two sections are mutually exclusive and they have independent fields of operation. It was further contended that the two provisions are mutually exclusive. The question was whether the two sections were mutually exclusive and therefore the two sections could be construed as one single and independent. HELD: (i) The two sections are concurrent. They cannot be interpreted in any manner so as to take away the effect of the several provisions of the Act. [801 G] (ii) The two provisions are interdependent and they operate in different fields. The two provisions can be harmonised with each other. If there is a conflict between the two provisions, the provision of one would prevail over the other. [802 B C] (iii) The two Acts are mutually exclusive, though the language of the two statutes may appear to be in harmony. The two Acts operate in different spheres. [803 D E] (iv) The two enactments are mutually exclusive if the language of both the Acts is clear and unambiguous. The two statutes operate in different areas. [804 F] (v) The two statutes are mutually exclusive
1940: The appellant was a shareholder of the Sangi Bank Ltd. and was allotted shares in the name of his wife, and two sons. The appellant filed an application for allotment of shares to the nominees of the Bank. The Bank decided that they or their nominees would subscribe for a large number of shares. In view of section 277(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, the Company was unable to carry on business unless the subscribed capital was not less than half the authorised capital. In order to comply with the requirements of section 276(1), the directors of the Company decided that theyor their nominees would raise loans from the Bank and the amount so advanced should be repaid by the Company. The directors of the Bank decided that the amount so raised would be paid by the Company on interest at 41/2 per cent per annum and the Bank also decided that the amounts so advanced should not be repaid by any one. The directors accordingly issued a notice to the appellant asking him to repay the amount within 15 days failing which he would pay the same along with interest at 41% per annum. The appellant 's father died in 1945 leaving behind his widow and two sons who were minors. The appellant applied for registration of the shares under section 277 of the Indian companies Act, 1913. The company refused registration of the share certificates on the ground that the shares had been purchased out of the funds of the family and that the appellant had no title to the shares. The appellant then filed a suit against the bank for recovery of the amount due to it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the allotment of 2000 shares to the nominee of the Bank was invalid and no title passed to the allottees in respect of the shares, and in the circumstances, there was a total failure of the consideration paid for the shares, that the appellant was not liable to repay the loan taken by him, that the allotment was invalid and that the directors of Bank were not justified in refusing to register the shares. HELD: (i) The allotment of 2000 equity shares to the appellant was invalid as the shares were purchased out of funds of the joint family. The appellant was entitled to the shares only if he had made a contribution
894: The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. He filed an election petition for a declaration that he had been duly elected to the Haryana Legislative Assembly. The respondent, Gian Chand, filed an election Petition under section 98 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, challenging the election on the ground that he had not complied with the provisions of section 81(3) and (4). The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the order of the Tribunal dismissing the petition had not been made under section 98 or section 117. The High Court held that an appeal lay from an order dismissing an election petition under section 90(3) without deciding the other issues framed in the case and that the order dismissing the petition was wrong because the terms of section 117 had been complied with. Held, that the order passed by the Tribunal dismissing an election Petition was correct and the appeal must be allowed. Section 117 does not provide that an appeal shall lie from every order made by an Election Tribunal under section 98. An order made under section 88 is by the terms of the section an order made at the conclusion of the trial of an election petition while an order dismissing a petition for any of the reasons mentioned in section 90(1) is an order made prior to the commencement of such trial.
6373: The appellant along with two others were convicted for murdering Kumari Mangala in furtherance of their common intention and causing disappearance of evidence of the offence. They were sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life under the first count and to pay a fine of Rs.2,500 each with a default clause. The High Court confirmed the conviction of all the convicts but reduced the sentence to seven years rigorous imprisonment. The State appealed against the said order of enhancement. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the High Court enjoys the power of enhancing the sentence either in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 read with Section 401 or in its appellate jurisdiction under Section 374 Cr. The High court enjoys the powers of revision under Section 397 Cr. The power of enhancement is not an inherent power. It is only an extraordinary power which is conferred on the High Court by the Code. [766A B] 1.2 Under Section 377(1) of the Code, the State Government in any case of conviction on a trial held by any Court other than the High Court is empowered to direct the public prose cution to present an appeal to the High Court against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy. However, the High court notwithstanding of the exerci se of its powers under the appellate jurisdiction under section 397 read with Sec. 401 IPC to enhance the sentence in appropriate cases while exercising its revisional jurisdiction even in the absence of an appeal against the sentence as provided under Section 377 Cr. The revisional jurisdiction under section 401 Cr. is available to the High court when it exercises its revisional jurisdiction over the findings of fact arrived at by the Trial Court. [767C D] Nadir Khan vs The State (Delhi Administration), ; , Nadir Hussain vs State of Assam, ; , Nairanjan Das vs State of Orissa, ; , and Nadir Ahmed vs State of U.P., ; , referred to.
1049: The petitioners, who were the owners of a bull or bullock in respect of which they had been granted a certificate under sub section (1) (b) of section 3 of the , filed an appeal before the State Government against the order of the Select Committee. The State Government dismissed their appeal on the ground that the petitioners had not produced any evidence to show that they had been issued a certificate under section 3(1)(b). The petitioners challenged the validity of the order of dismissal by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the petitioners were entitled to have the certificate set aside and quashed the order of rejection of the petitioners ' appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the petitioners could not be said to have been issued a certifica te under section 3 of Act 1 of 1959, because the petitioners had failed to produce any evidence to prove that they had actually issued a certificate. HELD: (i) The petitioners were not entitled to have a certificate under the Act. [847 E] (ii) The petitioners did not produce any evidence in support of their claim that they had issued a certificate as required by section 3 of that Act. They did not also produce any evidence that they had obtained a certificate under that section. [848 A] (iii) The petitioners had not established that they had applied for a certificate under Section 3 of the Act. The petitioners had merely relied upon the certificate issued by the State Government under section 3. [849 B] (iv) The petitioners could not, therefore, be said to be prejudiced by the refusal of the State Government to issue a certificate under s.3 of the Act, because the State Government had no power to refuse to issue such a certificate. [850 C]
1882: The appellant was convicted under section 409 I.P.C. and sentenced to three years ' rigorous imprisonment by the Sessions Judge, Ujjain, on July 20, 1963. He was also convicted in the other two cases of offences under section 467 read with section 471 and section 477A I.P,.C. The sentences imposed in the other case were directed to run concurrently with the sentence awarded in the other cases. In each of the other two appeals, the High Court reduced the sentences to one year 's simple imprisonment. In the fourth appeal, the High court said that the various acts of criminal breach of trust committed by the appellant in different cases were not so lumped together as no order had been made by the Sessions judge for the sentence in the other Case. In the fifth appeal, the appellant was sentenced to three months ' simple imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, the question for determination was whether the convictions of the appellant in the four cases could be sustained. Held: (i) There is nothing illegal about it. The courts below have held that the appellant was guilty of the offence under section 409 IPC and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for a period of three years. [801 G] (ii)The appellant was charged for committing criminal breach of faith with respect to different amounts, led to the appellant 's prejudice and harassment. The charge against him was therefore, proved beyond doubt. [802 D E] (iii)The appellant had been rightly convicted under section 467 I.P.,C. and he was sentenced to undergo imprisonment till the end of his life. The sentences were directed to be run concurrently with those of the other charges. [803 C D]
3794: The respondent was an employee of the State Electricity Board. He was promoted as Accounts Superin tendent on 30th December, 1966 and was posted at the Mysore State Electricity Board, which was a statutory body constituted under the Indian Electricity Act, 1910. On 1st October, 1957, the Board framed Recruitment and Promotion Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. In the year 1960, the Board issued a Notification calling for applications from eligible candidates for promotion to the post of Accounts Superin gent. The respondent 's name appeared at Sl. No. 2 in the list of eligible candidates. The appellant Board sent a letter dated 21st November, 1972 to the respondent stating that he had passed the S.A.S. examination and that he would be considered for promotion as per the Rules. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Board. The Single Judge who heard the petition dismissed it and the appeal preferred by the Board to a Bench of the Karnataka High Court. The Division Bench held that the respondent was exempted from passing the S. A.S. Examination and therefore allowed the writ petition. The Division bench also held that the Board could not have treated the respondent as an employee of an employee of a statutory body like the Board. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The respondent was entitled to be considered for promo tion as an Accounts Superintendent. [766C] 1.2. The respondent has been rightly denied the benefit of the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. [767D] 1.3. The respondent is entitled to be promoted as an Accounts Supervisor. [768E] 1.4. The respondent cannot claim that he should be given the benefit of his earlier service as an employee. [769F] 1.5. The respondent having been promoted as Accounts Supervisor, he cannot now be said to be an employee of any statutory body like Board. [770G] 1.6. The respondent being an employee of statutory body like board cannot be denied the benefit merely because he has passed the SAS Examination. [771B] 1.7.
4023: The respondent was an employee of the appellant Corporation. He had not sought or got the Chairman 's permission laboured under a legal ineligibility as contemplated by section 15(g) of the City of Nagpur Corporation Act, 1948. The appellant who was such an employee and had not sought any permission to take part in municipal elections, save with the permission of the Chairman, was disqualified for election as a Councillor under section 15(1)(g) of that Act. The High Court held that the appellant was disqualified under section 15 (g) of Act No. 1 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The disqualification provided in section 15(h) of the Act is a personal bar which can be overstepped by the Government servant at his own peril as regards his membership of a service under the Government. [901 G] The appellant was an employee and he had not sought to get the Chairman ' s permission laboured as a disqualification under section 15 of the Act. Therefore, the prohibition contained in section 15 (h) of Act 1 of 1951 did not apply to him. [902 A B]
2301: The appellants, who were the owners of certain lands in the State of Andhra Pradesh, filed a suit for declaration that the notification issued under sec. 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was not valid and that the Government had no power to acquire the land. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notification under sec.6 was bad as it did not state that the land was needed for a public purpose or for a company and therefore the acquisition proceedings were mala fide and in fraud of the Act and therefore null and void. HELD: (i) The notification under sec 6 is not a mere notification but an order made by the Government after satisfying itself about the purpose and need for acquiring the land. [683 F] (ii) The notification was not intended to be a piece of evidence against the Government. It was merely a direction to the Collector to make a report to the Government about the urgency of the acquisition. [684 G H] (iii) The notification does not show that the Government satisfied the requirements of sec. 6. The notification merely states that the land is required for a public purposes. The notification does mention that the land has been acquired for a public utility. [685 A B] (iv) The notification did not say that the land should be acquired for a private purpose. The notification only stated that the land would be needed for a 'public purpose '. The notification did nothing more than merely stating that the land had been acquired for the purpose mentioned therein. [686 C D] (v) The notification merely says that the land will be needed for public purpose. The declaration does not show such.satisfaction. [687 E]
4878: The assessee was a company in liquidation. In the assessment year 1960 60, the Income tax Officer took over the assets and liabilities of the company on the ground that the formula laid down in the Second Schedule to the Act for calculation of the 'standard deduction' was inapplicable on account of the fact that a company in winding up had gone into liquidation. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that after a company had gone into winding up there cannot be said to be in the hands of the liquidator any amount that can be distinctly designated as paid up share capital of the company or as 'reserve ' with respect to which the capital of the Company is to be worked out as provided in Second Schedule to section 10 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 (XI of 1922) or under sub section (3) of section 34 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (XLIII of 1961), or under sub sections (3) and (4) of section 10 of that Act, the capital of a company shall be the sum of the amounts, as on the first day of the previous year relevant to the assessment year which is long subsequent to the winding up. The High Court agreed with the view taken by the Tribunal that after a Company has gone into liquidation there cannot be no question of any amount that could be distinctly designation as paid up shares capital of the assessee company or as "reserves" with respect to it. The High court also held that after the winding up the assessee company would not be entitled to claim any additional amount from its shareholders. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the assessee company was not liable to pay any amount to the revenue because the company had gone in liquidation and the amount was not paid to the revenue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "paid up share capital" in section 10(2)(vi) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, means the aggregate of the sums payable to the creditors of the company. [775 E] 2. The word "pay" in section 40(1)(b) of the Act must be given its ordinary meaning. It is well settled that
5825: The respondents were charged with the offence of murdering Gulam Rabbani and injure others. The learned Additional Sessions Judge convicted the respondents under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. and under section 147 I.P,C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the convictions but reduced the sentence to one year R.I. The High court held that (1) it appears from the heads of the charges framed by the learned Additional Sessions judge that the principal accused Laisal Haque was charged along with other accused persons under section 302 r/w section 149 I P.C., and under section 148 I.P,.C. and (2) that the judgment of the High Court did not deal with the evidence separately in respect of each of the accused persons. The High 'Court further held that the charge against the accused persons under sections 302 read with Section 149 I.p. was substantially defective inasmuch as it was a rolled up charge, the common object of the unlawful assembly being to murder Gulam Rabani and injuring others. The High. Court also recorded a finding of guilt against the accused under section 302 simpliciter without making that charge as an alternative charge. The High, Court also recorded another finding of guilt in respect of the other accused persons. In the course of the judgment the High Court recorded a finding that the charge framed against the accused was materially defective inasmuch as the charge framed was substantially defective and that the trial of the accused was vitiated on account of non-compliance with the provisions of section 342 Cr. P.C. The High: Court also recorded the finding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The High _Court, however, found that the charge was substantially defective because it was not mentioned in the charge that the accused had caused any injury to the deceased or any other person. The High ·Court accordingly held that the case required a retrial against the accused. The State filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts' decision is based on erroneous appreciation of facts and law. [873B] 2. The High courts' decision is clearly unsustainable. [874A] 3
3872: The appellant was a occupant of the lands in question under the Bhopal State Land Revenue Code, 1959. He became a Bhumiswami under section 185(1)(i) (iv)(b). His name was recorded on the deposit of compensation money. On the coming into force of the M.P. Code of 1959, the appellant became a Bhumidar under clause (c) of section 158 and the respondent became an occupancy tenant under section 185 (1)(i)(iv)(b) of the Bhopal Act of 1932. The appellant filed an appeal before the Sub Divisional Officers Huzur, respondent No. 4 from the order of the Tahsildar. The revision petition was allowed on the 6th of July, 1965. The appellant preferred a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the respondent was not an occupant within the meaning of section 2(15) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was an occupant within meaning of section2(15) and hence he became entitled to conferment of Bhumiswami rights under section 185 of the Bhopal State land Revenue Code. [585C] 2. The appellant had no right to the land in dispute. The respondent was a sub tenant under the Bhopal Act. The appellant could not be said to be an occupant within section 2(14) of the Act. [586D] 3. The respondent is not an occupant under the Bhopal Land Revenue Code of 1959. The respondent has been rightly held to be an occupancy tenant. [587E] 4. The respondent had no right or title to the land. The respondent cannot be said to have any right to the property. [588B] 5. The respondent did not claim any right to any land in the disputed lands. The respondent claimed that he was an occupant under section 185. The respondent could not claim any such right. [589A B]
5255: The appellant was a public servant and was holding a post of a Banking Manager. He filed an application before the Metropolitan Magistrate, Hyderabad under section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for taking cognizance of the offence alleged to have been committed by him. The Magistrate rejected the objection raised by the bank that the appellant is not a public servant. The appellant challenged the order of the Magistrate in revision before the High Court which has been dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 197 are not attracted at all. [880C] 1.2. In the instant case, the appellant is a public servant, though he is not holding any office, nor is he holding any office of profit. Therefore, the view taken by the Courts below is not correct. [881D] 1.3. Section 197 of the Cr. P.C. is applicable only when a public servant is not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government. It does not mean that the appellant cannot be removed from service except by or with t he sanction of the government. [882E F] 1.4. The appellant is an officer who is removable by an authority which is not Government but the authority has been empowered under the regulations and these regulations have been framed with the sanction o f the Government. [883F G] 1.5. The appellant being a public servant cannot be removed by anybody except the Government. The appellant can be removed by the Government if it is satisfied that he is a public man. [884G] 1.6. The appellant was not holding any such office as would attract the provisions of section 19(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. [885A] 1.7. The appellant had no power to remove him from service. [886B] 1.8. The appellant could not be removed from his service by anyone except the Government or with the previous sanction of the Central Government. [881C] 1,9. The appellant cannot be said to be a public servant merely because he was a public man and was not holding a position of trust. [882D
418: The respondent was charged with having committed an offence under section 7 of the East Punjab Essential Services (Maintenance) Act, 1947. He pleaded guilty to the charge and was convicted by a Magistrate of the First Class for an offence under that section. The respondent contended that he had not been given any opportunity to explain his conduct or to prove himself as a foot constable in the Police Lines, Dharamsala, and that he had been wrongly convicted by the Magistrate. Held, that the conviction was wrong on the evidence on record and the High Court was right in setting aside the order of conviction and sentence passed against him. The fact that the respondent had been assigned duty as a sentry without rifle behind the Police Lalls in the rear of the armoury in the Police Station in which he was posted did not make him a police officer within the meaning of section 2(h)(i) of the Act. The fact however, remains that the respondent was not a police officer but was a member of the police force of the State. The respondent was not entitled to be discharged from service merely because he was a police officer. The mere fact that the appellant was a member or a member of a police force does not make him an accused person.
1886: The appellant company was a private limited company and the Government of India acquired land belonging to it under the Defence of India Rules. The Government of India, however, took possession of the land in pursuance of an order made by the Government on February 18, 1944. The Government did not pay any compensation for the land but only paid a sum of Rs. 2,000 as earnest money. The appellant company then filed a suit against the Government for recovery of the amount. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court in appeal upheld the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contract was not discharged because of the fact that its performance was rendered unlawful either for a determinate period of time or for an indeterminate period of lime. [440 D] (ii) The question whether the contract could be said to have been discharged because of its performance was still open to the Government. The question whether it was so performed would be irrelevant if the performance of the contract was rendered unlawful because of the circumstance that its performance had been rendered unlawful. [441 B C] (iii) The question as to whether the contract was discharged because of non payment of the balance of consideration within the meaning of section 74(2)(b) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, must also be decided in the light of the facts of each case. [442 A B] (iv) The question of the performance of a contract which is voidable under section 74(1) of the Contract Act does not arise in the instant case because the contract was not terminated. [443 F] (v) The question about the performance of an agreement which is void cannot be raised in a civil proceeding. [444 G H; 445 A] (vi) The question regarding the performance of contract which is illegal because of the absence of a provision in the contract itself providing for forfeiture of the deposit or security may be left open to be determined in appropriate proceedings. [446 E]
4291: The assessee was a firm of which the original assessment for the assessment year 1955 46 was completed long back. But it appears that some information was received by the Income Tax Officer, who had addressed two letters dated 14th January 1955 and 10th February 1955 to the assessee making inquiries about this remittance. Neither these letters nor their copies were brought on record. The Income Tax Officer did not disclose them in his order. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the letter of the Manager of the Punjab National Bank Limited was not disclosed to the assessee and that the letter was an unauthenticated letter. He also held that the assessee had failed to produce the relevant evidence before him. The Tribunal however held that the correspondence between the parties showed that the assessee was aware of the receipt of Rs. 1,07,350 from Madras and that the latter had made enquiries with the bank and found that the amount was paid to the employee of the assessee. In further appeal to the High Court, the High Court held that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the letter dated 9th February 1956 was not produced before the Income Tax officer. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the letter must be read as a whole and the income should have been included in the total income of the assessee for the purpose of computation of its income. Held: (i) that the letter is inadmissible under section 66(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because it does not contain any reference to the assessee 's account books or other documents. The letter merely states that the assessee has received Rs. 1.7.350 from the Madras National Bank Ltd., Bombay, and that the said amount was credited to the account of the assessee in the books of account. The letter does not refer to the assessee but only to the accounts of the assessee and does not show that the assessee ever informed the Income Tax Officers that the sum of Rs.1.7. 350 was remitted to the assessee. [801 D] (ii)The letter cannot be construed as an intimation to the assessee that the amount of Rs. I.7. 330 was remitted to him. The letter is not an intimation to him. It is an intimation to a person who makes an application to the Income Tax
6761: The appellant, a manufacturer of wagons, supplied to the respondent Railway Board, a wagon manufactured by it and sold to the Railway Board. The free supply items were not manufactured by the appellant but were fitted in the wagons manufactured by the Railways. The appellant claimed that the cost of the wagon as a whole should include cost of construction and furthermore, when sale is the charge and the same under charging section of the said Act would mean actual price of the goods viz. wagon as part of the relevant and necessary assessable value under section 4 of the said act. The central excise authorities rejected the claim on the ground that the cost was not included in the assessable value of the wagons. The appellant challenged the demand before the High Court which allowed the writ petition holding that the cost for the wagon was not included while determining the assessable value under Section 4 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The cost of the goods cannot be taken into consideration in fixing the assessable value. [963 E] 2.1 The cost of free supply items is not included in assessable value under the provisions of the Act as they are not part of the manufacturing cost. [964 B C] 3.2 The cost of manufacture of a complete wagon cannot be included in the value of the goods. [965 D] 3.3 The cost of supply of the wago or wagon is not included within the assessable value because the definition of "manufacture" in section 2(f) of the Act includes the process of making a commodity. [966 A B] 4.1 The value of the "free supply items" is not included under section 4(1)(a) of the said. [967 F] 5.1 The question whether the cost of free supplies items is included in the "value" of the goods will depend upon the nature of the goods and the purpose for which the goods are made. [968 B C] 6.1 The test for determining the value of a commodity is to find out the true nature of the commodity. If the commodity is a different commodity from what is adopted by another, the price at which it is charged must be the same as the price atwhich it is capable
4107: The appellant was an evacuee and the house in question was declared as an evacuee property on 15 11 1951. On 11 11 1960 the Central Government passed an order under section 20A of the Displaced Persons Act, 1950 directing that the house be restored to the appellant. The appellant filed an application under section 16(1) of the Act for restoration of the house. The Custodian, respondent No. 1 passed an order on 18 3 1957 restoring the house to the appellant, but before that Shri Ajjumal, respondent No 2 had been inducted as a tenant in the house by the Custodian after it was declared as evacuee property. The appellant came to know later that on 11 11 1960 he made an application to the Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property for restoration of his house under sub section (2) of section 16. The Assistant Custodian, respondent no. 1 passed another order on 19 6 1957 which was challenged by the appellant in Civil Suit No. 861 of 1957. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the order dated 18 3 1957 was not a decree within the meaning of section 2(2) of the U.P. Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the Assistant Custodian was a nullity because the property was not evacuee property and the appellant was entitled to compensation only under section 20 A of the Act. HELD: (i) The order dated 18 12 1957 was a nullity since it was passed without jurisdiction. [987 E] (ii) The order of the Custodian was a final order and could not be challenged in any court. The order of respondent No. I was a final one. It was not open to the Custodian to challenge the order of respondent no. I. If the order of Assistant Custodian was set aside, the order of Respondent No. I would become final. [988 F H] (iii) The order was a final decision of the Custodian. The order was not a mere formality. It was merely an interim measure. The order did not affect the rights of the parties. [989 G H]
2018: The Raja of Faridkot filed a suit against the respondents for possession of the land on the ground that they were the legal heirs of Raj Kaur and that the Raja was in possession of the entire land. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that as the Raja had adopted the son of the Raja, the suit was not barred by time. HELD: (i) Article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908 is applicable to suits instituted after the coming into force of the Limitation Acts. [851 G] (ii) Article 142 of the Limitation act, 1908 does not apply to suits for pre emption. The right to sue under article 142 arises only when the party claiming title has made out a case for enforcement of his right. [852 B] (iii) Article 142 applies only where the party claiming the right has made out an exceptional case for enforcement. It is not necessary that there must be a specific case or a case for the application of the rule. The question whether a particular case falls within the rule depends upon the facts of each case. [853 C] (iv) Article 142 is not applicable to the present case because the Raja of Faridpur was a tenant of the land in dispute and he died leaving behind him his widow, who was the respondent in the appeal before us. The Raja was a minor at the time of the death of Raj Kaur. He was therefore entitled to succeed to the land in question. [854 D E] (v) Article 142 does not apply if the person claiming the right is a minor. [855 F] (vi) Article 142 provides that the law of limitation shall apply to all proceedings in any court including execution of decrees passed in such proceedings. [856 A]
4192: The appellant and his brother were evacuees under the Custodian of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949. On March 11, 1955, the Assistant Custodian General declared the appellant 's property as evacuee property. The notice was issued by the Assistant Custodian on March 11, 1956 stating that there was "credible information in possession of the Custodian" that they were evacuating the evacuee properties from Pakistan and that it was necessary to declare them evacuee and their property as evacuee properties. The appellant and the brother preferred a revision before the Custodian General which was dismissed on August 30, 1956. The appellant moved the High Court by a writ petition challenging the notice dated November 22, 1955. The High Court held that the notice was invalid because the information in possession was not disclosed to the appellant and his brothers and that the notice did not contain any particulars about the possession of the evacuee properties. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The notice is invalid because the notice does not disclose the grounds on which the notice was based. [880C] (ii) The notice merely states that the information in the possession of Custodian was that he was evacuating evacuee properties from India. It does not state whether the information was that of the Custodian or that of the Deputy Custodian. The notice merely says that the information was not disclosed. The notice does not say that the information is not disclosed. It only states that the Deputy Custodian had decided to declare the property as evacuee. [881D E] (iii) The notice does mention that the Deputy Collector had decided to hold an enquiry into the matter and that the Deputy Commissioner had given him a copy of the order. The Deputy Commissioner had no power to give a copy of such order. [882F G] (iv) The notice cannot be construed as giving the details of the property. The Deputy Custodian has to give the details of that property. [883A B] (v) The notice must be read as a whole and not in isolation. It may be read along with other parts of the Act. But the notice must be one issued to the person concerned and not to the authority who issued it. [884B C]
4919: The petitioners in these petitions filed under Article 32 of the Constitution are various companies engaged in the business of editing, printing and publishing newspapers, periodicals, magazines etc. Some of them are trusts or other kinds of establishments carrying on the same kind of business. The petitioners contended that the imposition of customs duty on news print which had enjoyed total exemption from its payment till March 1, 1981, as the foreign exchange position was quite comfortable, was arbitrary and discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. It was also contended that there was no need to impose customs duty on newspaper circulating at the rate of 15% ad valorem. The petitioners further contended that the levy of auxiliary duty under the Finance Act, 1981 on newsprint is not justified because it has resulted in a loss of revenue to the Government. The petitioners inter alia contended that the impugned levy is unreasonable and excessive and is violative of article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposes an unreasonable restriction on the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by article 19(2). Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners have been subjected to a very severe and harsh treatment by the State in imposing a tax on news print. [574C] 2. The petitioners cannot be said to have suffered any prejudice due to the imposition of the impugned levy. [575A] 3. The petitioners are entitled to the relief claimed. [558B] 4. The petitioners do not suffer any prejudice due t o the imposition of a tax on the news print. They are not entitled to any relief. [567D] 5. The petitioners can claim the benefit of the doctrine of equality before law and equal protection of laws under Art.14 of the Constitution if they are similarly situated. [568E]
1604: The appellant, who was the son of his brother, filed a suit for partition and possession of his share in the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it on the ground that the Will executed by Chimpirayya was not proved to have been executed by Subbarao, the father of the appellant, and that the said Subba Rao had no knowledge of the said declaration. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Will is a valid document. It has been executed by the testator in the presence of two witnesses. The first respondent was present at the time when the will was executed and he signed as a witness. The second respondent was also present at the same time. The first defendant was not examined. The first appellate court was right in holding that the Will was a genuine one. [801 G] (2) The question whether the recitals in the will were true or not must be determined with reference to the circumstances of each case. If the intention of the testator was to separate himself from Subbaraopa Rao, the testator would have stated so in clear terms. But if the intention was to separate the plaintiff from Subbaratha, the testator could have easily said so in clear words. [802 B C] (3) The fact that the testator was not present at the date when the will came into force does not mean that he was not aware of the intention of his mother. He was not expected to know the intention of her mother. [803 D E] (4) The fact of the execution of the will by Subbarama Rao in favour of Subbaraobai, the daughter of the testator, is not conclusive evidence of the intention to separate himself. The fact that Subbaraosa Rao was present at that time cannot lead to an inference that he was aware of the said fact. [804 F H] (5) The fact, however, that the testator did not say anything about the intention of Subbrama Rao to separate himself, does not mean either that he was satisfied with the intention of subbrama Prasad, or that he was capable of giving effect to the intention of such Subbramaa Rao
4869: The appellant was the owner of a shop in dispute. He died on 31st August, 1974 leaving behind his widow and two sons. On 4th July, 1973, the landlord filed an application under section 12 read with section 16 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 for a declaration that the shop was vacant and he required the same for his personal need. The application was resisted by Jaspal Singh, the present appellant, on the ground that he was the heir of Naubat Singh deceased and was in occupation of the disputed shop after the death of Naubata Singh. The Rent Control and Eviction Officer rejected the application holding that Jaspal Singh had been living with the deceased Naubat singh since the death of the deceased and so he was entitled to get the benefit of section 14 as amended by the U. P. Act No. 28 of 1976. The appeal preferred by Jaspal singh against the order of the Rent Control and eviction officer was dismissed by the District Judge, Bulandshahr. The High Court held that the appellant could not be an heir on the basis of the will executed by Naubat Singhan and that the appellant was not even entitled to get protection of section 14 of the U P Act as it stood prior to its amendment in 1976. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court committed error in holding that the appellant had been living in the disputed shop with the deceased and was also assisting him in doing the business in the disputed premises to the full knowledge of the landlord. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that in order to get the protection of section14 as it stood before its amendment in the year 1976 would indicate that in order that the tenant should satisfy that (1) he was a tenant in occupation of a building with the consent of the landlord immediately before the commencement of the Act and that he was not a person against whom proceedings under section 7A of the old Act are pending immediately before such commencement, and (2) that the tenant had been helping him in doing his business in the property which he was carrying on. [892C D] 2
951: The appellants were assessed to income tax and super tax on the total income of their respective assessees. They submitted a return under the Income Tax Act, 1961, claiming that the amount of tax payable by them was Rs. 1,35,736 8 0 and that they were liable to pay that amount subject to credit for the tax already paid. The Income Tax Officer passed an order under section 5(1) of the Act directing the appellants to pay the amount of income tax and the super tax in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The appellants challenged the order before the High Court contending that the Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess or reassess the appellants as the tax due according to the findings recorded by the Commission was inadequate to prevent evasion of tax and to investigate into the matter in question. The High Court held that the Income tax Officer could not be said to have exercised his powers under section 5 of the Act without giving the appellants an opportunity of being heard. It also held that the Commission had no power to make any assessment after the expiry of the period prescribed by section 5(2). On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court erred in holding that the Income 'tax Officer had no power under section 5 to assess or reopen the assessments made by him. [447 C] (ii)The High Court was wrong in holding that section 5(3) of the Income Tax Rules did not apply to the case because the Income tax officer had no power at all to assess or reassessment the income of the appellants. [448 D] (iii)Section 5(3)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, which is similar to section 5(b) of the Travancore Income tax Act does not apply to cases where the Income tax Commissioner has been given the power to make an assessment after the expiration of the period specified in section 5(a). [449 E F] (iv)In the present case, the Income tax authorities had no power either to assess or revise the assessment orders made by them after the expiry Of the period specified by section 5 (a) of that Act. [450 A B]
3187: The appellants, who were the owners of a private stage carriage services in Rajasthan, challenged the validity of schemes approved by the State Government under section 68D of the (Act 4 of 1939) for inter State routes as a result of which private operators including the appellants had been granted permits by the Regional Transport Authorities of Rajasthan. The State Government, on the other hand, contended that the scheme was not approved by the Central Government and that the State Government could not issue a notification under section 68C of the Act for the purpose of providing road transport services on the route or portions thereof. Held, that the scheme did not fall within entry 21 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and the State Government was competent to issue a notification in respect of the scheme. The scheme was not sanctioned by the Central Legislature. The scheme, therefore, did not come within entry 21. The scheme did not come under entry 22 of List III. The scheme being a composite scheme, it would be open to the State Government to issue a direction under section 68 C of the Act to the effect that the scheme should be implemented in its entirety.
2711: The appellant applied to the Regional Transport Authority for a permit to run a passenger bus service on the route Dankaur. The R.T.A. rejected his application and granted him permits. He filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal. The High Court held that the R.T.,A. had no jurisdiction to entertain appeals against the orders of the R. T. A. under section 64(a) of the Act, and that the RTA was not competent to decide whether a proposed route should be opened or not. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the R.C.M. had power to decide whether an applicant should be granted a permit; (ii) the RTA had no jurisdiction under section 47(3), when read together, made it clear that the RTC could only decide whether a particular route should be open to the applicant; (iii) the RTC had no jurisdiction in the matter as the R. C.M. did not have the power to decide the question whether a proposed scheme should be opened; (iv) the RT.A., had no jurisdiction over the R. D.A. in the matter; (v) the R T.A. had not decided the question of granting or refusing permits to the applicants; (vi) the R TA. was barred by limitation; (vii) the RTI Act was not applicable to the R.TA. HELD: (i) Section 47(3) does not confer any new right upon the applicant. [247B] (ii) The R. T.,A. has no jurisdiction to decide whether the proposed route should or should not be opened. [248D] (iii) The R T. A., is a quasi judicial authority which has to decide the questions referred to it. It is not open to the R T to decide whether there is necessity for the proposed route. [249E] (iv) The RT. A. cannot decide whether a scheme should be framed or not. [245F]
6655: The appellant was manufacturing paper and paper board. It manufactured paper and paperboards in its factory at Pune. The excise duty payable on the said paper and paper boards was Rs.1,20,000/ as against Rs. 1,00,000/ paid by it. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise, Pune Division passed an order dated January 28, 1982 directing the appellant to pay central excise duty at the appropriate rate leviable on all types of eggs, including paper board, printed cartons, etc. under Item 17(4) of the old Tariff. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the aforesaid order of the Assistant Collector. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the products manufactured by the appellant were 'containers ' falling under Item 17 (4) of Schedule I of the Tariff. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "other similar products" used in item 17(4), is not defined in the Act. The term "articles of paper or paperboard" has been defined in section 2(c) of the Act to mean "any article of paper or form of paper". [326C] 2. In view of the definition of "article of paper" contained in section 2 (c) of Tariff Act, no duty can be levied on any article of paper other than those specified in the First Schedule to the Act. [326D] 3. The expression 'container ' would include a tray because it is a receptacle which contains articles and, therefore, an egg tray would fall within the meaning of the expression "other like goods of paper or of paperboard". [327E] 4. The expression, 'other similar products ' used in section 2 of the Act means, 'all such products of paper or substance as are made out of paper or ginned paper or unassembled paper or paper-board'. [327F] 5. The expression includes a tray. 'Container ' is a commodity which is made out of a paper or paper board. The word 'containment ' is defined in section 3(2)(d) of the Tariff
1506: The appellants were charged under section 302/149 I.P.C. for having committed the murder of one Gurcharan Singh and of another Gurcharan. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons but convicted them of the offence under section 302 read with section 149 I.P,C. The High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences imposed on the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the charge under section 302 I.P.,C. had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt; (ii) the charge was vague and lacking in material particulars and (iii) the evidence did not establish any common object of the unlawful assembly. HELD: (1) It is well settled that if two views are reasonably possible from the evidence adduced in a case of this kind, the view which favours the accused must be accepted. [880 A] (2) The prosecution has failed to prove its case against the appellants beyond a reasonable doubts. [881 D] (3) The prosecution case under section 302 IPC was fully established by the evidence of the eye witnesses and there was no reason why the High Court should have interfered with the order of acquittal. [882 E] (4) There was no reason to interfere with the order passed by the High Court. [885 F] (5) The High Court was right in holding that the charge under Section 302/34 had not been established against the appellants. [886 G]
3351: The respondent was charged with having committed the offence of cheating under section 420 read with section 511 I.P.C. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay fine of Rs. 1,000/ . On appeal the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed against him but reduced the sentence to one year 's R.I. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the High Court erred in setting aside the order of acquittal and convicting the respondent. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record. The High Court had not taken into consideration the fact that the respondent was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought washer plates in a taxi. [279 F] (2) The High court was wrong in holding that there is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agawalla. The report was lodged after the respondent was apprehended by the police. The part which is attributed to the respondent was that he was present along With Shanker Lal, when the latter came to the shop of Ram Avtars with whom he had been dealing. The part that was attributed to the accused was that he would be paid a profit of Rs. 3200/ . The High Court should have considered the matter from the point of view of the defence. [280 G H; 281 A B]
7070: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission issued a notification on May 28, 1984 inviting applications for the post of munsifs and requested the Government to initiate appropriate steps for selection of candidates. The appellants were not selected. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification and the selection process. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the government had no power to issue the notification and directed the Government to approve and publish the list of candidates recommended by the Public Service Commission. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in law in quashing the notification and directing the Government to consider the names of the appellants as suitable candidates. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has rightly held that the government cannot alter or temper with the order of merit determined by the commission but it is certainly open to the government to stop at a particular point where it feels that a particular candidate is not eligible to be considered. [908C] 2. The High Courts have been flooded with writ petitions seeking directions to the Government to prepare the select list of candidates. It is open to the Government, if it thinks fit, to reject the recommendations made by the Public service Commission. [909D] 3. The High courts are not justified in issuing any direction to the Government for approving the names of candidates who are found to be ineligible. [910E F] 4. The High Courl does not sit in judgment over the wisdom of the Government in framing the rules. It only examines the question whether the Government should frame the rules or amend them. It is not open to the High Court to do so. [911F G]
2362: The respondent was a tenant of the appellant under a rent note executed on February 27, 1947. He fell into arrears of payment of rent and the tenancy was to be for a period of one year from 22nd February, 1947. Under the terms of the compromise, the defendant became a tenant of a tenant in respect of the premises in dispute. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent on the ground that he had become a tenant of another tenant under a rent-note dated February 27, 1946. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent had disputed the municipal taxes and permitted increases and as such not entitled to the protection of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to protection of the provisions of section 12(3) (a) of the Act because the conditions mentioned in section 12(2)(b) were not present. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled under section 12(1) (a), to protection of section 12 (3) (b). [739 B] The condition under section 12 (1) (c) is not present. Section 12(3)(a) provides that if the amount of standard rent or permitted increases exceeds Rs. 20 per mensem the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if, before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2) he makes an application to the Court under sub section (3) of section 11 and thereafter pays or tenders the amount of rent or permitted increase recoverable under this Act. The words "at any time" are not to be read disjunctively but are to be read conjunctively. The word "or" in section 12 (2) (b) means "the date on which the order made by the Court is finally disposed of". [740 D E] Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory vs Subbash Chandra Yograj Kuverjee Oil Mills and Oghadwpramukh Niyamit vs Subodh Chandra Yograj Kanshi Ramji, ; , referred to.
7102: The appellant and respondent No. 3 were both appointed to the Service on May 26, 1977. Respondent No. 3 was a Mazhbi Sikh who was a Scheduled Caste in Punjab. The recruitment to the Service was governed by Punjab Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Rules'). Rule 8 A of the said rules provided that the quota for recruitment to the service shall be 20% of the total number of vacancies in the cadre strength of the service. The appellant and the respondent No.3 were both appointed on May 26. 1977. The Roster was further amended by notification dated June 14, 1977. By this amendment the instructions issued by the State Government from time to time in relation to reservation of appointments or posts for Scheduled Castes in a lot of 100 vacancies would be applicable for making appointments to the posts in the Service. The appellant was appointed on May 27, 1978. He filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High Court by its judgment and order dated October 9, 1991. The appellant challenged the aforesaid two orders of the High Court before this Court. The main contention of the appellant was that in view of the order dated May 5, 1975, 50% vacancies of the quota reserved for Scheduled Castes had to be offered to Balmikis and Mazhswars who belonged to a Scheduled Caste other than Balmiki and Mazhshas. The appellant contended that in view Of the order dated June 14.1977, 50% posts of the quota meant for Scheduled Castes should be offered to the Balmikas and Mazhswarans who belong to a Scheduled caste other than Balphise and Mazhsha Sikhs. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition filed by the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The Rationalisation of Reservation in direct recruitment in the Punjab Civil Services (Judicial Branch) Rules, 1963 is not applicable to the case of the appellant. [5G] 1.2. In the instant case, the Roster was introduced by the State of Punjab in the year 1977. The appellant belongs to a Schedule Caste in Punjab and he has been appointed in 1979. The Rhata of the State of Haryana is a
3607: The appellant was employed as a peon in the respondent 's establishment. He was charged with an offence under section 3 of the , and was convicted by the Magistrate. On appeal, the Sessions Judge acquitted him but the High Court confirmed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Explanation indicates that potteries industry includes the manufacture of articles of pottery including the manufacture of the following articles of potteries. [901 B] (2) The definition of "scheduled employment" is not exhaustive. It merely defines "scheduled employments". The expression "any employment specified in the Schedule or any process or blanch of work forming part of such employment" does not include "any employment in respect of which minimum rates of wages are fixed by the appropriate Government." [901 C D] (3) The Explanation does not cover all possible articles of potwales. The object of the Act is to provide for the regulation of employment of contract labour in certain employments. Section 2(g) defines "scheme" to mean "any scheme, frame or other instrument or document or any scheme, framed by the appropriate Govern ment". The definition is inclusive and not exhaustive. The definition of the word "schemes" is wide enough to include all possible articles or articles of pottion. [902 E F] (4) The definition is not exhaustive and the definition can be extended only to those articles or articles which are included in the definition. The definition is intended to enlarge the meaning of the word or phrase in order to make it more comprehensive. [903 A] (5) The definition does not include articles of potal mines. [904 G]
8: The appellant, a Hindu, was the adopted son of the testator 's nephews and was taken in adoption by the widow in terms of the will executed on 13th March, 1905. The adoption deed recites that the appellant 's wife had an infant daughter named Alamelu, who died on 25th April, 1905, leaving behind him as his near relations, his widow, and two daughters, and that the properties vested in the appellant as the adopted son and heir of the deceased on the date of the death of the testator. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain properties which were acquired by him during his life time from the widow of the testator, and claimed that the properties belonged to him as his adopted son and that he was entitled to get them in equal shares after the death of his father. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the adoption deed did not affect the rights of the appellant under the will. On appeal, the High Court held that the adoption was valid and that the appellant was entitled to succeed to the estate of the deceased. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The property devolved upon the appellant as his adopted daughter and as such the reversioners of the deceased, and therefore, the appellant was not entitled to claim any right under the will or under the will of the deceased in respect of the properties which were given to the appellant as a result of the will. [801 B D] (ii) The question whether the adoption is valid or not has to be determined with reference to the circumstances of each case. If it is found that the adoption is invalid, then the adoption must be set aside. [802 E F] (iii) The fact that the adoption has been set aside does not mean that the adoption itself is invalid. It only means that if there are more than one persons living at the time of the adoption, the adoption would be valid. But if there are other persons also living at the same time, then the adopted person can take the property of the adoptive father. [803 G H]
2608: The Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Ordinance, 1962 was promulgated by the President of India on April 27, 1962. The Act came into force on December 20, 1961. The Act was passed to enable effect to be given to the International Conventions and the provisions thereof were made applicable to Goa, Daman & Diu. The Act received the assent of the President on March 26, 1962. On April 27, 1963, the Constitution (Twelfth Amendment) Act, 1962 was enacted and was deemed to have come into force on March 1, 1963. The Act is now amended in 1964. The Act has been brought into force with retrospective effect from December 20, 1960. The Act provides for the establishment of a Commission to investigate offences committed under the Act. Section 2(a)(i) defines "commission" as meaning an offence punishable under section 3 or section 4 or section 5 or section 6 or section 7 of the Act. 4946: The appellant, a trade union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926, raised three demands and served notices of these demands on the Deputy Chief Engineer, Major Project, Chambal, Bhopal. The State Government refused to refer the dispute to the Tribunal by its order dated 15th March, 1969. The appellant took the matter before the High Court by filing Miscellaneous Petition No 29/69 for a mandamus to the State Government to refer the matter to the Tribunal for adjudication. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of the State Government dated 15th Mara, 1969. The Appellate Tribunal upheld the assessment but directed the Income Tax officer to make a fresh assessment after giving opportunity to the parties to produce evidence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (i) the Tribunal had erred in holding that the nonresident companies were entitled to the benefit of section 163 of Income tax Act; and (ii) the Tribunal having accepted the position that the non residents parties were not liable to be assessed as agents of the non resident company, the Tribunal should have remanded the case back to the Income Tax authorities for rehearing the matter. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that section 163 of Act is applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. [886C] 2.1. Section 163 of the Act provides that where any person chargeable with tax is under liability to pay income tax or penalty or both there shall be levied a tax or penalty which may be incurred by such person and such tax or penalty shall be determined at the rate or rates in force. The section does not provide that the tax or penalty must be paid before the Income Tax authority can determine the amount of tax or penalty. It merely provides that the tax/ penalty will be imposed if the tax or the penalty is payable before the Income tax authority. [887E F] 2.2. The expression "tax" has been defined in section 2(c) of the Act to mean "any tax on income or penalty". The word "tax" means a tax on income, or penalty. The word "duty" is used in section 2 (c) to include a tax
2081: The appellant Lakhan was convicted under section 302, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He appealed to the High Court which allowed the appeal of the appellant and set aside the conviction and sentence of Lakhan on the charge under section 302/149, Indian Penal code but maintained the sentence imposed upon him. The High Court held that it was competent to it in the appeal preferred by the appellant to alter the conviction of Lakhan from section 302/34, Indian Penal ' Code to a minor offence under section 326, Indian Penal Cod e, and regard being had to the gravity of the offence, the High Court altered the conviction of the appellant from section 302, I.P.C. to a minor one. The High court also held that it is competent to it to alter the finding of acquittal of Lakhan under section 302 read with section 149, Indian Penal, Code, but it did not do so in the present case because the High Court was not competent to alter the findings of acquittal of the appellant under section 302 or under section 326. Held: (i) that the High Court acted without jurisdiction in altering the finding of guilt of Lakhan as regards the appellant under sections 302/34 and 326, Indian Code, and relying on the evidence of the eye witnesses who were interested witnesses, convicted the appellant under s.302, Indian Penal Court, and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. (ii) that the appellant was entitled to have his conviction altered from section 302 to a minor punishment under section 326 I.P., Code, and the High Court erred in reducing the sentence of imprisonment on the charge of murder from one of five years rigorous imprisonment to one year rigorous imprisonment.
3944: The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of sugar. It had established its own factory at Bellary in the State of Tamil Nadu. During the assessment years 1959 64 and 1964 65, it paid commission to its salesmen for the year 1963 64 and 1964 66. In respect of the said payments, it claimed deduction under section 36(1)(iv) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, which provided that unless commission and bonuses are fixed periodical payments not dependent on a contingency, they were not covered by the term "salary" as used in Chapter IXA of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the claim but the Tribunal held that the commission paid by the assessee to its salesman was deductible under s.36(1)(v) of the Act and that the assessee was entitled to deduction under s.35(2) (b) of the Indian Income Tax Act. On reference, the High Court held that the expression "salary", as defined in Rule 2(h) of Part A of the Fourth Schedule to the Act included or excluded commission paid by an assessee to its Salesmen and that the definition of the expression "wages" as given in the said Rule 2(i) clearly showed that the commission payable by the assessee was nothing but a composite part of salary itself, and that the said payment was not a composite payment made by the assessee with its salesmen to its sales men. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "salaries" as used by the assessee in its books of account is not confined to remuneration only but includes remuneration for services rendered by the assessee. [790C] 2. The definition of the word "salary " as given in Explanation (ii) to section 2(d) of the said Act is inclusive and not exhaustive. The definition of "salary ", therefore, does not include commission, but includes all other allowances and perquisites. [795E F] 3.
2337: The appellant was a member of the Civil Service Class I and as such was an employee of the State Government. He was posted at the Civil Hospital, Ahmedabad and on February 18, 1950, he was in charge of the Medico Legal Section of that hospital. On March 14, 1952, the appellant made a representation to the State Government by his letter dated February 1, 1950, requesting that he should be placed under suspension pending further orders from the date of the receipt of the memorandum. On May 6, 1950, the appellant applied for leave to appeal to this Court against the decision if the High Court and on the application being rejected, the Government applied to this Court for special leave to appeal. Held: (i) Rule 151 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules, 1959, does not confer any power upon the Government to suspend a Government servant who has been dismissed, removed or compulsorily retired, but it merely confers a discretionary power upon the authority competent to order reinstatement. The rule is intended to prevent the Government from taking action for misconduct which may have taken place while the officer was in service. It is not meant to punish a Government servant without holding him guilty of misconduct. The power conferred on the Government under the rules is only to see whether the conduct of the Government servant during the period of his absence is such as would disentitle him to receive full pay and allowances. The Government cannot act arbitrarily or unreasonably so as to deprive the benefit of the opportunity of defending himself by imposing punishment of dismissal, removal or compulsory retirement. The Government can also take into consideration any other relevant material. If the Government decides to keep the record straight and objectively confidential, it will undoubtedly be open to the Government to disclose the material on the basis of which the Government decided to remove the appellant. But the Government cannot act mechanically or arbitrarily in taking action for blackmail or victimisation. The Government must show that the conduct of a Government servant is such as to give rise to serious financial liability. The Government may well come to the conclusion that the conduct complained of is such as could not be expected to result in loss of emoluments or in distress. 2405: The respondent brought a suit for pre emption of the land in dispute, which was sold under a sale deed dated February 6, 1942. The appellant contested the suit on the ground that the respondent had a right to pre emotion and that the appellant was not entitled to preemect the property sold. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the custom of pre encumber was not applicable to the city of Calcutta and that the vendor was not a resident of Calcutta. The definition of "land revenue", therefore, does not include the rent payable to the Government or to any other person. [560A B] 3. The expression "rent" in section 2 (1) of Bombay Land Revenue 'Act, 1879, includes the rent payable by the tenant to the landlord. [567B] 4. The expression 'rent ' in section 2 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, means the rent payable in kind or in cash or in kind. [569E] 5. The word "rent" is not defined in the Act. The word 'rent' is defined in section 3(2)(a) of the Act.
3961: The respondent was appointed as Sub Inspector of Police in the Uttar Pradesh Police Service on January 21, 1957. He was discharged from service by an order dated January 21, 1956. On March 13, 1957, he instituted a suit for a declaration that the order dated January 20, 1955 terminating his services was illegal and void and that he continued as Sub Inspector. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the enquiry was not made by a superior authority or by a competent officer, and that the order of termination was vitiated by mala fides. HELD: (i) The order of dismissal was passed by way of punishment because it was based on the allegations against the respondent. The order of termination had been made in accordance with the rules applicable to temporary government servants. [839 E] (ii) The order did not contain any stigma nor did it cast any stigmatio upon the respondent. It merely stated that the respondent 's conduct was unsatisfactory. The order was therefore bad. [840 F] (iii) The order was not made in the manner prescribed under the rules governing the conditions of service of the respondent. [841 B] (iv) The order is not supported by any reason whatsoever. It is only an administrative order which is made for the purpose of giving effect to the principles of natural justice. [842 C] (v) The order does not mention anything more than what was required to be done by law. [843 D]
40: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 147, 148 and 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on 29th November, 1949, a mob of about fifty persons came on the field armed with ballams, lathis and other weapons and that the first appellant Logendranath Jha, who was leading the mob, demanded a settlement of all outstanding disputes with the complainant and that the complainant had to pay a sum of Rs. 50 as settlement. The complainant alleged that the appellants had been demanding a settlement of the disputed land and that the appellants were trying to forcibly dispossess him from the land. The trial court acquitted the accused but the High Court set aside the order of acquittal. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the evidence in the case was not reliable and that the story of the prosecution was not acceptable. HELD : (i) It is well settled that if two views are reasonably possible on the evidence adduced in the case, one pointing towards the guilt of the accused and the other striking against the accus ed is no ground for setting aside the order acquit ted. [801 G] (ii) There is nothing in the provisions of section 417 of the Criminal Procedure Code which would prevent the High Court from interfering with an order of acquittal when there is some material on record which would justify the Court in taking a different view of the matter than that taken by the Sessions Judge. [802 B C] (iii) The High Court has not considered the evidence in its proper perspective and has not given any reasons for coming to the conclusion that the view taken by the trial court was unreasonable or perverse. [803 D E]
