2932: The respondent was appointed as a Special Officer in the Bihar Police Service on 25th January, 1937 and at the material time he was posted at Ranchi. He was transferred to Patna and appointed as Special Officer, Political, General and Transport Department on July 23, 1964. On July 23, 1963, the Government of India issued an order placing him under suspension. In June 1962, the respondent was reported to have contravened certain provisions of the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1954; and as such disciplinary proceedings were contemplated against him. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the order of suspension was not proper because the respondent had been questioned by section P. of the All Indian Services (Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1955; and since the enquiry was still pending, the order of his suspension was not justified. HELD: Rule 12 of the All india Services (Confidential) Rules, 1957, empowering the appointing authority to place an officer under suspension inter alia where a disciplinary proceeding is pending or contemplated or is pending and rule 7 of the All Indi a Services (Disciple of Appeal) Rules provides for the initiation of departmental inquiry against the delinquent officer. [718 E F] The Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules are concerned with the conduct of the officer and the nature of the charges and circumstances in any case. The rules do not provide for any specific procedure for holding the departmental inquiry. It does not also provide for any other procedure for conducting the departmental inquiries. [719 C D] The Central Criminal Investigation Commission has no power to suspend an officer under the All India Service (Disciplinary Proceedings) Rules, 1958. The Central Civil Service (Classification Control and Appeal Rules are concerned only with the conduct and punishment of officers of the State Government. [720 B] The Central Vigilance Commission has no jurisdiction over the matter. [721 A] The Central Administrative Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with the orders of suspension unless they are passed mala fide or without there being any allegation of bias or malafide. 6210: The appellant, a Hindu widow of a Hindu male who died intestate leaving behind her widow, the respondent, as his next heir. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties with mesne profits and a decree for possession of them along with mesnt profits. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decision of the trial court on the ground that the adoption of the appellant was not valid under section 16(1)(c) of the Bombay Prevention of Fragmentation and Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1947 (Bom. LXVII of 1947). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in reversing the decision of a single judge of the High Court which had affirmed the decision of another single judge of that court. HELD: (i) Section 16(1) (c) of Act No. XIII of 1947 is applicable only where the adoption is by a widow or by a person who has no near relatives living; and the adoption must be made before the commencement of the Act. [868 C] (iv) The High Courts were wrong in holding the adoption to be invalid because the adoption was not by a widow. [869 D]

245: The State of Uttar Pradesh was a part of the Indian Union. In pursuance of an agreement entered into by the Rulers of India and the Government of India, the United State of Vindhya Pradesh was merged in the Indian Union on January 26, 1948. By the Instrument of Accession, the Ruler agreed to be bound to the Dominion of India as from the date of his taking over the administration of the State. Under the terms of the Instrument, the Ruler was entitled to all the rights, powers and privileges which were enjoyed by the Ruler immediately before the date of the instrument. The Ruler was also entitled to the rights, duties and obligations of the Government of the Indian Dominion as from the said date. The Government of India Act, 1935, provided that "the rights, duties or obligations of the Crown of India shall cease and determine as soon as may be after the commencement of this Constitution." The Instrument of Accessions was executed on December 18, 1947, and the Ruler surrendered his sovereignty to the Dominion. On the merger of the State with the Dominion of Pakistan, the Ruler became the sovereign of India. The Government, however, did not accede to the Dominion and the Ruler continued to be the sovereign. The Government then took over the administration and the properties of the State including the properties of certain Rulers of the Indian States. The Ruler made a covenant on behalf of the Government that he would not be liable for any arrears of revenue due to the Government of any other country except the Indian Union and that he would be liable only to pay the taxes imposed by the Government of that country. The Ruler claimed that the income derived by him from the properties of his State should be assessed under the provisions of the Income tax Act, 1922, and that the income received by him should be assessed in the hands of the Government. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court held that the income was exempt from taxation under section 10(2) of the Income 'tax Act, 1922. Held: (i) The income received by the Ruler was exempt from tax under section 10 of the Income-tax Act, and the income received was not exempt from tax. (ii)The expression "property" in section 10
5358: The petitioners, who were members of the Administrative Tribunal, filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the orders appointing the Chairman and Vice Chair man and administrative members of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appointment of Chairman, Vice Chair men and administrative members should be made by the concerned government only after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The observations cannot be read as laying down any law. It is not necessary for the High Courts to give effect to the observations made by this Court in the cases referred to above. [941G H]

125: The plaintiffs in the suit for ejectment of the second defendant from the first floor flat of a building situate at Cumballa Hill, Bombay, filed a suit against the second defendant for possession of the said flat on the ground that he was a tenant of the first defendant and that he had sublet the said flat to the second defendant. The defendants resisted the suit on the grounds that the suit was not maintainable as the first defendant was a limited company and that the suit should have been instituted by him as his landlord. The trial Court held that the suit as against the second respondent was not a suit between a landlord and a tenant relating to the recovery of rent or possession of any premises to which any of the provisions of the Act applied and that the first defendant had no jurisdiction to entertain it. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) The suit as against a landlord was not a proceeding between a landlord 's landlord and a 'tenant ' within the meaning of section 28 of the Act. 5745: The Rajasthan State and Subordinate Services (Direct Recruitment by Combined Competitive Examinations) Rules, 1962 were framed under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution by which, in respect of the scheme of competitive examinations to be conducted by the Public Service Commission for recruitment to certain branches of the civil services under the state, certain minimum qualifying marks in the viva voce test was prescribed. Rule 15 provided that the Commission shall not recommend any candidate for the R.A.S./R.P.S. who had failed to obtain a minimum of 33% marks in the personality and viva voce examination and a minimum of 50% marks in aggregate. Rule 15 further provided that the candidates who failed to secure the minimum qualifying mark in the viva-voce test would not be eligible for selection. Rule 16 provided that the commission shall prepare a list of candidates selected for appointment to the service from amongst the successful candidates in the order of merit on the basis of the general suitability for the service. The appellants who were unsuccessful candidates challenged before the High Court the validity of the aforesaid provisions of the Rules and the corresponding provisions in the Rules pertaining to the other services. The High Court held that the provision of the Rules did not violate the guarantee contained in Article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the High Court in reaching such conclusions as it did on the constitutionality of Proviso (i) to Rule 15 of the '1962 ' and of the corresponding provisions of the '1963 Rules ' and the corresponding Provisions in the Rules relating to other services, wholly misconceived the thrust and emphasis of the pronouncements of this court in Ajay Hasia vs Khalid Mujib Sehravardi & Ors., ; , Lila Dhar vs State of Haryana & Ors., , and Ashok Kumar Yadav vs State of Rajasthan & Ors., etc. , that the High Courts were bound to follow the decision of this Court in Ajay Hasias case (supra), and that the High courts were not justified
3941: The appellant was a manufacturer of Vanaspati. It had set up its factory on the land in question and had installed a Vanaspathi plant. The State Government took a policy decision that new Vanaspaties in the State which go into commercial production by 30th September, 1970 would be given partial concession in Sales Tax for a period of three years from the date of commencement of production. The appellant was exempted from payment of sales tax for a period not exceeding three years from 2nd July, 1970. The appellant challenged the order of exemption before the High Court contending that the 4th respondent had given a categorical assurance to the State Government that the appellant would be exempt from payment of Sales Tax for the period of three year commencing from 1st July, 1970 and that the State Government was bound to grant such exemption. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the 4 th respondent had altered its position and the State Government had acted in reliance on it and the State was bound to give effect to it. [655C] (2) The State Government has no power under section 3 of the Act to make any law or issue any executive direction to the State to make any enactment or any notification or executive instruction or even to frame or amend or repeal any statutory provision. The State cannot, therefore, make any law in respect of the matter covered by the said statute. The State has the power to make laws with respect to matters enumerated in List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. The State Legislature has the power under Entry 54 of List I to legislate with respect to taxes on the consumption or sale of goods. The State legislature has the power, if it so desires
201: The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan who migrated to India after the partition of 1947. The petitioners had not acquired any right to continue in possession of the land allotted to them. 59: The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of aluminium products. In 1951, the Central Bank of India Ltd., a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, filed a suit against the Bank for recovery of its dues from it. The Bank contended that the Bank had no authority to make any law regarding acquisition or requisitioning of property for the purposes of the Union or the State, and that the Bank was not entitled to recover the amount claimed by it as compensation. Held, that the Bank 's action was barred by article 31(1) of the Constitution. The right to acquire property is a right to property and the right to property is a constitutional right guaranteed by article 19 (1) (f) and (g). The right to property cannot be said to have been taken away by an amendment of the Constitution which came into force on January 26, 1950. The amendment made by the President in exercise of his powers conferred by article 368 of the Constitution was not retrospective in operation but only prospective. The amendment was valid when it was made. The amendment could not affect the rights of the petitioner under article 19(1)(f) and article 31(2) of the constitution. The right of the petitioner to receive compensation was not a right to hold property but a right to acquire such property. The right was not a mere right to property; it was a right to compensation. The right must be a right to the property and not a right of property. The amendment did not take away the right of the petitione r to claim compensation because he had acquired it before the amendment. The amendment also did not take into account the right of a citizen to move this Court under article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of his fundamental right. The right under article 19 (l) (f), and article 31 (2) of Constitution was a right of personal liberty and not of property. It was not a personal right. The amendment of the,Constitution was not a new right nor a new right of property but merely a change of procedure. The amendment does not alter the existing procedure. The right is not a mere matter of procedure. It is a substantive right and has always been held to be a constitutional right. The
6749: The petitioner was appointed as Excise Sub Inspector on ad hoc basis in the Excise Department of the State Government. He was confirmed as Excise Sub-Inspector with effect from April 1, 1967. 5386: The petitioner was allotted a premises in the city of Hyderabad. The Government had declined to release the premises without giving an opportunity to the petitioner to show cause against the order releasing the premises. The Government rejected the representation made by the petitioner and passed an order on 19.3.1980 releasing the landlady 's premises. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Government could not review its own order, as it was not a party to the proceedings. In this appeal, it is contended for the appellant that the Government cannot review its own orders. It is further submitted that the Government did not take into account the subsequent events which were relevant on the question of release of the premises. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has rightly held that the Government can review its own decision. [880C] 2. The High Courts have power under Article 226 to issue appropriate writs or directions to quash the orders of the Government. [881D] 3. The High courts are not competent to correct errors of facts. [882E] 4. The High Cour t erred in entertaining the special leave petition without issuing notice to the respondents. [883F] 5. The High has no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the Government after having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case. [884G]
5172: The appellant was the owner of a building in Delhi. She let out the premises to the respondent for residence. The ground floor of the building was let out to the respondent on a rent of Rs.2,500 per month. The ground was that she required the premises for her residence. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 14(1) (e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The appellant contended that the landlady had no other reasonably suitable accommodation and therefore the land lady could not contend that she had no other reasonable accommodation. The learned single judge of the High Court dismissed the petition holding that the land lord had sufficient accommodation and he had bona fide need of the premises for his residence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the landlwall was not a suitable accommodation and the land lady had no other alternative accommodation. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The landlady has no other reasonably reasonably suitable accommodation. [285C] 2. The land lady having been residing in the suit premises for more than 12 years, it is not possible to hold that she had any other reasonably suitable residential accom pation. [286D] 3. The land lord cannot contend that she has no other reasonable suitable accommodation. The land witn esses have to be examined in the light of the facts mentioned hereinbefore. [287E] 4. The landlwalls are not suitable for the purpose of residence of the landladi ng. [288F] 5. The landlord has no other alternative accom pany available. [289G]
49: The respondent firm was carrying on business in cloth and was supplying to the appellant a large quantity of cloth. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent firm for supply of certain goods to the respondent firm, but the respondent firm did not deliver the goods to the appellant within the stipulated time. The appellant thereupon filed a suit against the respondent firm and its partners for damages for breach of contract. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent firm had failed to perform its part of the contract and that it was entitled to recover damages from the appellant. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the circumstances of the case afford no basis for the application of the doctrine of frustration of contract. In the instant case, the facts clearly show that the respondent had made out a clear and unequivocal promise to the appellant firm that the goods supplied would be delivered to them by the appellant 's firm, and that the appellant had paid more attention to the abstract legal doctrine than to the facts of the case.
4724: The appellant, a businessman of Dibrugarh District, was granted a licence under the Assam Excise Rules, 1945 for a period of three years. The licence was renewed from time to time and the appellant was given a fresh licence for a period not exceeding three years. In the meantime, the Deputy Commissioner, Sibsagar, by his order dated August 28, 1981, directed remitting the matter to the Board of Revenue for a decision afresh. The appellant challenged the said order in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court had no jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus or an order directing the Deputy Commissioner to settle the liquor shop with respondents Nos. 1 and 2. [307B] 2.1 It is not correct to say that the Deputy Commissioner has no power to review his own order. He can only modify it if he comes to the conclusion that there exist circumstances justifying it. The Deputy Commissioner cannot exercise such powers unless he comes to his conclusion on facts and on evidence. [308C] 3.2 The Deputy Commissioner has been conferred with the power to grant licences for a period exceeding three years but not exceeding one year. The Deputy Commissioners have been invested with the power of granting licences for a limited period. The Deputy Commis sioner exercises the power of revision as provided in section 36(4) of the Act. The Deputy commissioner does not have any power to review the orders passed by him. [309D E] 3.3 The Deputy Commissioner is not entitled to review his order merely because he has decided to grant a licence for a specified period. The power of review is exercisable within a reasonable time after the grant of the licence. [305E F] 4.1 The Deputy Commissioner, who is invested with the authority to grant a license for a specified term, cannot exercise the same power which the Deputy Commissioner exercises in respect of a class of cases. [306A B]
3219: The respondent was the owner of four ladies ' properties. He had two wives by name, one of whom was referred to as the father of his minor children and the other as the mother of his minor sons. The respondent filed a return under section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 stating that he had reasons to believe that income chargeable to tax for the assessment years 1955 56, 1956 57, 1957 58 and 1958 59 had escaped assessment within the meaning of sec.147 of the Act. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Income Tax Officers were not justified in initiating proceedings against the respondent under sections 147 and 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961; (ii) the Income tax Officer was not competent to initiate proceedings under section 147(2) of the Income 'tax Act, 1961 because the income of each of the four years was liable to be assessed separately in respect of each of those four years and (iii) the Income-tax Officer was not entitled to reopen the assessment for the year in question when the original assessments were completed. Dismiss
2587: The respondent firm purchased unginned cotton and after ginning the cotton by a mechanical process and removing the seeds sold the ginned cotton to customers outside the State. In respect of cotton seeds sold by it to registered dealers, the respondent claimed deduction from the purchase turnover under section 5 (2) (a) (vi) of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1948. The assessing authority did not allow the deduction holding that the goods sold were different commercial commodities and the respondent was assessed to pay a tax of Rs. 16,452 by the order of the assessing authority dated 11th September, 1963. The writ petition filed by the respondent in the High Court challenging the assessment was allowed by the High Court which quashed the assessment and directed the assessing authority to redetermine the tax in the light of its judgment. In allowing the appeal, the High Court followed its previous decision in Patel Cotton Company Private Ltd. vs State of Punjab & Ors.(1). On behalf of the appellants it was contended that ginning process was a manufacturing process and ginned or unginned and therefore the exemption granted by the High court should be upheld. The expression "manufacture", as defined in section 2 (d), means producing, making, extracting, altering, ornamenting, packing, pressing, breaking, shoving, purging or stealing. It does not include any process for making, altering, finishing, polishing, nature of etc. The term "processing" has been defined in section 3 (f) of the Act to mean "any process for making or bringing into or upon the wrapper or other thing of the nature described as making, altering or otherwise securing plainly contrary to the workings and usages of trade." The word "manufacturing" has not been defined in the Act. The expression manufacture implies a change but everything done so as to bring into existence of the new goods in the market. 2428: The appellants purchased the rights of the main lessee and sued the respondents for possession of the homestead. The trial court decreed the suit but the first Appellate Court reversed the decree. The High Court allowed the appeal as mentioned earlier, holding that the provisions of Bihar Tenancy Act (to be hereinafter referred to as the Act) do not apply to a lease of a homestead although that homestead was a part of an earlier lease which was admittedly an agricultural lease and to which the provisions of the Act applied. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the lease in favour of the appellants is governed by section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act and therefore they are entitled to evict the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 117 of the Act does not apply to leases of a homestshealthy tenure. [875C] 2. Section 117 applies only where a lease of an agricultural land is executed in contravention of the provisions of section 117. It does not apply when a lease of agricultural land is made in contravention of section 117 of Transfer of Property act. [876D] 3. Section 117 does not apply if the main lease is not covered by the provisions of Section 117 of Transfer Act. The question whether the lease is governed by Section 117 of Bihar Tenancy Law or not has to be decided in accordance with the provisions of law. [877E F] 4. Section 117 is not applicable to a lease in respect of a homotholder. The definition of "agriculture" in section 2(1)(a) of the Act includes cultivation of any land. The definition is not exhaustive. But if the word "agriculture", as defined in the Act, means cultivation of any other kind of land, then the word "agricultural" would include cultivation of any such land. [878G H; 879A B]
1859: The assessee was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It purchased a building and made substantial alterations, additions and improvements therein. The income of the assessee was received from subscriptions and donations collected from its members and rent received from the building. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was not a charitable institution and the income in question was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income was not exempt under section4(3)(ii). The Tribunal however held that the amount received by the assessee was exempt under Section 4(3) (iii), and that the assessee had failed to prove that it was not liable to pay any portion of the income. In further appeal to this Court, the assessee contended that the income received by it was not exempt as it was derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes and that the income in dispute fell within the purview of section 4(1)(a) of the Act. HELD : The income received by the appellant was not exempt from tax under section 4 (3) (i) of Income tax Act. [560 D] The word "derived" in section 4(2) has been used in the sense of an income which is derived from property so held under trust. The word "dividend" in section 2(6) of the Income tax Act means "any benefit or advantage derived or obtained by an assessee on the strength of a transaction or for use of money or profit". The word "income" in section 3(3) of the Incometax Act includes "any income derived from property referred to in section 3". The word 'income ' in section 3 (3) means "the income derived from any trade, business, profession or vocation". The word is defined in section 2 (7) of the Finance Act of 1950 as including "any income received from property held on trust or other authority for public charity." The word "compensation" in section 6 of the Income Tax Act means compensation paid out of profits or gains. [568 B C]
2736: The appellants who were the sons of one Kothandaraman, who died in 1943, filed a suit for partition claiming a share in the joint family property as successor in interest of one Kothavaraman. The main contention was that the adoption of the appellant was valid and that the adoption was not invalid. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the adoption had been validly made and that the appellant was entitled to a half share in the properties of the joint family. On appeal the High Court held that the adoption having been proved it was not necessary to obtain consent of the nearest sapindas of the family. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) The adoption of the appellants was valid. [502 B] (ii) The adoption was not valid because the adoption was made with the consent of the first three near relatives of the deceased. The first condition was that the consent of all the near relatives should be obtained before the adopted person can claim the benefit of the adoption. [503 C] (iii) The adoption is not valid unless it is shown that the adoption has been made with the knowledge or consent of the person giving it. [504 D] (iv) The adoption must be in accordance with law. [505 E] (v) The adoption cannot be challenged on the ground that it was contrary to the wishes of the persons giving it. It is only when the person giving the consent makes an attempt to interfere with the exercise of his right under the agreement. [506 F] (vi) The adoption does not require any independent judgment of the person making the adoption. It is not necessary that there should have been some other person who would have given the consent. [507 H] (vii) There is no evidence that the consent was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. [508 A] (viii) The adoption did not require any corroboration. [509 G]
1201: The respondent was granted a bilmakta of the village in 1901. In 1918, the Nizam granted a grant to his ancestor by the Nizam in 1787. In 1917, the respondent was only entitled to the pan muktara kiosk and the appellants were liable to ejectment as they could not claim to dispossess them from the village. On the question whether the village had been granted as bilmas or as bilams, the trial court held that the village had not been granted as a bilam or as bazar but as a bazar. The High Court on appeal reversed this decision and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The case of the respondent was that the village was granted as bhomatari and not as bazar. [1927 F] (2) The grant was not permanent. It was merely temporary. The grant was made for a fixed period. The grant did not create any title in favour of the respondent. The grant being permanent, it was not open to the respondent to assert a title adverse to the respondent. [1928 G H; 1929 A B] (3) The grant is not a bazar but a bazar grant. The grant does not create any interest in the bazar. It is only a bazar which creates rights in favour of persons who are entitled to possession of the bazar land. [1930 C D] (4) The grant does no doubt confer a title in favour the person who has obtained it. But it does not create an interest in favour of a person who is not entitled to the same. [1931 E]

3896: The assessee was a contractor. He carried out the works of construction of a building and sold it to the contractor. The cost of the stores or material supplied by the Government to the assessee was not included in the figure of cash payments received by the assessee on the ground that the stores (material) supplied by the military authorities to the assessee for being used in the works entrusted to the contractor, that the same always remained the property of the Government and that no profit could be said to have arisen to the assessee when such stores (materials) were merely handled and manipulated by the assessee in the execution of the works under the contract. The Income Tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee that the cost of the materials supplied by the Military Authorities to the assessee should be added to the total cash payments received from the Department under the contract for the purpose of estimating the income or profits derived by the contractor. In appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the cost or value of the stores/materials supplied by the Army Authorities to the contractor was not to be included in the amount of cash payments made by the contractor to the assessee. The High Court dismissed the reference. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the cost incurred by the assessee for the purposes of estimating his income or profits from the contract was not to include the cost of stores/material supplied by the civil authorities for being used as raw material in the works undertaken by the firm. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The cost or value for the purposes mentioned in section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, is the price paid by the contractor for the goods supplied by the Civil authorities to the contractor for being used by him in the works. [203C D] 2. The cost must be added to or deducted from the gross amount payable to the contractor under the contract entered into by the contractor with the contractor. [204E] 3. The cost to be added to any amount paid by the assessee under the contract is not to be added or excluded from the amount payable to him under the contract but only to the extent to which it is so added or excluded. [205F G]

The power must be exercised reasonably and in good faith. [1122E F] 1.4. The power cannot be exercised arbitrarily or mala fide. [1123F] 1.5. The power can be exercised for achieving the purposes specified in the statute. [1124G] 1.6. The power may be exercised suo motu or at the instance of the authority which would have jurisdiction to determine whether the action taken was reasonable or not. [1125A] 1.7. In the present case, the authority had no power to review its own decision. [1127F] 1,9.1. Section 15(2)(b) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 provides that the Vice Chairman shall be entitled to exercise all such powers as are vested in him under any law for the time being in force. 5965: The respondent assessee was a company incorporated in the United States of America. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income Tax Officer. On further appeal by the Department, the Tribunal held that the sale was effected with the object of earning profits and it was a relevant circumstance for the purpose of computing the income of the assessee. The High Court dismissed the reference. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the sale of the shares was affected only to the extent of the shares which were held on investment account or capital account but it was a trading loss and it was not the case of the Department that in arriving at its decision the Tribunal had taken into consideration any irrelevant material or failed to take into consideration any relevant material or failed not to take into considera tion any relevant material. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The Tribunal has rightly rejected the claim of the assessee for deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1961. [766F] 1.2. The Tribunal was justified in holding that the sale having been affected only in the manner indicated by the assessee, the sales were in the nature of a business transaction. [767A B] 1.3. The Tribunal also considered the fact that the shares were purchased in the name of the assessee and the sale was affected only in a few days. The Tribunal found that the sale did not have anything to do with the control of the companies concerned. It is true that the assessee had produced evidence to show that the shares had been sold in the name and style of the assessee but the fact remains that the shares have been sold in several places. The Tribunal had come to the conclusion that the sale took place in the course of the business of the assessee as a dealer in shares. [768B C] 1
4035: The appellant was detained under the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. He challenged his detention on the ground that he had been implicated in a case under section 3 of the Act which was pending against him and that there was no material to show that the appellant was involved in any other offence. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the possibility of a prosecution being launched was an irrelevant consideration which need never be present to the mind of the detaining authority. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of detention must always be made with or without prosecution and in anticipation or after discharge or even acquittal. [547D] 2. The object of preventive detention is not to punish a man for having done something but to prevent him from doing so. It does not necessarily imply that the person sought to be detained has to be placed under detention. The fact that the detenu may have some evil consequences on his future cannot lead to the inference that he was likely to indulge in similar activities again. The mere fact that the detaining authority may have reason to believe that the detenu might commit crime would not make the order of detention bad. [548E F] 3. The facts of the present case are quite different from the facts of the case in hand. The grounds of detention served on the appellant contain elaborate statement of facts. The fact of the matter is that the appellant had been arrested in connection with a case under sections 147, 148, 149, 307, 326, 324, 323, 504 and 506 I.P.C. and was released on bail. The fact remains that the appellant did not appear before the detaining authority at the time when the detention order was passed. The fact remained that the appellant could not be apprehended at the spot and was produced before the court. The fact situation is entirely different. [549F H; 550A B] 4. The fact whether the appellant was actually involved in any criminal activity or not is immaterial. The fact as to whether the appellant is a habitual offender or not is irrelevant. The fact about the appellant's involvement in a case of serious nature is irrelevant. [550G]

795: The appellant, a Hindu, filed an application under section 5(3) of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, for being impleaded as a party to the suit. He alleged that the temple was a public one and the properties were his personal properties. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the appellant 's case was that the temple and the properties belonged to him and he had no right or authority whatever in them. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to be joined as a party. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was estopped from making any claim against the deity. The appellant was not a party to any of the proceedings before the trial court. [684 B] (ii) The appellant could not be said to have been made a party to a proceeding before the trial judge because he was not a necessary party. [685 C D] (iii) The appellant did not make out a case that the temple itself was a public trust. [686 F] (iv) The appellant had not established that the temple is a public trust but it was open to the appellant to establish that the temple has come into existence for the religious and charitable purposes. [687 G] (v) The appellant cannot be said to be a person who can be said to hold an interest in the temple. [688 A B] (vi) The appellant is not a person who holds an interest in a temple. [690 E]

2436: The plaintiff bank advanced a sum of Rs. 12,000/ to the defendant for the principal and Rs. 2,769.37 nP on account of principal and interest. The defendant failed to pay the amount in spite of demand. The plaintiff filed a suit against the defendant for recovery of the amount due under the bond. The defendant resisted the suit contending that the surety had no right to restrain the creditor from recovering the amount from the principal debtor. The trial court decreed the suit against both the defendants. In appeal the Subordinate Judge held that the surety was not liable to pay the principal and the decree was passed as it was not executable against him. On appeal the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the surety became liable to pay only the principal and not the principal and that the surety must be discharged by the creditor from his liability to pay the entire amount. HELD: (i) The surety is entitled to recover the whole or any part of the debt due to the creditor. The surety has no right to enforce its dues in favour of the creditor. [635 D] (ii) The surety cannot be compelled to sue the principal before the creditor can enforce its dues. It is open to the creditor to enforce its debts against the principal. [636 E F] (iii) The surety has an independent right to recover the amount from his principal. The surety is bound to discharge the debt in question against the principal if he does not do so. He may then recover the amount in instalments as there are no sufficient reasons why he should not be made liable to pay. [639 G H]

Rule 12(2)(a) of the said Rules provides that the number of vacancies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes shall remain unfilled until all the posts in Grade I of the Central secretariat service are filled up by promotion from amongst the officers belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. The petitioners were included in the field of selection for the purpose of drawing up the select list for 1977 for promotion to the grade I posts. After an interview by the Selection Committee, ninety one unreserved vacancies were filled from the first 90 candidates in the general category. The petitioners along with several other officials were included in that list by the Department of Personnel & Administrative Reforms in the Cabinet Secretariat in accordance with the field of Selection determined by the Selection committee. The petitioners filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the Central Secretariats (Amendment) Act, 1979 and the Regulations made thereunder. The petitioners contended that the Central secretarial services (Amendment)

Rules, 1979 did not apply to the Central Secretariat services as they were not in existence prior to the appointed day and therefore, the provisions of the Central Government (Amendment) Regulations, 1979 would not apply to them. [1187 C D] 3.1 The petitioners cannot claim that the Central Secretar y Service Rules, 1965 should also apply to the State Secretariat Service. 3195: The appellants, small manufacturers of matches, have been subjected to excise duty at the same onerus rate as has been applied to larger producers who are unequal in their economic capabilities in the matter of production and marketing a sort of traumatic egality. The appellants ' contention is that the impugned notification was discriminatory because the appellants were not similarly situated with other big manufacturers who had already converted from 'B ' to C ' class units. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellants' contention that the impugned Notification was discriminatory is without substance. [413F] (2) The appellants are small manufacturers of Matches and they have been subjected by the impugned notification to excise duty on the basis of their investment in the manufacture of which the total clearance of match boxes exceeded themselves. The appellants are entitled to the benefit of the exemption under the notification. [414G H] (3) The appellants have been subjected only to the process of manufacturing techniques and the appellants cannot be said to be similarly placed. [415A] (4) The appellants ' case is fully covered by the decision of this Court in [Mohammad Yunus vs Union of India & Ors.] ; , and the appellants ' case must be held to be covered by the ratio of that decision. [416C D]
725: The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for declaration that she was the owner of the lands. The appellant contended that the respondent had not been able to establish her claim on a special custom entitling her sister to succeed in preference to the collaterals and the onus of doing this must, therefore, be on her. The trial court held that the respondent was not entitled to succeed in respect of the properties left by her deceased husband. On appeal, the District Judge held that the appellant was not entitled, as he was not a collateral of Sahib Singh of the eighth degree and that the respondent could not succeed in preference over the collaterals. In second appeal, the High Court held that the case was governed by the general custom of the Punjab in preference to collaterals and that the appellant as the agnatic relation or collateral of Sahib singh was entitled to succeed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The respondent was not a person who could succeed in preference than the appellant. She was not entitled under the general custom to succeed in favour of the collaterals in preference to her collaterals. [790 G] (2) The respondent had based her claim on the custom of the family of her father which was prevalent in Mauza Sultanwind. The custom of the community of the parties was not proved. The respondent was therefore not entitled to the properties under the general customs of the Punjab. [791 C D] (3) The respondent did not discharge the onus of proving any special custom entiting her sister to inherit the properties under her general custom of succession. [792 F H] (4) The respondent could not be said to have failed to discharge the onus. [793 A B] (5) The respondent 's contention that the appellant should have succeeded in preference to his collaterals was not correct. The respondent had relied upon the custom of Mauzadari in the Punjab. The custom was not proved because it was not proved that the appellant had adopted the respondent. [795 E F] (6) The respondent has failed to prove that the appellant is the heir of the deceased husband of the respondent. The respondent has also failed to prove the custom of inheritance. [796 A B]
5671: The respondent No. 3 was charged with having committed an offence under section 111 read with Section 135 of the Customs Act, for having committed an act punishable under section 85 of the Gold (Control) Act, 1968. The prosecution case was that the gold was imported within the Indian Customs waters contrary to a prohibition contained in the Customs Act and that the respondents were not guilty of having committed an offense under the said Act. The Chief Judicial Magistrate accepted the plea and ordered dropping of the proceedings against the respondents. The Sessions Judge confirmed the order of dropping. On appeal by the State, the High Court reversed the order of the Sessions Judge and held that the acquittal for the offences under the Customs Act would be barred on the basis of the undermentioned facts: i) that the respondents had been tried by a competent court for the offence of being in possession of gold under the Customs law; ii) that they were sought to be prosecuted under section 85(1)(a) of the Gold Control Act, 1968; iii) that they are sought to be tried since they were acquitted; iv) that they could not be prosecuted under the Gold (Prevention) Act because they were not charged with having been found in possession of any primary gold of gold which the offender was possessed or in keeping or concealing the control of any primary or primary gold. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The ingredients required to constitute an offence under the Gold Control act are altogether different from those required to be established for an offence under any other law. [947E] 2. The question whether the prosecution under the Customs act is barred on the ground that the accused has been acquitted by a competent Court of criminal jurisdiction does not arise at all. [948F] 3. The prosecution under the Gold Act cannot be launched unless it is established that the accused had been convicted by a competent Criminal Court for an offence punishable under the Gold Prevention Act. [949A] 4. The prosecution must establish that the accused was in possession of the gold under the customs law and that he was in possession thereof. [950B] 5. The prosecution should have proved that the accused knew that the gold seized from him was subject to confiscation under the Gold Prohibition Act. [99
2637: The respondent, a contractor, filed a complaint against the appellant, a municipal officer and a sub-contractor under section 20 of the , alleging that he was not competent to file the complaint. The Magistrate acquitted the respondent but on appeal the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the complaint petition was not made and signed by the person competent under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 to exercise powers of the Corporation in the matter of institution of legal proceedings. HELD: (i) Section 537 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923 as applied to the Municipality of Howrah is not applicable to the case. Section 537 provides that the Commissioners may institute, defend or withdraw from legal proceedings under the Act. It is clear from the language used therein that the Commissioner can delegate his functions to the Chairman and the Chairman may delegate their functions to the Vice Chairman or any municipal officer. [880 B C] (ii)Section 537 of that Act provided that the Commissioners could delegate their functions under the Act to the Chairman. The words "any other authority" in section 537 are wide enough to include the Municipal Corporation of Delhi. [881 D E] (iii)The word 'authority' in section 538 of the Act means the authority which has been conferred by law with power to make rules and unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context, the word 'authority ' includes the Municipal Corporation. [882 F G] (iv)Under section 537 of this Act the Commissioners have power to delegate their functions. Under section 537 the Commissioners can delegate their functions either to the Chairman or to any municipal officer, and under section 12 the Commissioners can delegation their functions to any municipal officers. [883 A B] (v)Under section 2(vii) of the Act, the Commissioner has been given the power to delegate his functions under the provisions of the Act to any municipal Officer. The words 'any other authority ' in section 536 of the Act do not mean the Municipal Corporation alone. The words, 'any other authorities ' in section 2(viii) of the said Act would only mean the Municipal Board. [884 B C]
3983: The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. They filed a suit for partition and separate possession of their share in the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs had no right to alienate the property in question. On appeal, the High Court held that the decree was not executable against the appellants as they were not in possession of the property in dispute at the time when the sale took place. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the decree passed by the trial court did not recognise any "pre existing" right of Bai Vajia in the property in issue. It was further contended that the sale by her in favour of defendant No. 2 was null and void because she had no title to the property in controversy. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "possessed by" is not intended to apply to a case of mere possession without title. [875C] 2.1 Section 14(1) of the Act does not contemplate a pre existing right of ownership of a person who has been dispossessed otherwise than by due course of law. The expression 'possession' in section 14(1), therefore, cannot be construed to mean possession which is capable of being taken by the person in possession. [876F G] 3.1 The expression "encumbrance" in section 14 (1) of Act means a debt or other interest in money or kind but not an encumbrance or charge on land. The expression is used in the same sense in section 14. [877A] 3.2 The expression "acquired by" in section 2(1)(c) of the Bombay Prevention of Fragmentation and Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1947 is not intended either to include a pre existing or a contingent right of ownership. [878B] 3.3 The expression "title" in section 4 of the Act refers to a right of ownership in the property. [879D] 3.4 The expression "liability" in section 5 of the Act is not intended merely to refer to a liability in respect of a debt or a share in the income of the property. The expression means a debt,
707: The appellant, a Head Master of a National Training School, was nominated for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Madras from Alangulam Constituency in the District of Tirunelveli. On February 1, 1957, he filed an application under section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, praying that the Tribunal be pleased to declare the nomination paper of the appellant as invalid and to direct the returning officer to reject it on the ground that the appellant had not qualified under section 7(2) of the Act. The Tribunal rejected the application holding that the question whether the appellant was disqualified under section 7 of the Act was open to appeal under section 116A of the Act and that the appellant could not challenge the decision of the returning officer. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) Section 100(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that no order or decree of any court shall be called in question in any manner, and no injunction shall be granted by any court in respect of any action taken or to be taken by way of revision or review of any such order or decree. [626 F] (ii) The words "any matter" occurring in section 100(l)(a) are used in a wider sense so as to cover all matters relating to proceedings before the tribunal. The word "matter" is defined in section 2(d) of the , to include all matters relating, to proceedings before a tribunal. [627 A B] (iii) The words 'any matter ' occurring in section 101(1)(b) of the Indian Penal Code do not take in the matter of the matters specified in section 100 (1)(a). The word 'matter ' means something more than mere matters of fact. [628 C D] Hari Vishnu Kamath vs Syed Ahmad Ishaque, ; , referred to.
1706: The appellants, who were the owners of certain lands in the revenue estate of village Kheri, claimed compensation for their lands on the basis that they had been in possession of the land since before the date of the notification issued under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act. The Land Acquisition Officer made a reference to the Court under section 18 of the Land Acquis ition Act and the High Court held that the reference was not maintainable as it was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the reference made by the Land Acquisition officer was not only limited to the apportionment of the compensation but was also with respect to the amount of compensation. [611 D] (ii) The High court was wrong in holding that in the absence of any reference upon the question of quantum of compensation by the Land Acq uisition Officer, the Court had no jurisdiction to consider that matter at all. [612 E F] (iii) The High Courts were wrong in holding otherwise. [613 A] (iv) The High courts were wrong in assuming that the reference is barred by limitation because the appellant did not raise the objection before the Land Acquisition Officer. [614 B]
4714: The respondent Corporation was a State Transport Undertaking. The appellant Corporation created under the State Act of 1950, an Industrial Dispute between the employees of the Corporation and its employees. The services of the respondents were terminated by the appellant Corporation on account of unsatisfactory service. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination order. The High Court held that the termination was bad for non compliance with section 25F of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the termination of the services of the employees was invalid as the services had been terminated on account of unsuitability and it was not a case of retrenchment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 2(oo) of the defines retrenchment to mean "any condition excluding the determination of his normal age of retirement which is either prescribed by the rules or by the employer 's instructions". The word "retrenchment" has not been defined in the Act. It means termination of service of a workman on the ground of continued ill health. [766 F] Hariprasad Shivshanker Shukla vs A.D. Shukla, ; , referred to. 2. The definition of retrenchment given in section 2(oo)(c) of the Act does not include termination of service on account of misconduct. The words "dismissal" and "termination of service" are used in the same sense in section 2 (oo) (a) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The word "terminate" is used in section 2A of the Act in relation to termination of service by the employer on account of any reason whatsoever other than those specified therein. The word retrenchment has been used in section 25F in the context of section 2(o) of the Workmen 's Compensation Act, 1923. [767 D E] 3. The expression "retrenchment", in section 2, includes termination of service otherwise than on account of some act or omission on the part of the employee but does not include discharge from employment on the ground that there has been a retrenchment. [768 C] 4. The word 'retrenchment' in section 2 is used in a wider sense so as to cover termination of service without reasons. The word `retrenchment' is
4687: The respondent was detained under the provisions of the Act. He made a statement before the Customs officer admitting that he was a member of the crew but denied any knowledge of the contraband goods. A Division Bench of the High Court quashed the order of detention on the ground that the respondent at the time of joining the vessel as a member of crew had no "full knowledge that the vessel was to be used for smuggling activity". In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of the fact that the maximum period of detention mentioned in Section 10 of the Act has expired, and as such the appeal has become infructuous. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The order of detention against the respondent is clearly erroneous. [847F] 2.1. It may be mentioned that the maximum sentence prescribed under section 10 of the is one year and not the maximum. [848G] 2.2. The order passed by the High Court quashing the order of the detention on the basis that the respondent was a member, of the crew, is clearly erroneous and cannot be sustained. [849A] 3.1. In view of the facts that the maximum detention mentioned in section 10 of Act has expired the appeal has been rendered infructuous. [850B] 4.1. Section 10 of Act provides that if the person against whom an order of detention is made under section 3 of the Act, he can successfully abscond till the expiry of the period and altogether avoid detention. If he has served a part of the period of detention, he will have to serve out the balance. The order is clearly erroneous, and cannot be justified. [851C D]
6019: The appellants instituted a suit for declaration of their homestead right to the land comprised in plot nos. 59 and 70 in village Dhansar, District Dhanbad, which was acquired by the Central Government under the Coal Mines (Nationalisa tion) Act, 1973. The Company claimed that the disputed land formed part of the coal mine which had vested in the Central Government and thereafter in the company under the provisions of the Coal Mines Act, 1957. The Company contended that the disputed lands formed part of a coal mine which was not vested in the State Government and therefore, the vesting of the estate in the Central Govern ment did not take place. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the lease granted to the plaintiffs in respect of the land formed part and vested in the central Government under the provisions o f the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act, 1973 and that the suit land was an encumphated one. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit lands were not part of the land acquired by the central Government and that the vesting of estate in the State of Bihar took place with the notification issued under sec tions 3 of the Coal mines (Nationalisatio ns) Act, 1972. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The suit lands are adjacent to a coal mine and are being used for the purposes of the mines and that the intermediary interest in the land is not vested in any State Government. [326C] 2. The suit land forms part of a mine which has been acquired by the State Government. The State Government is the owner of the land. The State of Bihar is the owner. The State is the owner and the State of the suit land is the owner thereof. [327D] 3. The suit property is not a part of the mine. It is a part of a colliery. The State cannot be said to have taken over the possession of the suit property. [328F G] 4. The suit is barred by limitation. [329E] 5. The suit filed by the appellants is barred by time. [330G]
3467: The appellant was the sole transporter of the cement manufactured by the Cement Company at Sindri. The appellant was engaged in transporting the cement from the Sindri to different stockists at various places in Bihar and West Bengal. The appellant used to engage thirty six trucks for the purpose of transport of the cement. The appellant had also engaged twenty six trucks out of which twenty six were hired by the respondent for transporting the cement. In the course of transportation, the appellant used to charge the truck owners and other trucks for transporting the goods to the stockists. The appellant 's contract with the manufacturing company commenced some time on October 12, 1963. Since the appellant did not have its own fleet of trucks for use in his (sic) transport work, it used to engage 30 trucks for carrying the cement bags. The appellant paid Rs. 1,00,000 as freight charges to the respondent for the transportation of the cement bags and the appellant was liable to pay the balance amount. The respondent issued a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the appellant to show cause why the appellant should not be asked to pay the amount due to the respondent. The appellant replied that he was not the owner of the truck and that he was only a carrier of the cement and that he had no concern with the truck. The respondent passed an order under section 80(1)(b) of the Code directing the appellant to pay the entire amount due to him. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the appellant was in charge of the trucks for a period of three years prior to the date of the order and that the appellant could not be called upon to pay the amounts due to the respondents. The High court accordingly set aside the order of the Tribunal and restored the order of assessment made by the assessing authority. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition of owner as given in section 2(d) of the Act is not exhaustive but includes all persons who are in the business of buying or selling goods. The definition is inclusive and not exhaustive. [901 G] 2. The definition does not include a person who has been in-charge
3375: The respondent was a carpenter employed by the appellant. He fell down from the elbow of the respondent and suffered injuries resulting in amputation of his left arm. He served a notice on the appellant demanding compensation under section 4A of the , but he did not respond to it. The Commissioner held that the injury had resulted in ampulation of the left arm of the respondent, and imposed a penalty on him under section 4 A of the Act. The appellant appealed to the Labour Appellate Tribunal which dismissed the appeal holding that the injury was caused by accident arising out of and in the course of employment. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the Commissioner committed serious error of law in imposing a penalty on the appellant under section 4(3) of the Act as the compensation had not fallen due until it was settled by the Commissioner under section 19 by his impugned order dated May 6, 1969. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) Section 4A of Act provides for payment of compensation to the workman who has sustained any injury during the course of his employment. It is not possible to accept the argument that the employer 's liability to pay compensation under section 3, in respect of the injury, should be determined with reference to the facts proved or admitted by the workman. [876F] (2) The Commissioner was therefore justified in imposing a fine on the appellant. [877G H] (a) The Commissioner committed serious illegality in imposing a sentence on the appellant because of the fact that the injury which occurred arose out of and/or in the course o f the employment. The Commissioner could have easily done so if he had been satisfied that the injury complained of had been caused by the accident which arose out of or in the course' of the employment. [878B C] (b) The Commissioner could not have imposed a penalty without giving the employer 'S knowledge of the nature of the injury. [879C D] (c) The Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose a penalty on an employee who was not covered by the definition of 'workman ' in section 2(g). [880D]
5898: The respondent was posted as Executive Engineer in the Industrial Supply Section of the Directorate of Industries, Punjab. He retired from service with effect from October 31, 1982. The appellant filed a complaint against him under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 alleging that he had purchased sign boards from the respondent and had also purchased some other goods. The respondent submitted an application to the High Court for quashing the prosecution against him on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of sign boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume II, the First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1979 and the prosecution against the respondent was quashed by the High Court relying on the decision in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Punjab, AIR (1967) SC 647. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 2. 2 of the Punjab Rules is not applicable to the case because the said rule has no application to the facts of the present case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The view taken by the High court is correct and in view of Rule 2 2.2, the First information Report against the respondent being lodged within four years of his retirement and the prosecution having been launched against him, the High Court committed an error of law in taking the view which it did. [917B C] 1.2. In the instant case, the High court was right in holding that the First Information Reports were instituted after the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said rule and the High Court was wrong in taking the said view. [918D E] 1.3. The view expressed by the High 'Court is correct and the impugned judgment of the High Court cannot be sustained. [919F G]
5256: The assessee carried on the business of manufacture and sale of woolen textiles, cotton textiles and hides and leather products. For the assessment year 1959 60, under the Income tax Act, 1922, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs.50,000 paid to Messrs Textile & General Supplies Private Ltd., London as its distributor for meeting the initial expenditure for establishing it as distributor of the assessee 's products. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the assessee was bound under an agreement with the firm in which it was stipulated that the distributors would receive a discount of 15% of the sale price fixed by the assessee and that the agreement would extend for the period of seven years. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Tribunal. On reference, the High Court held that the assessee had not been able to prove that the amount represented capital expenditure incurred by it for the purpose of acquiring the technical know how or technology and that the assessee could not be said to have discharged any part of its obligation under the agreement. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The assessee was obliged to appoint the distributor of its products for the sale of industrial leather manufactured by it in India. It is clear from paragraph 7 of the agreement between the assessee and the approved officers of the assessee that the distributor would receive a commission of 15% on the sale price of the industrial leather. [739E F] (2) The agreement between the parties clearly provided that the distributorship would be for a period of seven yeas. The agreement was entered into after referring to the agreement with Charles Walker & Co., London. The agreement also contained a clause that the distribu tor would permit the use by the assessee of a number of registered trade marks specified in the agreement and further disclosed and make known to the approved officers the technique, practices and application of specialised tanning processes. The agreement did not contain any condition that the distrib ution would be for the period mentioned therein. The agreement expressly stated that the distribur tion would be for seven years. There was no mention of any term in the agreement that the distrib urer would be entitled to the benefit of the agreement. [740G H
3259: The appellants were licensees under section 10 of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961. They were licensees under Section 10 of the Act in Form 'B ' as kacha arhtiyas or commission agents. The appellants were found to be selling gur and shakkar in their own shops within the notified market area without submitting accounts and without payment of fees. The appellants had been demanding fee for the period from April 1, 1964 to March 31, 1969 on the basis of the best judgment assessment made by the Committee. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of fee on the ground that they were liable to pay market fee on the basis that they were not liable to pay any fee. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellants were not liable for payment of fee under the Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellants are not liable to payment of fee. [330G] (2) The appellants were not entitled to levy fee under the provisions of the Act. [331A] (a) The appellants have no right to demand fee under the Rules. [332C] (b) The appellants could not claim that they were entitled to collect market fee from the licensees. [335E] (c) The appellants cannot be said to be liable to pay the fee. [334F] (d) The appellants do not fall in any of the categories mentioned in sub sections (i), (ii) and (iii). [345D] (e) The appellants did not fall in either of these categories. [345E] (f) The appellants had not been exempted from payment of fee by the rules. [346H; 347A] (g) The appellants can only be held liable to pay fee under the rules. The appellants are liable to pay fees under the Act if they are not exempted by the rules but are liable to make good the loss suffered by them. [348B] (h) The appellants would be liable to make full payment of the fee. The appellants will not be liable to refund the amount collected from them. [329C]

The Advisory Board considered the case of the detenu and also the representation and submitted its report. The Advisory board considered the matter and rejected the same. The detenu 's representation was not considered before confirming the detention order. The State filed an appeal against the order of confirmation of the detention. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In this appeal, it is contended by the detenu that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the question whether the detenu should be detained or not. It was further contended that the representation made by the detenu was not considered by the detaining authority as early as possible before any order is made confirming the detention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Advisory Board has not been constituted in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 3(2) of the Act. [845C] 1.2 The Advisory Board is required to consider the entire material placed before it and make its recommendations thereon. The Advisory Boards are required to take into account relevant factors such as the nature and gravity of the offence, the social position of the parties, the means adopted by the detenu, the circumstances which were prevailing, the likelihood of the detenu's release on bail and so forth. [846E F] 1.3 The Advisory Board must give its opinion within 15 days from the date of detention. The decision of the Advisory Board must reflect application of mind to the facts of each case. The Advisory Committee is to submit its opinion within fifteen days from the receipt of the reference. The Advisory committee is to submit the report to the appropriate government. The Advisory Advisory Board is to submit a report to the Government after considering the report. The report of the Advisory board is to be forwarded to the appropriate Governments. The limitation of six month prescribed in section 131 is not applicable to the case of non levy or short levy of duty. [989 D] 5. 3247: The prosecution alleged that the respondents were responsible for the death of one Gulabkhan and his wife, a close neighbour. The prosecution case was that a she goat of Gulabkhana went to the house of respondent No.1 on 27.6.1968 at about 5 p.m. when he was showering blows with a stick on the deceased and the latter was caught hold by respondent No. 1 and sent her back to her house. The prosecution alleged further that the respondents had been threatening her not to disclose the incident to anybody else but they had also threatened her not to report the matter to any person. The prosecution examined two witnesses in support of its case. The trial court acquitted the accused holding that there was no evidence against them. On appeal the High Court set aside the order of acquittal and convicted the respondents under section 302 read with section 114 I.P.C. and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Court has erred in acquitting the respondents on the ground that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable; (ii) the High 'Court has exonerated respondent No. 2 from the charges levelled against him and hence the acquittal should be set aside. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has exonerated respondent No.2 from the charges framed against him. The High. court has externing respondent No. 5 from the charge and the acquittal of the other accused. [978 G H]

4667: The detenu was detained under section 3(2) of the with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community. The grounds of detention were supplied to him on October 12, 1971. The High Court dismissed the petition filed by the detenu under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that without the particulars of supplies and service which according to the detenu had been served on him, the order of detention could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The requirement of the specification in the order of the detention is mandatory and not merely directory. It is open to the detaining authority to take note of the past conduct of the detenu and apprehend repetition of such conduct in future an order of detention can be made known properly to the public. [959 E F] (2) The non specification of the required particulars in the order would not vitiate the order as long as the particulars are provided in the grounds in support of the order of preventive detention. [960 G H; 961 A] (3) The requirement that the particulars should be specified must be read into the order of order of detention. If the past conduct or antecedent history of a person is not disclosed at the time of his detention in order to enable him to make an effective representation against the order of his detention, the order will have to be struck down as invalid. [962 B C] (4) The requirement about the specification of the particular material in the order is mandatory and cannot be regarded as a part of the order. [964 D]

The trial court decreed the suit holding that the will had been validly executed and that the appellant could not claim any right over the property. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The object of section 14(1), as pointed out by this Court in Badri Persad 's case, is to remove the bar of limitation on the rights of a Hindu woman to claim maintenance from her husband. The object is to prevent such misuse by the Legislature. [275G] (4) The object is not to deprive a Hindu female of her right to claim maintenance but to prevent the abuse of the position by the husband of his legal obligation to maintain her. [276A B] (5) The object being to prevent the use of the property of a Hindu male by a female Hindu, the legislature cannot have intended to confer upon her a restricted estate in the properties of a Hindu lady. [277D] (6) The object and purpose of section
992: The appellant was a shopkeeper and a commercial establishment. He had been working in the shop for more than one year, but he did not disclose his name as a member of the staff of the shop or any other person who could be said to have been employed by him. The Inspector of Shops and Commercial Establishments, Ferozepore Circle, visited the appellant 's shop on the 29th January, 1954, and found that there were no employees. The Inspector also found that the appellant ''s son was selling articles at a distance of about 20 yards from the shop. On the same day, the Inspector sent a report to the Additional District Magistrate stating that the appellant had committed an offence under section 16 of the Act. The appellant pleaded that the Act would not apply to his shop because he had engaged no strangers as employees but that the entire work in the shop was being done by himself and by the members of his family and that his son was selling goods at a distance from the shop and that the provisions of the Act would be violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The word "employer" in section 7 of the Act is used in a wider sense to cover all persons who may be employed in the business of doing any kind of work. The word 'employer ' has not been defined in the Act and it is sufficient if it includes all persons who can be said to be employed in a particular business. 3978: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, and was further ordered to undergo imprisonment for life. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the death penalty was not a bar to the exercise of the power conferred by section 302 I P.C.; (ii) the sentence of death was excessive; and (iii) the circumstances in which the crime was committed were not sufficient to justify the imposition of death penalty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether the death penalty is a bar to judicial review is a difficult and controversial subject, long and hotly debated and it has evoked, during the past two centuries strong thoughts and reiteration.
