It is not legally permissible for this Court while hearing an appeal in a particular case where capital punishment is now seated with the death penalty. [139B C] 1.3 The death penalty can be imposed only if the accused has acted in a cruel and unusual manner and has acted in such a manner as would render the exercise of discretion futile. [140E] 1.4 The death penalty cannot be equated with the sentencing policy of the court. [141A] 1.5 The death penalty does not offend the constitutional guarantee of Article 21 of the Constitution. [144B] 1.6 The death penalty may be inflicted in extreme cases but the death penalty must be proportionately applied to mitigating circumstances. [144D] 1.7 The death penalty has a direct bearing on the criminal justice system. The death penalty should not be used as a weapon of reprisal to deter others from committing crimes. [144E] 1.(a) The death penalty must not be disproportionate to the offence committed. 1543: The assessees were the shareholders of a company in which the public are substantially interested. In the year 1941 42, the shareholders of the company at the material time were Kishinchand and Murli Tabilram each holding three shares. The companies were assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1941 42 to 1943 44 on the basis that they had paid dividend to their shareholders. The Income Tax Officer held that the dividends were not paid by the company but were paid by the shareholders themselves. He therefore issued notices under section 34(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, to the shareholders of their companies. The assessees appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who upheld the assessments. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that the dividend was not paid by a shareholder but was paid by the companies themselves. The High Court held that the assessees were entitled to relief under section 66 (2) of the Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the dividend could be taxed only when it is declared or paid by the assessee and not otherwise. HELD: The dividend was not payable by the company as soon as it became due. It was paid by a person who was not a shareholder. The payment of dividend was made by the company after the resolution was passed. The dividend was paid by an individual member of the company. The payment was made by a person other than the company. [279 B] The payment of the dividend was made before the resolution was signed by the members of the company and the payment was made after the resolution had been signed by the directors. The payment made by the directors was not made before the general meeting of the company was convened. The payment in the case of a company was made before its general meeting. The payment must relate to the period prior to the date of the resolution. [280 C D] The payment was not made within the period prescribed by law. The payment could not be said to have been made before the General Meeting of the company, because the payment was not in respect of any particular period. [281 E F] The payment cannot be said to be made before the meeting of the general body of the company took place. 4401: The appellant was the Judge of the Senior Sub Judge cum Chief Judicial Magistrate. He had been attending a case in which he was charged with offences under section 406 and 420 I.P.C. The Judge issued a warrant against him for his arrest. The appellant filed an application before the Rent Controller under section 15(2) of the . The Rent Controller dismissed the petition on the ground that the appellant 's version was false. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant had not paid the process fee and had managed to prevent proceedings being taken by the Judge for the contempt of his court. The High court also held that the Judge had made a reference to the High court of Himachal Pradesh under section 15 (2) of . The High Court, however, set aside the order of the Rent Controller and directed the Rent Controller to proceed under section 228 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the Judge has to be satisfied that the person making the allegation is making a false statement. [817B] 2. In the instant case, the appellant did not desire to take a lenient view of the matter since the Judge had not given any direction for furnishing complete address of the respondent before him. The High courts were therefore wrong in holding that the Judge was guilty of contempt of court. [818D E] 3. The High Cour t erred in taking the view that it was not necessary to give notice to the respondent when the Judge had already passed an order for payment of costs. [819E F]
6138: The Bombay Municipal Corporation for admis sion to post graduate degree and diploma courses in its medical colleges framed on June 18, 1973, for admission to the postgraduate courses in its Medical Colleges. Rule 4(A) of the Rules framed under the Government Resolution dated June 18, 1983 provided for collegewise institutional preference for admission in the M.D. By the impugned rule 4(A), the State Government had made a provision for collegewise counselling to be held by the Maharashtra Public Service Commission. The appellant, who was a candidate for admission to M.D., by the impugned rule, challenged the validity of the rule in whole and rule 5 (wrongly stated as rule 6 in the High Court judgment), in so far as it applied to the Government Medical College, both the rules providing for collegewise intake of seats in the MD. By its order dated March 31, 1979, the High Court allowed the writ petitions and struck down the impugned rule in whole. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1. The rule is discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. It is not only arbitrary but also discriminatory. [923F] 1.2. The rule has been made to provide for collegewise admissions to the post graduate courses in the institutions situated within the jurisdiction of the same university. This is not discriminatory. [ 922G H] 1.3. The rule does not violate Article 14 of tile Constitution. [924B] 1.4. The rule cannot be said to be unreasonable or arbitrary. It is reasonable. It is based on intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from those that are left out of the group. [925C D] Nidamarti vs State of Andhra Pradesh, ; , referred to.
1045: The appellant was a commission agent and pucca aratiya and had been acting as such for the respondent since November 7, 1951. On March 18, 1952, two of these contracts were outstanding, one of which was in respect of groundnuts and was a forward contract. Eventually on July 17, 1953, the arbitrators made one composite award for Rs. 22,529 15 9 against the respondent in respect of the said disputes. Thereafter, on July 17. 1953, the respondent made an application to the Bombay City Civil Court for setting aside the award contending that forward contracts in groundnuts between the parties were illegal as the making of such contracts was prohibited by the Oilseeds (Forward Contract Prohibition) Order, 1943, issued under the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, and hence the arbitration clause con tained in the forward contract in groundnut and was null and void. The appellant contended that forward contracts were illegal as they were not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and therefore the award in terms of the arbitration clause contained in it was a valid and enforceable award. Held, that the appellant could not be allowed to raise the question whether forward contracts were invalid or not because the Indian Parliament had passed an Act on March 26, 1946, providing for the continuance of forward contracts in certain specified areas of Bombay and Bombay, and that the Central Legislature had no power to make laws with respect thereto after September 30, 1946. The Act did not apply to the Bombay Act but only to the Bombay Acts. The Central Legislature had power to enact the law relating to forward contracts in the Bombay Act and the Bombay Act had no retrospective operation.

1251: The appellants were in unauthorised occupation of a house. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Deputy Custodian on the ground that the Deputy Custodian had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the appellants were in possession of the house or not. The High Court held that the Deputy Collector had no jurisdiction under section 18(1) of the Act to decide the matter and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The right of a non proprietor to occupy a village site was a right in property though it might not be an interest in property and that this right vested in the Custodian if the non proprietor left the country and became an evacuee. [205 D] (ii) The right to retain possession of a house is a right in rem and cannot therefore over ride the provisions of the Act. It is only where the non proprietor has been in unauthorised occupation and the house is in danger of being occupied by him, that the right can be said to have been extinguished. [206 F G] (iii) The right which the appellants had to vacate the house was not an interest in the property but was a right which could be exercised by the Custodian when he decided to dispose of the property. [207 B C] (iv) The right conferred upon the appellants by section 18(2) of the evacuee property Act, 1954, is not an interest which is capable of being transferred or assigned. [208 E] (v) The right given to the appellants by the Act is not an absolute right. It is a right to retain the possession of the property after the death of the owner. [209 A B]
6183: The plaintiffs filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to them from the owners of the vessel. The defendants were not parties to the suit and, therefore, they did not appear in the Court on the date fixed for hearing. The plaintiffs filed an application under Order IX Rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aside the ex parte decree passed against them. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their case. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the trial court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the first Special Leave Petition was not maintainable as the first Special Le tter dated 23.3.1989 was passed without notice to the plaintiffs and without giving them an opportunity of being heard; and that the suit was decreed on 6.4.1989 on the unrebutted testimony of the plaintiffs. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The first Special Leave petition is dis missed. [947E] 1.2. The first special leave petition is against the judgment and decree of the High Court confirming the order of dismissal of the suit. [946F] 1.3. The first appellate court has held that the first special leave peti tion was not maintainable. The first Appellate Court has also held that the second special leave petition was not maintainable because the first Special leave petitio ner had died during the pendency of the appeal. [948G H] 1.4. The first appeal was dismissed as abated. The first Second Appeal was pending before the High Court. The first First Appellate Court had no jurisdiction to decide the second appeal. The first Additional District Judge had no jurisdiction in the matter. [949A] 1.5. The first additional Civil Appeal No. 946 of 1992 is allowed. The first appellant is entitled to costs.
2172: The appellants were vendees to the sale of their land which was preempted under the Punjab Preemption (Haryana) Act, 1949. The vendees sold the land in suit to the appellants on January 15, 1955. The vendee purchased the land in dispute from the appellants on February 15, 1955 and the appellants filed a suit for preemption against the vendees on March 31, 1955. In the plaint it was stated that the land was purchased by the appellants during consolidation proceedings in lieu of the land which was the subject matter of the sale deed and that the vendees had no right to preempt the land which they had purchased under the sale deed. The appellants contended that the suit was not maintainable as the preemption decree was obtained by fraud and misrepresentation of facts. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the preemption suit was not competent because the preemption suits were governed by the provisions of the Punjab Preferential Purportance Code and that the pre emptor could not be said to have been misled by the preemption decrees. The appellants appealed to this Court with special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the preemptive rights of preemption conferred upon the vendees by section 24 of the Punjab preemption Act, 1949, were not available to preemptors who were co sharers in the land in question and that the appellants could not be deprived of the preemption rights if they were not co sharers. HELD: (i) The preemption suits are not barred by section 24(1)(a) of the Punjab Act. [867 F] (ii) The preemptors were co sharer in the land and the preemptors had no right or title to preempt it. [868 A] (iii) The pre-emptors were not co co sharers but were co sharners in the land. [869 B] (iv) The pre emptors were co co sharer and not co sharer. [870 C]
2148: The Assam Primary Education Act, 1947 was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under entry 45 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. Under section 15(1) of the Act, the State Government may appoint a Board for Basic education and such number of officers and servants as it thinks fit. Section 16 provided that "all teachers existing or to be appointed in any Elementary School recognised under the Act, except in the case of the Autonomous Districts, shall be deemed to have been employed by the State Board". The respondent teachers were not appointed by the State Government but by the Deputy Inspector of Schools. They were inter alia authorised to operate the fund placed at their disposal by the State. The State Government had also issued instructions regarding the appointment of teachers. The respondent teachers challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the State Government had no power to terminate the services of the teachers who were appointed by the Deputy Inspectors of Schools. Held, that the State Legislature had no power under entry 45 List III of Seventh Schedule to tile Constitution to make laws with respect to the matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Sche dule to the Constitution and that the State legislature had no power even to frame rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act. The State Legislature had power to enact legislation in respect of matters enumerated in Entry 45 of List II of the Seventh Schu pl to the Constitution, and the State Government could not, therefore, pass any order terminating the services of teachers who were not appointed either by the Deputy Inspectress of Schools or by the Deputy inspectors of Schools.
6927: The appellant assessee was a company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of aluminium products. [566G]

The auction proceedings were illegal and void. The auction holder was not bound under section 97 to pay the amount of tax due. The auction pawner was not bound. 3522: The appellants were convicted under section 2(i)(a) read with section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (hereinafter called the Act). They were sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250 each and in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one month. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence to a fine. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the provisions of the Act did not apply to the facts of the case. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code are not applicable to the proceedings before the Magistrate. [703C D] 2. Section 2(i) of the Act is an inclusive definition and does not contain any provision which would enable the State Government to make rules or orders in respect of any matter relating to food. It only provides that the State Government may make rules providing for the imposition of penalties on persons contravening the provisions of section 2. [704E F] 3. The Act does not provide for any separate procedure for the trial of offences under the Act. The Act has been enacted to deal with the adulterated food. The Act is intended to deal with adulteration of food within the meaning of section 2(ia) of the Food Adulterat e Act. The provisions contained in sections 7(1), 8 and 16(1) of the act are not exhaustive of the matters covered by them. The Act deals with the punishment for adulteration. The Act also contains a non obstante clause. [705F G]
231: The plaintiff, a Hindu undivided family, was the nearest agnate of the family. He executed a will in favour of his father who died in 1903 leaving behind him his widow, and two sons. The plaintiff claimed that by reason of his adoption he had become a preferential heir entitled to divest the properties standing in the name of his adopted son. The trial Court held that the plaintiff was entitled to a half share in the family properties on the ground that they belonged to the family as ancestral properties; but the High Court held that it had not been established that the acquisitions standing in the names of the plaintiff were made with the aid of joint family funds, that the evidence adduced by the defendants did not establish that the acquisition was made with the help of joint family fund, that the presumption in favour of the plaintiff stood unrebutted, and that the presumption arising from the fact that the plaintiff had acquired the property under the will was rebutted. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the plaintiff could not be said to have acquired any title to the properties which had been inherited by his adoptive father from his father. 2027: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It is a subsidiary of the respondent company. 2519: The petitioners who were working in the sweetmeat shops of the respondent State, filed a writ petition in this Court for an order directing the Chief Minister to show cause why he should not be committed for contempt of court on the grounds (1) that the speech was likely to prejudice the Court and the public against the cause of the petitioners, and (2) that it was likely to have the effect of misrepresenting a piece of illegal legislation before the Court had an opportunity to decide the matter, and that the Chief Minister did "not like to use any affidavit showing cause". The petitioners contended that the speech amounted to defamation and that the action of the Chief Minister was mala fide. Held, that the speech must be made with a view to preventing the mischief or injury complained of by the person making it, and that if the object of the speech is to promote feelings of enmity or hatred between different classes of the citizens of India on grounds of religion, race, caste, community or language, it would be calculated to interfere with the due course of administration of justice. The object of the Act was to prevent the publication of the speeches which were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The object was to prevent people from resorting to violence and to insult their authority and dignity. The object could not be said to be to promote feelance of enmity or feelings of disaffection among members of the public or to lower down the esteem of one section of the people. The object can never be achieved without the support of law. The object may well be to secure obedience to the orders of the Court but the mere fact that the Chief Justice of the High Court has been moved by the Chief Minister after the order was passed does not make the speech bad merely because the Chief Minister had no intention to defend himself. The object is to prevent people against the Government from exercising their right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. The object cannot be said to have been achieved unless the Chief Minister knew what the object was and how he intended to achieve it. The object need not necessarily be to see that the object does not become oppressive or harmful to anyone. It is enough if the object is to promote feeling of enmity or interest

96: The appellant was charged with the murder of his wife and son. He was convicted under section 201, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to seven years rigorous imprisonment. The prosecution case was that Sardar Jaspal was administered potassium cyanide poison by the appellant and Mohinderpal Singh (a fugitive from justice) who was responsible for this. The prosecution evidence showed that the appellant and his father were not in a position to administer potassium phosphate to Jaspal and the evidence regarding the murder was purely circumstantial. The High Court acquitted the appellant but allowed the appeal of the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the convictions were based solely on circumstantial evidence and that the circumstances relied upon by the prosecution did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant or Mohinderpal had administered potassic phosphate at the deceased 's residence. It was further contended that the alleged confession made by the appellant was inadmissible in evidence as he was not examined by the police during investigation. HELD : (i) The High Court erred in holding that the circumstantial evidence in the case was incompatible with the innocence of the accused. The fact that the appellant was not examined in court was not conclusive of the guilt of the appellant. The appellant was entitled to an acquittal. [947 E] (ii) The High court was wrong in law in holding that there was no direct evidence to prove that the appellant had administered potash to Jaspal. The appellant could not be said to have been prejudiced because he was not produced before the trial court. The appellant had been given opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and if he failed to do so, the trial court would have been justified in acquitting him. [948 F H; 949 A B] (iii) The High Courts judgment was erroneous in law. The appellant did not produce any material to show that the appellant ever administered potassica phosphate. The appellant also did not produce the evidence that the deceased had died due to poisoning. The appellant has not been able to explain how the death of the deceased occurred. [950 C D] (iv) The High courts order was correct. [951 G]

333: The plaintiffs were partners of a firm known as Harnam Singh Jagat Singh. In the course of their business they used to make lump sum payments to the defendant against their purchases. When there was an adverse balance, the plaintiffs paid the defendant interest on the amount due and the defendant 's claim for interest was decreed for Rs. 12,496 6 6 and this was upheld on appeal to the High Court. The plaintiffs ' case is that they carried on business with the defendant company for some three or four years before 1947 and purchased cloth from the defendant ''s bankers. The defendant 's banker had no authority to sell the cloth. The plaintiffs flied a suit for recovery of Rs. 12496 6 7 and Rs. 1,000 respectively. The defendant admitted the facts set out above but pleaded that when India was partitioned on 15 8 1947, Lyallpur, where these transactions took place and where the money was situate, was assigned to Pakistan, and the Pakistan Government froze all evacuee assets and later compelled the defendant to hand them over to the Custodian of Evacuee Property in Pakistan. The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to recover the money under the contract of sale. Held, that the plaintiffs were not exonerated by the defendant from the liability of payment of interest under the contract. The contract of sale did not create any title in favour of the plaintiffs nor did it confer any title upon them. The contract was not voidable at the instance of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs were not entitled to recover interest on the money advanced by them. The plaintiffs could not be said to have been exonerated because the debt was not payable at the time of the contract of purchase. The plaintiffs had not acquired any title to the money advanced. The plaintiffs did not acquire any title to it. The plaintiffs are not entitled to sue for the money advanced as a security. The plaintiffs cannot be said to be exonerated merely because the debt is payable at the date of the contract.
904: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of carding and drawing embroidery. It had a factory at Bombay and its workmen were paid wages on piece rate basis. The company claimed that the workmen were entitled to receive from the company an additional amount of Rs. 1,000 as bonus for the year 1955, and that the company should pay to them an additional amount calculated at the rate of Rs. 2,000 per month. The company contended that the additional emoluments payable by way of production bonus and incentive bonus were " wages even if not ordinarily understood to be basic wage" and that the Government order did not require or justify the company in including the additional emoluments being paid by way of Production Bonus. Held, that the Government Order did not require the company to include the additional emoluments in calculating the rates of basic wages for the purpose of the order. The words " basic wages" in cl. 8 of the order did not mean " basic wages". The word " basic wages " is used in the sense of basic wages which means basic wages plus dearness allowance. The word " wages " does not necessarily mean basic wages. The word ' basic wages ' has been defined in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to mean " all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would, when fixed, give rise to some obligation or obligation attached to such employment." The word " minimum wages" in the definition of "wages" in the Industrial disputes Act, 1947 includes dearness allowance, and the Tribunal was right in holding that the company was liable to pay the additional amount of bonus.
2946: The appellant was appointed as Head Mistress of a school run by the Madras Government. She applied for recognition and aid to the school under the Madras Elementary Education Act, 1920. The High Court reversed the decree passed by the District Court and ordered that the appellant be reinstated into service. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the school was receiving grant in aid from the Government; (ii) the order passed by the Manager removing her from the post of Head Master was illegal because the Manager was bound by rr. 13 & 14 framed under the Madras Act, and (iii) the order of the District Educational Officer refusing to reinstate her was illegal because she was not given an opportunity of hearing before passing the order. HELD: (1) The order passed by a competent authority is a quasi judicial order and the order must be supported by reasons. It is only when the order is shown to be arbitrary or mala fide or based on wholly irrelevant grounds that the validity of the order can be challenged. [1066 D] (2) The order of the manager removing the appellant from the post was not bad because the Manager refused to give an opportunity of being heard before passing the same. The order was therefore bad. [1067 F] (3) The order was not vitiated by any error of law apparent on the face of it. [1068 B] (4) The order did not suffer from any infirmity. [1069 C] (5) The order does not violate Article 14 of the Constitution. [1070 E]

On the 3rd December, 1947 sanction was given by the Central Government under section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, for prosecuting the appellant. The appellant was produced before the Special Magis trate on the 28th of November, 1947, but he was released on bail on the 31st January, 1949. On the 31st of January, 1949, the Government appointed a Special Magi tate to try offences under the Act and on the 1st of December, 1947. the appellant was produced in court and was granted pardon. The case against the appellant was split up and the appellant was tried by the Special Judge. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had committed an offence punishable under section 161 I.P.C., and section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Preventionof Corruption Act, and section 5 (3) read with sections 161 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 161 and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that when the Magistrate issued the warrant of arrest on the 22nd of October, 1948, the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence under section 161 or 165 of the Code and section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, which is a penal provision, and therefore the order of the Magistrate dated the 22nd October, 1948 was illegal. HELD : The words "in respect of" in the proviso to section 6 of Act II of 1947 are very wide and include all cases where the accused person has been prosecuted for criminal misconduct. It is only when the Magistrate takes cognizance of the criminal misconduct under section 161 of the Indian Code that the bar of section 6 would apply. [801 D] Emperor vs Sourindra Mohan Chuckerbutty, , applied.

38: The appellant was tried before the Sub Divisional Magistrate of Guntur in respect of offences under the Motor Spirit Rationing Order, 1941. In the first case, the charges against him and the employee were that they on 27th June, 1945 at Guntur, supplied petrol to a cars without taking coupons, in contravention of clause 22 read with clause 5 of the Order promulgated under section 81 (2) of the Defence of India Rules and that they, on the same day and at the same place, accepted coupons relating to two other cars without taking vouchers, in contravention thereof. The plea of the appellant before the Magistrate was that he was the presiding officer of the sub divisional court, Chirala, that he was not guilty of an offence under rule 81 of the Defence Of India Rules, but was proved to have known of the unlawful acts of the second appellant. Held, that the conviction of the appellant for the offences under the Act was legal and valid. The conviction was not liable to be set aside merely because the appellant had been acquitted by the Sessions Judge. The acquittal was not honourable as it was based upon the evidence adduced by the prosecution which consisted of the testimony of the witnesses examined by the prosecution and the statements made by them during their examination. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the appellant was liable to be convicted for the offences charged.

2624: The appellants workmen employed in the respondent company were working as depots of the Company. They were doing the work of collecting tobacco, selling it at a small scale. On 16th August 1963, the Company gave a notice to the Union of the appellant workmen that out of 21 depots mentioned therein would be closed down with effect from 30th September, 1963. Thereafter, an industrial dispute was raised by the workmen which related to the closure of these depots. The State Government referred the dispute for adjudication under section 10(1)(d) of the to the Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad. The Tribunal held that the closure of the depots was not justified and directed the Company to pay compensation to the workmen. The Company challenged the award of the Tribunal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the closure was genuine and real and that the Tribunal had no power to adjudicate on it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal has rightly held that the reference did not amount to closure of business of the Company and that the Industrial Tribunal was right in its view that the closure is genuine and real. [880C] (ii)The Tribunal has given reasons for arriving at the conclusion that the closure took place bona fide and real. It cannot be said that the closure does not amount to retrenchment. [881D] (iii)The Tribunal was right when it came to the conclusion that there could not be any industrial dispute over such closure. The Tribunal also considered the evidence of the witnesses examined by the workmen and found that the closure did not amount either to closure or closure of business. [882E F] (iv)The Tribunal had given reasons for coming to the conclusion. [883F] Pipraich Sugar Mills Ltd. vs Pipraich Coal Corporation Ltd., Calcutta, ; , followed. (v)The Tribunal having given reasons for the decision, it cannot be said to have committed any error of law in interfering with the finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal. 3112: The respondent was a citizen of India and had applied for and obtained an Indian visa. He returned to Pakistan on April 25, 1954. On January 27, 1955 he again applied for and obtain a Indian visa which was valid upto January 26, 1955. But the Additional District Magistrate, Silchar passed an order No. 2155 dated December 31, 1947, releasing him from service with effect from January 26, 1950. The respondent then applied for and got a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. The Additional District Magistrate held that the respondent 's application was not maintainable as he had not been able to prove his citizenship and that he was not entitled to be registered as a foreigner. The respondent thereupon filed a revision petition before the High Court which allowed the revision holding that the respondent was a foreigner when he entered India in April 1955 and was not required to obtain a permit under cl. 7 of the Foreigners Order, 1948. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that the respondent having left India after March 1, 1950, could not be deemed to be a foreigner even if he had migrated to Pakistan during the period between March 1, and January 26, 195 1; (ii) that the Additional District magistrate erred in taking into account the fact that the respondent had left India for Pakistan in August 1947 after he had served out the sentence of imprisonment; and (iii) that the High Court should have relied on Fida Hussain 's case (1). HELD : (i) The High Court was right in its view that the respondent could not be said to be a foreign national when he left India for Africa. It is true that the respondent did not leave India for Pakistan but he had gone to Pakistan by air. If he had returned to Pakistan, he would have been a foreigner within the meaning of section 2(e) of the Act. But the fact that he had left India after he had left the country cannot lead to the inference that he was a forever person. [867 B C] (iii) The respondent
490: The respondent company was carrying on life insurance business and the appellant issued annual fire insurance policies and received a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as premiums thereof, the whole of it would be shown as income in the statement for the year 1939, and a sum of r. 2 of Sch. 11 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, provided that "the profits of a business other than life insurance for the chargeable accounting period ending December 31, 1940, and December 31, 1941, shall, subject to the provisions of this Schedule, be computed on the principles on which the profits of a company are computed for the purposes of income tax under section 10 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and the balance remaining after deducting the depreciation actually allowed to the assessee during the previous years." The premium was paid for the purpose mentioned in the policies. [643 A] (vi) The High. Court
3116: The appellant was tried for offenses under section 120B IPC. He was acquitted by the special judge, Ganganagar. The State of Rajasthan filed an appeal against the acquittal of Ram Swaroop and Bhagat Ram in respect of all the charges. The High Court dismissed the appeal against the conviction of Ram Swaroo P. for offenses Under section 161 IPC. The State appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the case against him had not been proved and the State appeal in that respect also was liable to be dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [306C] 2. The evidence of the two witnesses clearly established that the appellant had demanded bribe from Puran Chand. The evidence clearly showed that Puran Chand had agreed to extort Rs. 7000 from Niranjan Dass and as such were guilty of an offence under section 161 IPC and 5 (1) (a) of Prevention of Corruption Act. Court was wrong in coming to the conclusion that the material was insufficient to establish the charge. [309F G]
3668: The appellant was the sole proprietor of a Hindu Undi vided family consisting of himself and his wife. In the assessment year 1955 56, the Income tax Officer passed an order under section 25A(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, directing the Income tax officer to partition the joint family property in accordance with the partition made by the High Court. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order on the ground that the order was without jurisdiction as it was not made in conformity with the provisions of section 25A of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order could be challenged only by way of appeal under section 25B of the Act and not by way of writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order is not made in violation of the principles of natural justice. [116G] (2) The order does not give any reason for refusing to record partition and direct the Income tax authorities to make a partition. It merely directs the Income tax Authorities to record the partition and to proceed to recover the taxes so assessed. [117C D] (3) The order cannot be said to have been made in breach of principles of natural jus tice. The order is made in exercise of the power conferred upon the Income tax Officers under section 25 A of the Act, and is not in the nature of administrative or quasi judicial orders. [118D] (4) The order has to be made in conformity wit h the provisions of the Act which governs the case. [119F] (5) The order can be challenged only under article 226. [120E]
2272: The respondent Club was carrying on the business of running two race courses, one in Bombay and the other at Poona. It obtained a licence from the Government of Maharashtra for a period of 30 years commencing from June 1, 1948 at an annual rent of Rs. 3,75,000. The respondent Club had obtained a licence to hold racemeetings at both the bars and for which it paid a sum of Rs. 22 lacs as licence fees. The respondent club was assessed to tax under section 154(2) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, by the Deputy Municipal Commissioner who is the assessing authority disallowing the expenses actually incurred by the respondent Club. The respondent filed an appeal before the Small Cause Court, Bombay, under section 217 of the Act. The Small Cause Court allowed the appeal holding that the proper method for determining the annual rent was the profits basis method but upheld the respondent 's objections as regards the disallowance of the several items of expenditure. The High Court held that considering the unique nature of the use of the premises by the Club, the proper method of determination of the annual rent being the profits basis, the proper way of fixing the net rateable value under section 154 (1) would be to deduct therefrom the percentage deduction allowable under section 15.4 of the Act, and not to add the same to the gross annual rent. In this appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in its view that considering the peculiar nature of the user of the premises, the proper methods for determination of the rent were the profits basis. [1301 G] (ii) The High court was wrong in holding that the method adopted by the respondent was not correct. The High court has rightly held that the proper way for determining the rent is to deduct therefrom all the expenses incurred by the landlord in connection with the race course. [1302 B C] (iii) The High Courts decision is based on the assumption that the proper test for determining the amount of rent is the profits or income of the property. [1303 D E] (iv) The High courts decision is based upon the assumption that if the premises are let out for the purpose of trade, the rent will be the real consideration. [1304 F]
364: The petitioners, who were the owners of the disputed properties, filed a suit against the State Government and the State Government for declaration that the properties had vested in the State under the provisions of the 990 Bihar Land Reforms Act 1950. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act declaring that the estate of the petitioners was vested in the state. On the date of vesting the disputed properties stood on the land in the notified estate. The petitioners claimed that they were the owners only of the disputed lands and not of any building on it. The State contested the claim contending inter alia that the properties did not vest in the State on the publication of the notification under section 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1950. The question whether the properties stood on land which was used as office or cutchery for the collection of rent of such estate was a mixed question of law and fact. Held, that the property was not land within the meaning of section 2(g) of the , and the notification under s. 3(1), therefore, could not be challenged on the ground that it was not published in the Official Gazette. The word "land" in the context means land which is capable of being converted into an ordinary building. The word 'land' in the context must mean something which is capable or capable of being brought into existence at some point of time before the acquisition. The word land has been defined in the General Clauses Act to include buildings, houses, structures and other things attached to such buildings. The word is used in the sense of a building or a house, or a share of a building in a building. The expression "land" includes both movable and immovable property. The word must be construed ejusdem generis with the word "land". The word "lands" in the General Clause Act means land which has been used immediately previous to the date of the vesting. The word has been used in the context of the Act and the word "building" in the definition of "estate" in the Bihar Land Reform Act, 1950, has been defined to include buildings and houses. The word means buildings and houses does not include buildings and house sites. The word includes buildings and houses cannot be confined to buildings and
2670: The assessee was a registered shareholder in the assessment year 1945 45. In the accounting period of the previous years, the assessee received certain dividends and the assessee credited the same to its profit and loss appropriation account and thereafter transferred the same to a reserve fund in the accounting year ending September 30, 1955. The assessee claimed that as the arrear dividends pertained to the years 1945 to 1954, the amount of Rs. 43,925/ should be treated as dividend and should therefore be assessed under section 12 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not claimed any dividend income from the shares held by it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee acquired the shares on which the arrear dividends were paid in the accounting period amounted to Rs. 43 925/ and that the assessee was not liable to tax. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1922 is not applicable to the facts of the case. [857 C] (ii)The assessee was entitled to deduct the sum of Rs.43,925/- from the profits and gains of business arising out of the assessee 's share dealing business. The assessee was not entitled to the deduction of the said sum. [858 D] (iii)Section 12 of the Act does not apply to the facts and circumstances of the case because the assessee was a member of the assessee firm. The assessee had been carrying on the business of shares and securities and had been receiving dividends from the companies. The assessee did not have any interest in the shares or securities. It was only a shareholder who had received the dividends. The assessee could not be regarded as a registered shareholder for the purpose of section 12 of Income tax Act. [859 E F] (iv)In the instant case, the assessee was entitled only to the benefit of section 12(1)(b) of the Act. [885 G]
5086: The assessee, a company owned an estate from which it derived agricultural income liable to be assessed in the year 1963 64. In assessment proceedings for the year 1963 63, the assessees claimed a deduction of Rs.33,747.09 from their agricultural income on the ground that it was payable towards interest on a loan of Rs.4,00,000 taken by them from M/s. Associated Planters Ltd., and credited to the revenue accounts of the assessees. The assessing authority brought the amount to tax. The Tribunal held that it was not agricultural income. The High Court took the view that it was immaterial that the assessees followed the mercantile system of accounting, because the case was not one of actual receipt or any receipt at all but only one of remission. The High court also held that it could not be considered as amounting to the receipt of agricultural income. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. Section 3 of the Kerala Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950 provides that agricultural income shall be charged for each financial year on the total agricultural income of the previous year of every person at the rates specified in the Schedule. It is not disputed that the interest allowed to be deducted in the assessment of the present assessees fell under one of those clauses and was, therefore, rightly deducted in computing their agricultural income. [168B] 1.2. The remission in the present case could not amount to agricultural income. It was not necessary that the assessee should have paid the interest to the assessee. The remission cannot amount to agricultural incometax. [169C D] 2.1. The High Courts decision and after exhaustively surveying several decisions came to the conclusion that the remission in the case could not be treated as amounting to agricultural income and that it did not arise from the agricultural operations carried on by the assessees. [165E] 2.2. In the instant case, the High Court has taken the view that the remission cannot amount either to agricultural income or to agricultural income within the meaning of section 3 of the Act. [166F]
6032: The respondents were declared evacuee property under the Act. They filed an application before the Custodian General for restoration of their properties to them on the ground that they had migrated to Pakistan during the disturbances of 1947 and continued to live there as an evacuee. The Custodian rejected the said application holding that the application was not maintainable since the property was evacuee property and belonged to one Shah Mahmood who had migrated from Pakistan during the disturbed period of 1947 and had continued to live in the house allotted to him. The respondents preferred a revision petition before the High Court which dismissed the same by its order dated 5.2.1973. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 8 of the Evacuee (Administration of Proper ty) Act, 2006 has no application to the facts of the present case because the property was not evacuee property. [474C] 1.2 In the instant case, the property was admittedly evacuee property and it was not evacuee land. The Custodian had rightly held that the sale was invalid since the property had been acquired by the State Government after the Act came into force. [475D] 1.3 The High Court was justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact rendered by the Custodian and the Custodian General. [476E] 2.1 The High Court is right in observing that the property was an evacuee property and hence the possibility of a person having migrated to India cannot be ruled out. [477F] 3.1 The question whether the property was a evacuee property or not must depend upon the nature of the property. If it is a evacuee property, it would continue to be an evacuee property even now. [478G]
1432: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 149 and section 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. They challenged their convictions in appeal to the High Court which set aside the convictions and acquitted them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Court had erred in holding that the eye witnesses had seen the occurrence; (ii) the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable as there was no other witness who could have been present at the time of the occurrence; and (iii) the High Courts ' findings were perverse and should be interfered with. HELD: (1) There is no legal bar for convicting a person under section 302 I.P.C. if the murder has been committed in a dwelling house belonging to the husband or to any member of his family. [947 E] (2) The High Court was right in holding that there was no reason why the eye witnesses should have been present when the occurrence took place. [948 F] (3) The High Courts ' finding that the eye witness had seen the incident and their evidence must be accepted but there are certain circumstances proved by the evidence of eye witnesses which, when considered substantially affect the force of the finding in regard to oral evidence and which have to be considered in order to adjudicate on the correctness or otherwise of the prosecution case. [949 C D] (4) The High court was wrong in holding that in the absence of any independent witness the trial court could not have recorded the statement of the eye witness. [950 A B]
3853: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. He was also convicted under section 302 I.P.C. for causing the murder of one Hari Singh, who was a distant relative of the deceased. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the evidence of the eye witness Hari Singh and Chandra Pal was not reliable; (ii) the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt; and (iii) the conviction was based solely on the testimony of the eye witnesses. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The evidence of Hari Singh and Chander Pal is corroborated by the medical evidence. The first information report was written by Bharat Singh at 8.00 p.m. on the dictation of Hari Singh. The injured witness Hari Singh stated that he went to the place of the incident with his cot and the torch was burning. The doctor found two injuries caused by fire arm on Chandra Pal and one injury on Hari Singh. This resulted in Deena being killed. The evidence clearly established that Hari Singh and Chandan Singh were the persons who shot Hari Singh. There was no reason why the other two accused should have been falsely implicated. [108 B C] 2. The evidence establishes that Hari Singh was one of the assailants who fired his pistol. The fact that the deceased was shot dead shows that he was an interested witness. The evidence does not establish that the deceased died as a result of the gun shot injuries received by him. The evidence further indicates that the deceased fell down after receiving the gunshots injuries. The evidence also shows that the deceased sustained injuries as a result thereof. The evidence thus establishes that Hari was one of those who shot the deceased. [109 D E]
3072: The Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (Amendment) Act, 1970 was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 26(2) of the Constitution. By section 55 of that Act, the State Government made rules providing for qualifications to be possessed by the Archakas or Mathadhipatis of some ancient Hindu Public temples in Tamil Nadu. Section 55 provided that every 'ulthurai servant ' whether hereditary or nonhereditary whose duty it was to perform pujas and recite mantras, vedas, prabandams, thevarams and other invocations shall, before succeeding, or appointed to an office holder, obtain a certificate of fitness from the head of an institution imparting instructions in Agamas and ritualistic matters and recognised by the Commissioner, by general or special order or from the head or head of a math recognised by the commissioner by general or specific order or from any other person as may be designated by the Commissioner. Under this rule making power the State Government had made the Madras Hindu Religious Institutions (Officers and Servants) Service Rules, 1964. Rule 12 provided that every "ulthoivasal" servant, whether hereditary or not, who was entitled to appoint a fit person to perform the functions of the office or service after having due regard to the claims of the members of the family, Power to make rules providing for the qualifications to be accomplished, and the like, were given to the Commissioner, from time to time, for the purpose. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Charitable Institutions (Officings and Servants) Services (Amendment) Ordinance, 1970 on the ground that it violated their fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(g), 19(6), 25 and 26 of the Constitution of India. It was contended that the provisions of the Principal Act applied only to those institutions which were established for religious worship and not to all such institutions which were not established for religious purposes. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the principal Act are not applicable to the institutions established for religious ceremonies and observances. [819G] 2. The provisions relating to appointment of office holders and servants in the religious institutions do
5205: The petitioners in the writ petitions were employed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They were appointed by the Government of Andhra Pradesh on deputation from the State Government to the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission. Their services were governed by the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, r/w Rule 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Government Servants 'Service Rules, 1975. The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Organisation of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order, 1975 was issued under Article 371 D of the Constitution. The petitioners challenged the validity of this order before the Administrative Tribunal. The Administrative Tribunal held that the Administrative Tribunal had no jurisdiction to deal with the service matters specified in the order of transfer and accordingly dismissed the petition. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by the High Court holding that the Administrative Tribunals constituted under the Andhra Pradesh Act were competent to deal with service matters specified therein. The petitioners contended that the Administrative Tribu nal had no power or authority to pass an order modifying or nullifying the decision of the Administrative Tribunal and that the Administrative tribunal had no jurisdiction. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Administrative Tribunals created under the Andhra pradesh Act are competent enough to deal with all cases coming within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunals. [886C] 2. The Administrative tribunals created under the Act have been given the powers of judicial review. It is not at all possible to say that the Administrative Trus ts created under the statute are not effective or efficacious because the State Government can defeat its exercise by just passing an order modifying, or nullifying its decision. [886D E] 3. The Administrative Tribun al has got the power to modify or annul any order passed by it. But the power of judicial review conferred on the Administrative Tribunal is by reason of the Proviso to Clause (5) of Article 371 D subject to the veto of the State Government and it is not at par with the power of Judicial Review. [887E F] 4. The Administrative Tri bunal has got the same power as the Administrative Tribunal under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. [888G H; 889A B] 5.
5302: The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the sale deed executed by her mother in favour of the appellants was invalid and was not binding upon him. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that the alienation was not something which a man of ordinary pru dence would have effected had the properties been owned by him and thus held it not binding on the plaintiffs. In second appeal, the appellants contended that the question of improvements having been concluded by the judgment of the High Court in the second appeal, they were not bound to make any improvement and hence could not be ordered without payment of the value of improvements. The High Court rejected this contention holding that the alienation being not something which is prohibited under section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act or Section 4 of the Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958, could not be made without payment of compensation. The appellants moved the High Court for grant of certificate of fitness. The High court allowed the appeal and granted the decree directing delivery of the properties from the possession of the Judgment debtors. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The High Courts decision does not lay down the correct law. [875C] 2.1. It is well settled that the provisions of the Transfer o f Property Act are not applicable to proceedings under the said Act unless the provisions of that Act are complied with. The provisions of the said Act do not apply to proceedings under that Act. [876D] 2.2. The High courts decision does not give rise to any substantial question of law. [887E] 3.1. In the instant case, the High Courts decision is based on the finding that in case of eviction, the defendants would be entitled to Rs.4,164 as compensation for improvements. His further submission is that the appellants were tenants within the meaning of Section 2(d) of the Kerala Preferential Ownership Act, 1957. [886F G] 2.3. The High Cour t has held against the appellants with the following observation: "The basis of the claim has not been stated anywhere, and no averments of fact necessary for attracting Section 51 of the Act or Section
5814: The petitioners in this case were appointed as Assistant Engineers (Civil) in the Central Public Works Department and were promoted to the post of Executive Engineer. They were promoted to higher posts on the basis of seniority subject to fitness. The Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs issued a letter dated 11.7.1968 stating that the policy regarding reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in posts filled by promotion/promotions on the basis Of seniority subject to suitability was being adopted by the Government of India in supersession of all earlier orders issued from time to time. In the said letter it was also stated that the Government had decided to implement the policy contained in the letter dated 23.12.1983. The petitioners challenged the aforesaid order before the High Court contending that the Government of Indias decision to adopt the policy contained therein was not applicable to the present case because the Government had not taken into consideration the fact that the scheme of reservation of posts for Scheduled Castes & the Scheduled Tribes in the posts filled by promotions/promotion was introduced only after the issuance of the letter dated 11th July, 1968. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Government could not have taken into consideration any other material which would be relevant for the purpose of determining whether the Government had considered the matter objectively or properly. The present appeal is against the judgment of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government of India has taken a conscious decision to adopt a policy of reservation in the posts of Assistant Engineers (Civ.) in the Central Engineering Services (MES). This policy was adopted by the Union of India in consultation with the Ministry of Law and Justice. [628B] 1.2 The Government of Indian has taken a decision to adopt this policy in respect of the recruitment to the post in question. The Government has taken a policy decision to give effect to the policy of reservation of the posts in the Central services. The Government cannot take a stand that the policy of reservations of posts in the State services should be made applicable only to the Central services and not to the Central Services. [629E F] 1.3 The Government of india has taken the decision to give an opportunity to the employees belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes
4741: The petitioners who were registered as lottery tickets of the State of Maharashtra, had been selling lottery tickets in the State of Madhya Pradesh. They had been selling lotteries organised by the Government of India or the Government of a State. The Government of Maharashtra imposed a ban on the sale or distribution of lottery tickets of other States without the express consent of the State Government. The ban was not for the purpose of carrying out the policy of prohibition but only for the purpose to prevent the sale or the distribution of lottery ticket in any manner. The ban is sought to be spelt out from a Press release of the Director of Publicity, Sachivalaya, Bombay dated September 24, 1970 addressed by the Government Of Maharashtra to some of the petitioners individually. 1089: The appellants were assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1945 46 on the basis of their profits and gains. The Income tax Officer, in his order dated March 31, 1945, accepted the return of the company as valid and the excess profits tax was also worked out on the same basis for the chargeable accounting period ending March 31, 1946. The appellants filed a petition under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, challenging the validity of the order of assessment on the ground that the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to take action under section 34 of the Act. The High Court held that the Income Tax Officer could not take action under s. 34 of the Income tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, but he should have taken action under section 15 of the Act before he took action under section 1 8 of the Act and that the Income 'tax Officer was not competent to do so. Held, that the Income-tax Officer was right in taking action under section 23A of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The provisions of section 23A are mandatory and they must be strictly complied with if they are not observed. The words "in accordance with" in section 23A(2)(b) mean that the Income Commissioner is bound to follow the procedure prescribed by the law for the purpose of making an order under section 23 A. The Income Tax Officer cannot take action under the said section after he has made the order under section 1 6(2). The Income tax officer can take action only when he has reason to believe that the income of the assessee has been concealed or has been suppressed. The Income 'tax officer can take such action only when there is some material on which it could be established that the income has been supplanted or has been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. The Income-tax officer can act on the basis that the income had been suppressed or that there has been suppression of any fact. The Income, tax Officer can take action under sections 23A and 23B only when there exists a reasonable belief that the income was derived from property belonging to the assessee. The Income. tax officer can proceed to assess the income without resort to the procedure laid down in the Act.

It is true that the notice must contain the name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff, but the fact that the notice has been delivered or left at the office of the defendant cannot be said to be conclusive proof of the service of the notice. 532: The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police in the State of Bihar. He was dismissed from service by an order dated December 20, 1948. The order of dismissal was confirmed by the Inspector General of Police on June 7, 1949. On April 22, 1950, the respondent filed a revision application under section 435 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the High Court challenging the order of his dismissal and the order of the Inspector General dismissing him as being bad. The High Court allowed the revision application holding that the order of dismissal passed by the District Superintendent of Police on December 20, 1947, had not become final until the Inspector General had given his assent to it and that the order had been validly made by the District Sup erintendent of Police. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court erred in law in interfering with the order of dismiss al of the respondent. The High court could not interfere with the order merely because the subordinate court or tribunal had taken a different view of the matter than the one which had been taken by the subordinate court. [608 B] (ii) The High court was wrong in its view that the order passed by the Inspector general of Police on May 7, 1949, had become final until he gave his assent to the order of punishment. The High 'Court was wrong in holding that the Inspector General could not be said to have acted without authority. [611 C D]
2083: The Mysore Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1957, were made by the Governor of Mysore under article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 4(2) provided that the Commission may invite Government to nominate an officer to represent the service or the Department for whom recruitment is being made to be present at the interview referred to in clause (3) to assist the Commission in its work of selection. The High Court held that the words "shall be as set forth in the rules of recruitment" in r. 4(1) of the Mysore State Civil Services General Recruitment Rules, 1957 and the other sub rules are really administrative arrangements apparently arrived at between the Commission and the Government as to how the Government and the Public Service Commission will take steps to recruit persons for the State Services or posts. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The words "shall he as set forth" in rr. 3 and 4 mean that till the rules are made in that behalf no recruitment can be made to any service. The High court was therefore right in holding that r. 4 did not apply to the case of the Mysore Public Service Commissiion. [158 D E]
1631: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, executed an agreement to sell the property in favour of the respondent. The respondent made a gift of the property to his wife and two children. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of the agreement. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court reversed the decision of the courts below holding that the appellant had not obtained a valid title to the equity of redemption by the sale deed in his favour. In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the respondent 's right to redeem the property under the agreement was not extinguished by reason of the fact that he did not obtain any legal title to the property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the respondent had obtained a valid right to the equity or not is essentially a question of fact which has to be decided on the basis of evidence adduced before the court. [539E] 2. The question as to whether the respondent could have obtained a valid mortgage decree of the District Court, Trivandrum, in his favour, is a pure question of fact depending upon the facts of each case. [540F] 3. The question of limitation does not arise in the instant case because the respondent had not obtained any legal title from the appellant. [541G] 4. The question about the validity of the sale deed is a mixed question of law and fact. It is open to the parties to lead evidence in support of their respective cases. [542A] 5. The question regarding the validity of a sale deed arises only when the parties are ad idem on the question of title. [543B]
6788: The appellant imported the goods detected defects and the foreign supplier accepted the defects. The Assistant Collector of Customs, after considering the report of the expert, rejected the refund application on the ground that the damage was discovered after the goods were out of customs control. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Collector of Customs which was dismissed by the Collector of Central Excise on 23.12.1982. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Collector of Excise dated 19.7.1982. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the damage suffered by the appellant was not due to any wilful act or omission on his part but it was due to the negligence of the importer. The Division Bench of the High court held that the appellant was entitled to the refund of the customs duty paid under Section 22 of the Act for reasons set out therein. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended for the appellant that the appellant is entitled to the benefit of Section 22 of The Act for reasons given in the judgment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant is entitled for refund of customs duty on account of the compensation given by the seller to the appellant on supply of goods. [817E] 1.2 The appellant had claimed that it would be entitled to refund of customs duties under Section 22 if the goods were found to have been damaged at any time prior to the import when the assessment has to be on the basis of the real value of goods. The appellant had not disputed the finding of the Assistant Collector that the damage had become due to any deliberate act of omission or commission on the part of the importer or his agent. The appellant was not liable to pay any amount as the loss suffered by it was not due. [818F G] 1.3 The appellant was entitled for refund. [819G]
4749: The petitioner was a Judge of Madhya Pradesh High Court. He retired from service on 31st January, 1982. On the recommendation of the High Court he was paid an amount of Rs. 2,000 by his communication dated July 17, 1982. The Accountant General of Madhya Pradesh authorised the petitioner to draw cash equivalent of leave salary in respect of the period of earned leave at their credit subject to the ceiling of five months. The petitioner informed the Accountant General that he was drawing the amount as indicated in the communication without prejudice to his right to claim Rs. 24,000 to which sum under the law he was entitled. The petitioner made representation to the Government for release of the balance payment but it was rejected. The petitioner moved this Court by way of special leave. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the provisions of section 5 (3) of the Act, the limit has to be confined to five months equal to 150 days and not 120 days as in Rule 20B. [657E] 1.2 The petitioner is entitled to the benefit of rule 20B of the Leave Rules. The petitioner is also entitled to interest on the amount due to him. [658A B] 1.3 The petitioner is not entitled to any relief. [659C] 1.4 The petitioner is, therefore, entitled to the benefits of the leave rules. [660D] 1.5 The petitioner is directed to pay the difference between the amount payable to him and the amount already paid to him. The arrears shall be paid to him within two months. [661G] 1.6 The petitioner is held entitled to interest @ 6% per annum on the amount withheld from the date of retirement till the date of payment. [662F]

1550: The appellant was the owner of a car which met with an accident. The car was insured against a policy issued by the Bharat Fire & General Insurance Co., Ltd., and the policy was due to expire sometime in April, 1953. The car met with an unnatural death on February 9, 1953. On March 10, 1953, the appellant made a claim for compensation under section 4(1) (d) of the , and the claim was repudiated by the Insurance Company on the ground that the car had not been insured against a valid insurance policy. The appellant contended before the High Court that the concept of fraud would include not only deceit but also some injury to the person deceived and that the appellant could not be found guilty under any one of those sections. The High Court held that the concept was not applicable to cases where the accident occurred within the meaning of section 464 of the Indian Penal Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the concept would include not merely deceit but other injury to the persons deceived and as in the present case the appellant had never had the intention to cause injury to the insurance company and as in her own name she was entitled to compensation under section 464. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the concept did not apply to cases where there was no actual injury caused at all to the person who died or injured. [598 D] The word "fraud" is used in the wider sense in which it is understood in law. It includes not only deceive but also some wrongful gain. It may mean either a wrongful loss or a wrongful withholding of something. It does not include any wrongful gain. The word "wrongful gain" has been defined in section 24 of the Code to include any fraudulent or dishonest gain or an unfair or unlawful act done to a third party. The word 'fraud' is not defined in the Act. It is well known that the word "fault" is not defined. It means a deliberate and conscious failure to do something which a reasonable man, guided upon the facts in issue or probabilities, willfully exceeded the right of doing. It is a concept which requires consideration of various aspects such as whether the wrong was done to the insured or not
273: The respondent, a national of Pakistan, was allowed cash credit limit of rupees three lakhs by the Central Bank of India Ltd. on the 23rd June, 1947, shortly before the partition of India, and thereafter acquired the status of a citizen. On the application of the respondent, the bank filed a complaint against him under sections 380 and 454, Indian Penal Code, and also under section 412 of the Code before the District Magistrate of Gurgaon. The trial magistrate held that the respondent had acquired the citizenship of Pakistan and accordingly convicted him under sections 406 and 420, Indian Penal code, and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent could not be tried in India as he was a national of India and therefore the offence committed by him was an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life. HELD : (i) The respondent was a national within the meaning of section 2(d)(ii) of the Indian Penal Code. He was a national in the sense that he was a citizen of India at the time when the offence took place. [708 D] (ii)The respondent was a foreign national and therefore the question whether he was a foreigner within the meaning Of section 2(c) of the Act did not arise. [709 B C] (iii)Section 412 of Indian Penal Code is applicable only if the person who has been a foreigner is a citizen of Pakistan. It does not apply to a person who has ceased to be a citizen of Nepal. [701 E F] (iv)The respondent had no right to continue to hold the bank account of the appellant. His name was struck off from the account maintained by the Bank. [702 A B]
387: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 435 and 436 of the Indian Penal Code. They pleaded that they had been wrongly convicted by the Assistant Sessions Judge, but the High Court disagreed with the jury on the question whether the charge was defective or not. Held, that the convictions were wrong in law and the appeal must be dismissed. The trial court had jurisdiction to convict the appellants for offences under sections 427 and 436 read with section 34 of the Indian penal code. The trial Court had no power to alter the sentence without giving due weight to the opinions of the assessors. The evidence was such which could be relied upon by the prosecution and if it was found that the assessors had given false evidence, the conviction would have been upheld. The High Court had jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the trial court. The High Courts decision was correct and the appeals should be dismissed. A person who is tried for an offence under section 435 cannot be sentenced to imprisonment unless he has been acquitted. The High 'Court had jurisdiction to examine the correctness of the verdict of the jury and to give its own reasons for coming to a different conclusion. The High court had jurisdiction only to consider whether the verdict of guilt was justified.
6683: The appellant was prosecuted for offences punishable under the provisions of the Gold Control Act 1968.
