Sharma, Assistant Collector of Custom, against the appellant and two others. After examination of the prosecution witnesses and recording of the statements of the accused under Section 342 of the new Code (corresponding to Section 540 of the old Code) the Trial Magistrate allowed the application of the appellant for recalling the witness for further examination. The High Court allowed the second revision petition filed by the respondent and set aside the order of the Trial Magistrate allowing the two other complaints. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court has gravely erred in allowing the second revision petitions filed by the Union of India, which were also allowed by the High Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court should not have allowed the second revisional petition filed by Union of India without examining the case of the appellant as required by Section 540(2) of the Old Code. [717C] 1.2 The High Court ought to have considered the merits of the case and ought to have allowed the revision petition filed on behalf of the Union of Indian. [718D] 1.3 The High Court was wrong in permitting the prosecution to bolster up its case by filling up the lacuna and plugging the loopholes which if carried out would be detrimental and prejudicial to the appellant. [719E F] 1.4 The High Court could not have permitted the prosecution to fill up the lacunas which if carried through would be detrimental to the appellant, even though the case may be pending before the Trial Court for considerable length of time. [721G H] 1.6 The High Court is right in allowing the two applications of the Union Government and the State Government. [722A B]

The dismissal order was challenged by the workmen in the Industrial Tribunal which set aside the dismissal order on the ground that the enquiry was not proper and some of the witnesses were re examined before the Tribunal whose verdict was against the Company and hence this appeal. Held: (i) The Labour Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the order of dismissal under cl. 10(XVI) of the Standing Orders for the employees of the Dual Automobile Mills. The Labour Court could not have set aside the discharge order on the basis of the evidence adduced before it because the evidence was not properly appreciated. (ii)The Labour Court had jurisdiction to set-aside the dismissal order. The Labour Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction. (iii)The Labour Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with the decision of the Labour Court. (iv)The Labour Courts are not courts of limited jurisdiction but they are tribunals created by statute. (v)There is no provision in the Act which makes the award of an Industrial Tribunal unenforceable or void. (vi)The Labour Tribunals are not courts though they are invested with inherent powers. (vii)The Labour Tribunal can set aside the findings of fact recorded by the Labour Court if it finds that such findings are perverse. (viii)The Labour appellate Tribunal cannot go into the question whether the findings of facts are based upon no evidence or are perverse. (ix)The Labour court had no jurisdiction under cl.10(XVI). (x)The Labour courts are not courts subordinate to the High Court and therefore the jurisdiction of the Labour Courts is excluded. (xi)The Labour authorities are not courts within the meaning of section 2(k) of the Act. (xii)The Labour Authorities are not courts. 6474: The appellant, a resident of the State of West Bengal, was allotted a certain area in the Eastern India as a part of the Eastern India. The appellant challenged the validity of the said allotment by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the Calcutta High Court on the ground that the said allotment had been made without any Gazette Notification fixing any "appointed day" within the meaning of section 3(1) of the . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there being no Gazette Notification fixing the date of commencement of the Act, the same could not be held to have come into force and the appellant could not claim any benefit therefrom. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the notification dated 26th November 1949 issued by the Governor General under article 394 of the Constitution did not apply to the Eastern India and that the said notification was not applicable to the Eastern Indian territory. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The notification dated 26.11.1949 is not applicable to Eastern India. [939E] (ii) The notification does not purport to extend the operation of the Act to the Eastern Indi a but only to the Berubari Union which was situated in the Police Station Jalpaiguri. [940F] (iii) The Act was passed with the object of providing for the partition of the country and for the division of the area of the Eastern Indian Territory into two parts, namely, the Eastern India, and the Eastern India was to be divided into two parts. The Act was intended to provide for the division and integration of the areas in the two parts of the Eastern Indio. It was not meant to apply to the East India. [ 941A B] (iv) The Act has been enacted to give effect to the policy of the Government of India to secure to all its citizens 's rights and obligations under the Constitution. The Act is intended to be effective from the appointed day. [942C] (v) The Act is not intended to be operative from January 26, 1950. [943B C] (vi) The Act does not make any provision for the division or integration of the territories of the Eastern States into two parts of India. [993D

3630: The appellants purchased raw hides and skins as well as dressed hides and kins from the State of Bihar. The sales tax authorities included the sale price of those goods in the taxable turnover of the appellants. The appellants challenged the validity of items 7(a) and 7(b) of the Second Schedule to the State Act on the ground that they were not liable to be taxed under the Central Act. The High Court upheld the contention of the appellants but dismissed the writ petitions filed by the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The State legislature has power to levy tax on the purchase of raw hides or skins at the rate of 1 1/2 per cent under item 7(a). The local sales of dressed hide and skins are declared goods under section 14(i) of the Central Act and the State legisla ture is competent to impose tax on such purchases. [766 D] (2) The State legis lation is competent to levy tax only on the purchase value of raw hide and kins. [767 F] (3) The State Legislature has power to tax the purchase of goods other than raw hides, skins and dressed hood which are sold in the State. [768 A B] (4) The State law is a taxing statute. It is for the State to determine what should be the rate of tax. The State legislature cannot fix different rates of tax on the basis of the sale price. [769 C] (5) The State 's power to levy taxes on the purchase or sale of raw hull and skins is not subject to any limitations. [770 E]

3971: The appellants were importers of certain goods. They had imported the goods in question and paid for them on payment of customs duty according to the amended provisions of the Act. The Customs authorities, however, rejected their applications for refund on the ground that the amended provisions were applicable to the consignments in question. The appeals filed by the appellants before the Central Government failed. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the amended provision was not applicable to the goods which were imported into India and therefore the appellants could not be allowed to clear the goods without payment of duty. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The amended provision is applicable only to those goods which are imported into India. [766 F] (2) The rate of duty applicable to the imported goods has to be determined according to the law which was prevailing at the time when the goods were actually removed from the warehouse. If a bill of entry is presented before the date of removal of the goods, the proper duty payable would be the duty which would have been chargeable on the goods if they had been imported. [767 D E] (3) The amended section 14 of the , as it stood prior to its amendment, provided that "the rate of duty" or the tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the date of the presentation of the bill of entry. It was not disputed before us that the goods which are the subject matter of the appeals before us were cleared from the warehouse after the amending Ordinance came into force on July 7, 1966. Therefore, the amended provision would apply to the goods imported into India even though the goods were not imported within the period of limitation prescribed under the amended provision. [768 B C] (4) The amended provisions were not applicable to imported goods because the goods were imported into the country much earlier than the date of their import. [769 A] (5) The amended Section 14 of the Act does not affect the position as it stood before the amendment. The amended provision was applicable to the consignment in question because the goods which had been imported into India were not imported but were subsequently sold to the appellants. [770 B C]

7045: The petitioner, a police constable in the State of Orissa, was treated as a Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation made therein consequent upon his death. The said Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1st December, 1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police of Jaraikela Police Outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. The allegation made is that it is a case of custodial death since Suman Behal had died as a result of multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police custody; and thereafter his dead body was thrown on the railway track. The appellants contended before the High Court that they were entitled to be placed in the higher scale of Rs. 300 25 450/25 600 with effect from November 1, 1966, that they were not qualified to hold the post of Lecturer 's grade and that they should have been given the benefit of revised scales of Rs. 400 25 450/ 25 600 with effect form January 1, 1973. 5268: The respondent was appointed as a Subedar in the Central Reserve Police Force on 1.6.1976 and he was confirmed in the post of Commandant with effect from 20.9.1985. He applied for absorption in the Force. His application was accepted by the Director General of the C.R.P.F. and his services were absorbed w.e.f. 1.1.1986. He retired from service on 31.12.1987. The appellants, however, issued orders absorbing him in the Force, but he was not given any benefit of the said order. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for a direction to the appellants to consider his case for permanent absorption in the force. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that there was nothing in these rules to disentitle a retired or released army officer from absorption, directed the appellants to absorb him in the cadre with effect from the date the amended rule came into force and he was, therefore, entitled to the benefit of the amended provision from 20.09.1985. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal of the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In regard to the category of officers, benefit of absorption would be admissible only if they have put in continuous service of more than 20 years in the Force and it would be totally unjustified to deprive them of credit of service. [387B] 1.2 In regard to persons who are already in service, the benefit of absorption is not admissible. The respondent has been given a promotion and in the promotional post he had worked for about 16 years. Therefore, he should be deemed to have been absorbed in the cadre from the date of the amended rule coming into force. [388C D] 1.3 In regard to those persons who have been given temporary promotions, their past service shall be counted for the purpose of seniority. [385E]

159: The appellants were convicted under sections 297 and 500, Indian Penal Code, on the charge of trespassing upon a cremation ground. They filed a petition in the court of the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Uluberia, for taking cognizance of the offence. The Magistrate dismissed their application but he held that the offences were not triable by a Court of Sessions. The High Court set aside the order of conviction and acquitted them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the complaint did not disclose any offence of which cognizance could be taken by the magistrate because of the special provisions of section 195, Criminal Procedure Code, and (ii) the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offences mentioned in section 190, Criminal Procedure, Code, as the offences alleged were committed after the information given by the complainant was received at the police station and before the report was submitted to the Magistrate. HELD: (i) Section 195, Criminal procedure Code, is not applicable to the facts of the case. It applies only where the facts are disclosed in the complaint or information received by the police. [901 D] (ii) The Magistrate has no power to take cognizance if the facts stated in the complaint disclose an offence. [902 G] (iii) The Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence only when the complaint discloses a cognizable offence and not otherwise. [903 C] (iv) The Magistrate cannot take cognizance of any offence without a complaint in writing by some other person. [904 E]
2605: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of certain articles. It claimed a sum of Rs. 8,910/72 P as over time allowance for the period from 1st January 1964 to 30th June 1965 and cost of uniform at Rs. 40 each from 1st July 1964 to 30 th June 1965 in respect of 18 of those workmen. The Labour Court allowed the claim on the ground that the Act had no application to the appellant company. On appeal by the appellant company, the High Court held that the Act did not apply to the appellant and dismissed the writ petitions filed by the workmen. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act was a self contained Act making provision for relief in such cases, the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under the general Act, viz., the was taken away and excluded. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) Section 20(1) of the Act is an independent provision providing for relief in cases where the Act is a self contained one. [739 E] (2) The Act was a piece of social legislation making provision for remedy in such cases. The Act was enacted to provide for relief in respect of certain specified matters. The Act is a complete code relating to the remedies provided in the various labour laws. The Act has been enacted with a view to give effect to the policy underlying the Act. The Act does not exclude the jurisdiction of other courts or Tribunals. [740 F G] (3) The Act is not a self contained enactment dealing with the subject matter covered by the Act. It is a selfcontained Act dealing with the matters covered by the provisions of the Act. Therefore, the Act cannot be said to have any overriding effect on the provisions of section 20(1). [741 B C] (4) The Act being a self contained statute, the jurisdiction conferred upon the Labour Courts under the general law is not barred. [742 D]

The object of the provision is to give a fresh opportunity to the parties to adduce the same evidence as they may have done before the court. The object underlying the provision is that the accused should be given a fair chance of hearing after he is acquitted and after a punishment falls short of the authority of the law. [717D E] 5. The court has to take into consideration all relevant factors, and without giving any further details, the court cannot be justified in exercising its discretion in favour of the accused. [718F G] 6. The object behind the provision is not to punish the guilty but to make the criminal work more difficult. The provision does not provide for any formality to be observed by the trial judge. The provision is intended to meet special cases where the appellate court or the lower appellate court finds that the judgement of the trial court

The Selection committees are to be constituted of the Principal and Head of the institution. The selection is to be conducted by the
5006: The appellants were the owners of certain documents seized during the search. They were directed to deliver them to the respondent, who was the custodian of those documents. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the search and seizure made by the appellants on the ground that the said documents had been deliberately withheld from the authorities for reasons which are not relevant to the case. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was nothing illegal in the issuance of search warrant, the consequent search and taking over of the documents by the Income Tax Department under section 132A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent acted in a manner contrary to law in issuing a search warrant when there was no material before him on which he could entertain a reasonable belief that any documents which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any investigation or proceeding under the Act were secreted in the house of the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred on an officer of Enforcement is not to act arbitrarily but only according to the procedure prescribed. It is not a judicial discretion exercised by him. [766F] 2.1. The power to issue search warrant is not to be lightly interfered with except for compelling reasons. It is a discretionary power. It is to be exercised in public interest. [767G] 3.1. Section 132A of Income Tax Act confers power on an officer not below the rank of Assistant Director of Enforcement to search premises. The power is discretionary. [768C] 3.2. The power of search is not to bander the authority to seize the documents. It is only to facilitate the exercise of such power. [769D] 3.3. The power under section 132B of the Income tax Act is not to make search without a valid authorisation. [770E] 4.1. If the authority has reason to believe that any document which in his considered view would be useful for, or relevant to, any investigation or proceedings under the Act are secreted in any place, the authority cannot be said to have committed an error apparent on the face of the record. [771F]
6378: The workman was detailed to work in the first shift for picking up certain employees of the second shift and general shift. On that day, the management sought approval from the Industrial Tribunal, Karnataka at Bangalore under section 33(2)(b) of the Act of the action taken and towards meeting the requirement of the provision paid to him before hand a sum of Rs.607.90 as wages for one month, before hand a pavilion amount of Rs.6000. [993 G] (d) The two questions which arise for consideration are: (i) whether the two items fall within one or the other category of workmen specified in the Schedule to the Act; (ii ) if so, what is the nature of the employment, and (iii ) whether the employer has been given sufficient opportunity to put forth his case. [994 H; 975 A B]
5478: The appellant was appointed as a Principal of the College on January 27, 1986. She was suspended by the Vice Chancellor of the University on January 29, 1986 and an order of suspension was passed against her. The appeal filed by the appellant under section 68 of the U.P. State Universities Act, was dismissed by the ViceChancellor of the University. Thereafter, the Authorised Controller of the Institution issued a notice to the appellant asking her to show cause why she should not be removed from service. The appellant replied that she had been removed from service in exercise of the powers vested in him by Statute 17.06 of the Statutes of the University and that she would be entitled to continue in service till the end of the academic year. The High Court also directed the Authorised Controller to reinstate the appellant with full back wages. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the order of suspension did not amount to punishment within the meaning of section 68 of U.P., (ii) the order was passed by the Managing Committee without any authority or power; and (iii) the order being passed by the Registrar, the order could not have been passed by the Director of Higher Education. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of suspension does not amount to dismissal from service. [361F] 2. The order is not an administrative order. It is only an administrative order which can be challenged under Article 226 of the Constitution. [362B] 3. The order does not amount either to dismissal or removal from service. It is merely an administrative order and not a quasi judicial order. [363C D] 4. The order has no legal sanction. [364E] 5. The order cannot be sustained because the order is not made by the Director or the Managing Committee. [365G] 6. The order was passed in collusion with the Authorised Controller. The order passed by the Manager was not in accordance with law. [366D] 7. The order having been passed by a person who was not authorised to
2126: The appellant, a religious endowment, was the owner of certain properties in suit. The properties were acquired by the Government under the provisions of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. The properties in suit were held by the appellant as marfatdars and to have been acquired either by purchase or 'krayadan ' or by way of gift subject to the charge of some offering to Lord Jagannath. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Orissa, hereinafter called the Commissioner, demanded contribution under section 49 of the Act and took steps to enforce certain other provisions of the Act against the plaintiff and the properties in suit, and the Commissioner decided against him on July 20, 1952. The Commissioner found that the properties in dispute did not constitute 'public religious endowments ' within the meaning of the Act which applied to them. He therefore issued a writ directing the Commissioner to pay the contribution. The Commissioner filed an appeal before the High Court and contended that the properties were public religious endowments and were not private properties. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the properties had been acquired for the support of the institution which was partly of a religious and partly of secular uses and that the properties constituted a 'religious endowment ' within the definition of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the properties did not constitute "public religious endowments" within the meaning Of the Act and that the Commissioner could not be said to have been authorised to demand contribution under section 6(13) of the Act, and that the order passed by the Commissioner was illegal. HELD: (i) The property in dispute was not a public religious endowment but was a private property. It was not a private property and the Commissioner was not competent to issue a writ of mandamus directing the Commissioner. [440 D] (ii) The Commissioner was not entitled to ask for any direction from the court to the Commissioner to make payment of the contribution. [441 A] (iii) The Commissioner had no authority to direct the Commissioner to collect the contribution. He was merely exercising his powers under section 6 of the Act for the purpose of collecting the contribution. His acts were not judicial acts. [441 B C] (iv) The Commissioner could not claim to be a trustee of the temple
3656: The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the Municipal Corporation of Delhi. He made a written complaint to the Education Officer of the Corporation alleging therein that the appellant had been misbehaved with his son, while he was on duty at the time when he was posted at the school premises during the recess. On September 6, 1967, Dhan Raj made a written statement before the Deputy Commissioner (Education) stating that the appellant bad sensually misbehaved with him in the School Premises during the recession period and that he had not taken any action against the appellant for his misconduct. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition challenging the order of dismissal from service being a quasi judicial order. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the disciplinary authority having regard to its findings recorded by it as required by regulation 8(9) of the Regulations, could not have passed the order of removal from service. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned order of the High Court is set aside. [10] 2. The appellant has been dismissed from service under Regulation 8(9). The only conclusion at which one can arrive is that the dismissing authority has applied its mind and had provisionally come to some conclusion either way. The order of dismissal does not expressly state that the finding of the dismissing authority or the finding recorded by the enquiring officer are accepted by the appointing authority. It is only if the finding of guilt is accepted by the appellate authority that the delinquent employee would be able to challenge the correctness of the finding of fact. [11] 3. The appellant was given an opportunity to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The appellant did not avail of that opportunity. Therefore, the order of the dismissal was not valid. [12] 4. The appellant had no right to continue in service after the date of superannuation. The appellant therefore cannot claim that he should be reinstated in service. [13] 5. The appellant is entitled to reinstatement with full back wages. [14] 6. The appellant shall be deemed to have retired from service w.e.f. 31st March, 1971. The respondent shall pay to the appellant the amount of gratuity payable to him within three months from today. [15]
4018: The appellants filed a suit for declaration that the notification under section 4 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 was illegal and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents from proceeding with the acquisition of the lands in possession of the appellants. During the pendency of this suit the then Government of Bombay, after considering the report submitted under section 5A of the Land acquisition (Amendment and Validating) Act, 1966 declared, inter alia, that final plots 41, 43 were required for the purpose of State Transport. The legislature had therefore provided that in case of a notification under sections4 and 6, the apprehended arbitrary exercise of power is thwarted and the Court should not further restrict or curtail the power of the Government to issue notification under sections 3 and 4. [876D E] 1.3. The Government could have issued a fresh notification under section 3 of the Land acquiring Act, 1894, after the expiry period of two years prescribed therein. But the Government did not do so. [877F G] 1.4. The Government cannot go behind the notification under s.6 and say that the notification was bad because the notification was
547: The appellant company was a public limited company. On November 20, 1952, an occurrence took place in the said house where the respondents were involved. An industrial dispute between the parties was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The respondents filed their application under section 33 of the , before the Labour Appellate Tribunal for permission to discharge the respondents from its employ with effect from the date of the order on payment to the respondents of one month 's pay in lieu of notice. The appellant contended that the dismissal of the respondents was illegal and bad as it had not been made by the appellant within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act. Held, that the dismissal was illegal and void ab initio. The word "retrenchment" has not been defined in the Act but it is well settled that the definition of the term "retrenchment", which includes termination of service by way of punishment or otherwise, must be given the same meaning as in the ordinary acceptation of the word "termination" used in the definition clause. The word retrenchment means the termination of service of an employee either by way of penalty or on account of the non-payment of his wages or of the remuneration payable to him during the period of his employment. The word 'retrenchment' is not confined to termination of service simpliciter; it extends to termination of the service itself. It does not include termination of service for any misconduct or other oblique reason. The word retrenched is not confined only to termination of services by way of disciplinary action or punishment. The word termination of service is not intended to give protection against disciplinary action. The word `retrenchment' has not been used in the Act. The word is used in the wider sense to cover termination of service without proper sanction or without due process of law. The word has been used in a comprehensive sense to cover all kinds of termination of service except those mentioned in cls. (a), (b) and (c). The word retrenchment has not been held to mean termination of service. The word transfer is used in a wider sense to include termination of services of an employee on account of misconduct or inefficiency. The word appointment is not used in the narrow sense of termination of services simpliciter. The word may also have different meanings depending

[98C D] 4. The expression includes a person who holds or has held any office including that of a member of the armed forces of the Union or any post connected with the defence of India, or who is a member of any armed forces of any Union or of any service or post connected with defence of India. [99E F] 5. The expression used in section 14(l)(a
347: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life under section 302 I.P.C. and a fine of Rs. 100/. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that he had an opportunity to show cause against his conviction but nobody will contend that because he had lost the appeal in the High Court he could not be heard at that stage to defend himself when the State or other interested person applied to the High court in revision under section 439(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, for enhancement of the sentence. HELD: (i) The right conferred by section 439(6) is absolute and unqualified and does not exclude the jurisdiction of the appellate court to enhance the sentence. [1019 D] (ii) The right to appeal is a creature of statute and its exercise can be controlled only by law made by the legislature. It cannot be exercised so as to nullify the provisions of the statute which are otherwise valid. [1099 E] (iii) The right of appeal is a substantive right and the procedure prescribed by the statute has to be followed before any statutory remedy of revision is availed of. If the accused has been deprived of his right of appeal under the statute then the procedure laid down by the statute must be followed. [1097 F G]
1969: The assessee company was a firm carrying on the business of land development in Calcutta. By an agreement dated July 7, 1948, the partners of the firm agreed to sell all the business of the firm and the sale consideration was fixed at Rs. 2,50,000. The vendor firm sold all the assets including the goodwill of the business to the Amalgamated Development Limited, which was the vendee. The vendor 's firm was promoted by the partners of that firm. The vendor entered into an agreement with the vendor firm for the purchase of certain shares of the vendor firm. The vendors were also authorised to sell the shares of the vendee firm. The vendee sold the shares of certain other persons who were not parties to the agreement. The vendor purchased the shares of some of the other persons. The vendor sold the shares to the vendee and the vendee paid the price of the shares to them. The vendees paid the price to the vendees but did not pay any interest. The vendor filed a suit against the vendor 's vendee for recovery of the amount due under the agreement. He claimed that the sale was not taxable as it was a sale within the meaning of section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the sale of the entire business of the vendor 's firm amounted to a sale within section 4(2)(d) of the Act and accordingly he assessed the income from the sale of its income. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the profits arising out of the sale of a business could be taxed only if the sale was a sale in the course of the assessee 's ordinary trade or profession. In further appeal to this Court, the Revenue contended that the sale being a sale within s.4(2)(e), the profit arising from the sale must be deemed to have been made in the course. of the assessee "as the asset" and that the sale would be covered by the expression "in the course of his trade or profession". HELD: (i) The word "sale" in section 4(3) has to be construed in its popular sense and is not confined to the concept of sale in section 4. It means transfer of property in goods
4656: The appellant was convicted under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for murder and other capital offences. He was sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, and a sentence of death was imposed on him by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) the circumstances that the appellant was previously convicted for murder and committed these murders after he had served out the life sentence in the earlier case did not constitute "special reason" for imposing the death penalty as required under Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973; (2) the fact that the appellant had undergone imprisonment for more than seven years during the pendency of his trial before the Sessions Court constituted an exceptional ground for awarding the death penalty; (3) the fact of the appellant having been acquitted by the High court of all charges and the convictions were set aside by this Court; (4) the fact whether the appellant was a member of the armed forces of the Union or not was a matter which could be decided only by the Supreme Court and not by the High Courts; (5) the fact about the appellant having undergone imprisonment for over three years during the trial of the previous case did not amount to any special reason for awarding the extreme punishment of death penalty; and (6) the fact regarding the appellant having already undergone imprisonment for a period of more than six months during the trial before the High Court did not constitute any special reason. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The facts found by the courts below are sufficient to justify the imposition of the death penalty. [358B] 2. The question whether the circumstances that there has been a violation of Section 354(a) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, is a matter which can be decided only on the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution and not by taking into consideration the other relevant factors such as the nature of the offence, the position of the offender and the possibility of his getting involved in a criminal conspiracy, etc., is a matter that requires to be determined by the court on the basis that the facts proved establish the offence. [359C D] 3. The fact that the accused was acquitted by the Sessions Court does not mean that the acquittal is wrong. It is open to the
2373: The appellant, a company owning several properties in the municipal borough of Godhra, was assessed to property tax by the respondent under section 73 of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925. The appellant challenged the assessment on the ground that the valuation made by the respondent was not correct and that the value of the properties should be taken as the capital value of the lands for the purpose of the companies Act. Held, that the word "rate" used in section 73 of Bombay Municipal Borne 's Act, was not intended to include the cost of construction of buildings or the cost of acquiring land for the purpose. The word "rate " is defined in section 2(1) of the Bombay District Municipalities Act, 1876, to mean "the annual rent payable by the owner of any building or land required for his own use or the value of such building or land which he is entitled to acquire." The word "rates" is defined in the Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, to mean the annual rent payable in respect of any building, land or premises. The word 'rate ' is defined in s.2(1) to mean "a rate or other charge levied upon lands and buildings for the time being occupied or held by them". The word "taxable", therefore, means the annual rent or the annual rent which is payable by the tenant to the landlord. The word tax has been defined in section 3(3) to mean a tax on lands and buildings and does not include a tax on buildings. The word taxes is also defined in section 4(4). The word 'taxable ' means the annual amount of the annual rent of the land or building assessable as such. The word is used in the sense of a tax on land and buildings and is not used in the same sense as a tax on houses and buildings. The expression 'taxable area ' is defined to mean the area in which the land or the building is situate. The word has been defined to mean "all lands and buildings, all open lands and buildings belonging to the Government, local authority or to the owner of such lands and buildings; all open lands, buildings and lands appurtenant thereto, but excluding any land or building which may be let separately from the land or land on which it stands".
4079: The appellant filed a suit for possession of the land in dispute on the basis that he was in possession of the same. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 146 of the Criminal Procedure Code empowers the Magistrate to attach the subject of dispute pending his decision under section 145(4). This power is not conferred by any statute but is subject to the provisions contained in Chapter XXXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [780C] (2) The Magistrate has no jurisdiction to attach the property which is subject of dispute. He can only proceed against the person who is in actual possession of the property. [781D] (3) The Magistrate cannot go behind the decree passed by the Civil Court. If he proceeds under section 145 Cr. P.C., he has no jurisdiction at all to attach the said property. [771E F] (4) The Magistrate could not have attached the property without the aid of a receiver appointed under section 145. [772F] (5) The Magistrate had no jurisdiction to order attachment of the property in execution proceedings. [773G]
6363: The Karnataka Contract Car riages (Acquisition) Act, 1976 received the assent of the President on 11th March, 1976. The Karnataka Contract Carriage (Acquisition) Ordinance, 1976 was promulgated by the Governor on 30th January, 1976 and came into force from 30th January 1976. The Act was brought into force with effect from 30th of January 1976. Section 20 of the Karnataka Act provided that the Act shall be deemed to have come into force on 30th of December, 1976. Section 21 of the Karnataka General Clauses Act, 1977 provided that the repeal of any enactment shall not affect any legal proceedings which were commenced under the repealed enactment before the commencement of the Act. The Karnataka Act was amended in 1976 and the Karnataka Act was again amended in 1976. The validity of the Karnataka Contract Carri tage (Acquisition) Bill, 1976 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 31st May, 1976 and it was declared to have come in force on 30.1.1976. The Karnataka State Legislature passed the Karnataka Contract Carriage( Acquisition) Act, 1977 (Karnataka Act No. 21 of 1976) which came into force on 1st April, 1976. By section 2 of the Karnataka State Act, the Act was made applicable to the whole State of Karnataka. The Karnataka General Clauses (Amendment) Act, 1978 was enacted on 30th November, 1978. The Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1976 was enacted on 31st December, 1976 and the said Act was also amended in 1976 by the Karnataka Act No. 9 of 1979. The Karnataka High Court struck down the Karnataka Contract Lines (Acquisition) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1979 as unconstitutional and held that the Act was an 'acquisi tion Act ' within the ambit of Entry 42 of the Concurrent List under Schedule VII of the Constitution. 6452: The appellant was appointed as a lady Principal of the college. She applied for the post of lady Principal in the degree section of the college and she was selected by the Selection Committee. 940: The appellant, a company incorporated in the United State of Rajasthan, claimed exemption under section 14(2)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it stood before the amendment of 1953, contending that the said section was applicable to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the income tax law in force in Kotah State had been amended by the Finance Act, 1950, and that the exemption granted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1950 was not affected by the amendment. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the income of the appellant was exempt from taxation under section 14 (2)(c). The High Court dismissed the application for revision filed against the decision of the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The contention that the Explanation to section 14(1)(c) should be confined only to the assessment year 1950 51 must fail. The Explanation to section is not intended to enlarge the scope of the exemption granted under section 14. It is intended to enlarge time limit for the purpose of determining whether the income has escaped assessment or not. [560 D E] The Explanation to sub section (2) of section 14 does not extend the operation of section 14(3) to any other period. The Explanation applies only to cases where the income tax authority has already determined the amount of tax due from an assessee after the date of the amendment. [564 F H] The Explanation cannot apply to cases where there are no assessments pending at the commencement of the amendment made by the Finance Acts of 1950 and 1951. The Explanation is intended to cover cases where the Income tax authorities have already determined the tax payable by the assessee after the amendment. There can be no saving. [566 B C]

In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the proceedings commenced with the filing of a return by a person holding on the appointed date land in excess of the ceiling area prescribed by the Act, (ii) the proceedings were pending immediately before the commencement date in any court or tribunal or before any authority for the purpose of determining the extent of surplus land, Chapter IV contained provisions (Sections 12 to 21) for determining the extent to be surrendered and (iii) the total area and particulars of land which is in excess of ceiling area, and the total area of land which has been declared surplus under section 20, and the area and particulars thereof in pursuance of the provisions in the original Chapters II and III of the Act. HELD: (1 ) The proceedings commenced with a declaration regarding the surplus land in pursuance of section 20, the effect of which is that the ceiling area in respect of which is deemed to have been determined under section 20 is to be the ceiling area. [225 D] (2) The proceedings are not concluded within the period of limitation prescribed by the Limitation Act, 1963. The period of limitation provided in section 20(3) is one year from the date of the notification under section 21. The period during which the proceedings are stayed by an order of a court or tribunal is excluded in computing the period of one year prescribed by the proviso to section 20(4). [225 E F] (3) The proceedings cannot be continued after the expiry of the period of two years from the date when the Collector takes action under section 21, and the period of six months from the date on which the Collector takes such action would commence only if the Collector does not take action within the time prescribed by the statute. [226 B C] (4) The proceedings must be completed within the period prescribed by the Statute.

4904: The appellant tenant had obtained a decree for possession of the premises in question against the respondent landlord. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for recovery of possession of the suit premises on the ground that he was not entitled to the benefit of the provision contained in section 15(1) of the Act. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the proviso to sub section (2) of section 14 is applicable only to cases where the tenant has made default in payment of rent for three consecutive months. The High Court held that though the first ejectment proceeding was withdrawn by the respondents on the ground of nonpayment of rent, no order for recovery of the possession of the tenanted premises could be passed because the proviso to section 14(1) does not apply to the instant case because, in the first ejectment proceed ing, the tenant had not complied with the order passed by the Controller under section 15 of the Act and, therefore, the proviso to subsection (2) would not have any application to the instant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proviso cannot be applied to the instant proceedings since the tenant had committed default in payment or deposit of rent for more than three consecutive months and the proviso to Section 14(2), which provides for the grant of a decree for eviction, must be read subject to the proviso to Sub section (2). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to sub sections (1) and (2) is not intended to take away the right of the tenant to claim the benefit of Section 15(1). [395D] 2. It is intended to give protection to the tenant from eviction when the tenant makes default in payment. [395E] 3. The proviso is not intended as a rule of construction to defeat the provisions of the Act but is intended to be a part of the enactment itself. [396B] 4. The proviso cannot be construed as an exception to the main provision

2086: The appellant was the tenant of a non residential premises No. 281, Old Tharagupet, Bangalore City. He had installed some machinery in the premises. The landlord tiled an application under section 8(3)(a) (ii) of the Act for the eviction of the tenant on the ground that he required the premises for his own use and occupation. The Rent Controller held that the landlord was not entitled to possession of the premises in dispute unless and until he was prepared to vacate the shops in which he was trading at the time. The Appellate Authority reversed this finding and dismissed the appeal. In revision before the High Court it was contended that the landlord 's right to recover possession of the building from the tenant was not affected by the provisions of the Act and that the landlord could not be said to have a right to evict the tenant merely because he was a tenant of the non residential premises. HELD: The expression "tenant" in section 2(g) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 includes a person who is a member of the family carrying on business in the building. [875 B] The definition of the word "tenant" is wider than the ordinary meaning of the word and includes a person,continuing in possession after the termination of the tenancy in his favour. Therefore, the landlord ' s right to recover the possession of the non premises from the tenant is not affected by section 4(2)(a)(i). [876 C D] The expression "any person" in section 3(c) of the Mysore Act means a person who has been in actual possession of the house or part thereof for a period of not less than one year prior to the date of the suit. The expression "all other persons" in section 4(1) (b) includes a person in possession of the whole or part of the house. [877 E F]
3366: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the appellants on the ground that the dying declaration was not made to an independent person, but was made by a person who had no reason to falsely implicate the accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the oral statement which Bahadur Singh made could not be relied upon as a dying declaration because he did not give full account of the incident or its tenor. HELD: (1) The first information report which is lodged at the police station does not contain any recital about the occurrence. It is only in regard to the first information report that the deceased stated that he saw the appellants assaulting Bahadur Singh and that he did not see Munnu Raja at all. [766 D E] (2) The second statement which has been treated by the High Court as a dying one cannot be treated as a dying statement. The first information was lodged after the attack took place and the deceased died. The second statement was recorded by the police after the attack. The third statement which has also been treated by this Court as a second dying declaration was made to an Executive Magistrate when the attack took off. [767 F H; 768 A B] (3) The High Court was right in holding that the oral evidence of the eye witnesses cannot be accepted without corroboration from other evidence. [769 C D]
3199: The plaintiff, a carrier, was entrusted with the goods of the defendant. The goods were to be delivered at the destination named in the bill of lading. The goods arrived at the port on the midnight of March 31, 1964 and were to be despatched by the carrier to the defendant. On the arrival of the goods at the port, the defendant sent a letter to the plaintiff stating that the goods had been delivered to him at the destination mentioned therein. The plaintiff claimed that the goods were delivered to him without any delay and that he should pay the value of the goods as per the invoice. The defendant contended that the suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the suit must fail because the defendant did not have knowledge of the goods being delivered to him. The fact that the goods are delivered to the defendant is no ground for postponement of the accrual of the right to sue. The rule is that if there is an act done or intended to be done under the authority of the Act, and if so done or intended, the defendant is entitled to notice of action. A person who has no knowledge of the thing being delivered to another cannot be said to have knowledge of it.

826: The respondent company was a textile mill. It had a total factory at Jalgaon and its factory was situated in Jalgaon. The respondent claimed that the said factory should be closed down for a period of 15 years, but it did not give any credit to the rehabilitation amount. The appellant contended that the respondent had not been able to prove that the reserves were used as working capital and that the respondent could not claim that the said reserves were utilised as working capital. Held, that the respondent was entitled to deduct the said amount from the available surplus for the year in question, and that the Industrial Court was right in holding that the said amount should be deducted from the available available surplus. The respondent was entitled only to the benefit of the statutory depreciation which was allowed by the Act. The respondent had not proved that the said reserve was used as working Capital. The respondent failed to prove that it had actually utilized the said reserves as working capital, and therefore, the respondent was not entitled to deduct any amount from the rehabilitation amount which was paid to it.

On August 5, 1952, the Government issued a notification declaring that as the petitioner had succeeded his father as Ruler, the village Pithadiya should, pending final orders be treated as Khalsa or Khas village of the State for enjoy as ' Kapil Giras '. On September 3, 1953, the Government cancelled the grant on the ground that the petitioner had failed to establish his title to the property. On October 9, 1953, a petition under article 226 of the Constitution was filed by the petitioner challenging the validity of the order cancelling the grant. 2685: The appellant, a partnership firm carrying on business in partnership at three places (1) Pipliya in Madhya Pradesh, in the name of the Jaora Slate Pencil Works; and (2) Nagpur, in the names of Partap Brothers; and (3) Nagpur, the respondent in the appeal. 53: The plaintiff brought a suit for possession of the ghatwalis ' estate on the basis that she was entitled to be maintained in possession of the estate. She claimed that she had been in joint family and were entitled to succeed to them in preference to the plaintiff under the Mitak shara school of Hindu law which admittedly governed the family of the parties. The defendant denied this claim and contended that the properties being the exclusive property of the ghetwars, they could not be regarded as joint family property. The trial court held that the plaintiff was entitled to the benefit of the rule of survivorship and decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the status of the family in the present case was such that they could not have been excluded from inheritance; (ii) the rule of especific cs is applicable to such estates and (iii) the rule was applicable to the estate of the deceased father in the present ease. HELD: (i) The rule of es pecting the joint family property from the moment of death of the last male holder is applicable to the facts of the instant case. [875 C] (ii) The rule applies only where the estate is joint family property and not where the estate has devolved upon the other heirs. [876 D] (iii) The rule is applicable to all the heirs of the deceased and not to the heirs who are not alive at the time of his death. [877 E] (iv) The rule does not apply to the estate in question. It applies to the estate which is joint family estate. [878 F]
176: The appellants were prosecuted for offences under section 120 B and 161 Indian Penal Code (Act XLV of 1860) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial was held by a Special Judge under the Vindhya Pradesh Criminal Law Amendment (Special Court) Ordinance No. XLVIII of 1949 which came into force on the same day. The appellants contended that the convictions were invalid as they had not been made in accordance with the provisions of article 20(1) of the Constitution. Held, that the conviction was valid and the sentence imposed was adequate. The presumption arising from the absence of a right of appeal is a presumption of law and does not operate as a bar to the exercise of such jurisdiction. The presumption is rebuttable and the burden of proof is on the accused to prove his innocence. In the present case, the prosecution has failed to discharge its onus of proving its case beyond reasonable doubt. The presumption arises when an accused person is convicted of one offence and the conviction is based on the evidence led at the trial. The presumption therefore arises only when the accused person is able to establish his guilt. The presumption may be rebutted or rebutted by other evidence but it cannot be raised until the contrary is proved. It is not necessary that there must be an interval between the acts complained of and the criminal act resulting in the offence. The presumption can also arise where the facts are proved by the evidence of a number of witnesses or the evidence of one witness alone is sufficient to sustain a conviction. Where the prosecution fails to prove the essential ingredients of the offence, the acquittal of the accused may result in a miscarriage of justice. Where the defence raises a very important question and the court believes that the existence of the prosecution case is established, it will be open to the appellate court to consider whether the view taken by the lower court was justified. Where the accused points out that certain circumstances existed which rendered it impossible for the prosecution to adduce evidence the court should acquit the accused. Where the evidence has been recorded in the form of questions and answers, the accused is entitled to rely upon the answers given by him and the prosecution is bound to lead evidence in rebuttal. 4581: The appellant, a dealer in respect of sales of goods to the State of Orissa and to the public at large, was liable to pay tax under the Orissa Additional Sales Tax Act, 1975 (Orissa Act 24 of 1975) as amended by the Orissa Additional Sale Tax (Amendment) Act, 1979 (Orissa Act 14 of 1980). The appellant challenged the levy of additional tax on the ground that it was not a single point levy but a multiple point levy. The High Court held that the levy of the additional tax was a single point levied or a multi point levy. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "turnover" used in section 2(dd) of the Principal Act is a single point taxable under the Act. The rate of tax is prescribed by the Act. If the turnover exceeds Rs. 50,000, the tax would be payable at the rate of 5% of the gross turnover. [550C] 2. The expression 'turnover ' in section 2 (d) of the Act means the aggregate of the amounts of sale prices and tax. if any received and receivable b, a dealer who is liable to pay sales tax under the Act on every dealer whose gross turnover during a fiscal year exceeds Rs.50,000, otherwise than in his own name, the tax shall be payable at a rate equal to the amount of tax payable by him on the total turn over of all the dealers. [551F H; 552A B] 3. The expression turnover means the aggregate amount of purchase prices paid and payable by a dealer in his own behalf. The expression gross turnover means the total of the amounts which a dealer is liable to make up the total of his gross turnover. The expression is defined in section 2 of the Principal, Act as the aggregate of amounts of purchase prices and tax, if any, received and receivable by a dealer. The expression has been defined in section 4 A of the Principal. Section 4 A provides for the levy of tax on the turnover of purchases. Section 4 B provides for the imposition of tax on dealers who are liable to pay the tax. Section 4 C provides for the assessment of tax on persons liable to pay such tax. Section 6 provides for the determination of the amount of the tax payable
1614: The appellant was a cashier of the Municipal Board, Hardwar. He had been working as such since 1932 and had been working in that capacity for the last several years. On his conviction under section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, he was sentenced to three months rigorous imprisonment and to pay a fine of Rs. 100 or in default to undergo further rigorous imprisonment for one month. The Special Judge took the view that the joint trial of the appellant and his brother was not possible with respect to some of the moneys which were the subject matter of the charge (except for two items). The High Court set aside the order of acquittal on the ground that the joint trials were not possible with the appellant 's money. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Special Judge had erred in holding that the joint proceedings were not possible without the appellant ' 's money being deposited in the Bank or the treasury at Roorkee as required by rules. HELD: The Special Judge was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the appellant was using the bank 's money in order to advance it to the officers and servants of the Board. [94 E] The Special Judge could not have taken the view that there was any evidence to show how much money was actually received by the appellant. It is true that the appellant had not produced any evidence to prove that he was using the money in order that he might be able to get it back from the bank. 4503: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Sessions Judge ignored the provision contained in section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which provides in so far as is relevant, that when the accused was asked on the question of sentence, he did not say anything; (ii) the Sessions judge overlooked the provision contained under section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, while recording the conviction for murder and the sentence of death. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A conviction for murder is based on circumstantial evidence. It is well settled that the law does not require that the accused must be questioned only on the circumstances appearing against him or proved against him. The Magistrate must give due weight to the opinion of the Sessions Judge and should also give due regard to the provisions of section 354(4). [768A B] 1.4 Where the accused is charged with the commission of a heinous crime and the court is prima facie satisfied that the case is one of such heinous crime then the court can confirm the sentence imposed upon the accused. 5785: The petitioners in the batch of writ petitions are direct recruits and promotees. They were appointed as Assistant Engineers on ad hoc basis by order dated 8th June, 1984. The Chief Engineer of the respondent State issued a circular dated 6th July, 1984 directing that the direct recruits should be regularised with effect from 1st April, 1965. The petitioners challenged the said circular by filing a Writ Petition before the Andhra Pradesh High Court which was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the retrospective regularisation made by the Chief Engineer of their services to the posts of Assistant Engineers was without authority and was in gross violation of the prescription of the Rules. It was further contended that the rules were not applicable to the posts within the limits of 37 1/2% of the substantive vacancies and even if the promotees were placed in those posts, no seniority had been given to them. Seshachalam; , and the decision of this Court in the case reported in [State of Bihar vs Dr. Birendra Kumar Sinha & Ors.] ; , wherein it was held that the rules of recruitment are not applicable to appointments made by transfer from the cadre of A.E.E. and the direct recruits are entitled to be considered for appointment to the post of Assistant

It is not necessary that there should be an intention to inflict such injury; but that the injury must have been intended to be inflicted. [746F G] Virsa Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

1769: The petitioners, a company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of certain goods, filed writ petitions under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the State Trading Corporation 's order imposing sales tax on the transactions effected by them. The Sales Tax authorities held that the transactions were inter State sales and not intra State sales and accordingly they levied sales tax on them. The petitioners contended that the sales in question were inter State transactions and had been effected in the course of inter State trade and as such, were not liable to be taxed under the relevant provisions of the Sales Tax Act. Held: (i) Article 286(1)(a) does not apply to the facts of the present case because the petitioners are not citizens within the meaning of article 19(1)(b). The petitioners have no fundamental right to carry on business in a State. The petitioners cannot claim protection of article 286(2) of the Constitution. (ii)The petitioners are not entitled to invoke the protection of article 301 of the Constitution for the reason that they are not citizens but are merely instrumentalities of the State. The State Trading Corporation is not an agent of the State and it is only a corporation owned and controlled by the State. It is not a mere agency or agent of the Government. The petitioners are not holders of any office of profit under the State Trading Corporations. The petitioners do not fall within the category of persons who can enforce their fundamental rights under article 31(2) and are therefore not entitled to maintain the petition.

[498 A B] (7) The words used in sub section 4(a) are intended to refer to proceedings in the executing court and not to proceedings in execution of a civil court as such. 5869: The petitioners in the three appeals were candidates for admission to post graduate courses in various Medical Colleges affiliated to the Rajasthan University. They applied for admission to the post graduate courses and appeared at a competitive examination conducted by the Rajasthan University, which was held on May 27, 1979. The result of the said examination was declared on June 30, 1979. In the result sheet of the examination, the petitioners who had passed their final MBBS Examination from the same institution for which selections were being made, were shown as qualified. The petitioners challenged the validity of the provision contained in note (d)(ii) of Ordinance 278 E contending that they had been wrongly denied admission to postgraduate courses in the colleges affiliated to the University of Rajasthan. There is no merit in the contention that the provision in note (b) is unconstitutional or void. The provision is not unconstitutional merely because there is no provision in the statute for making such a provision. [314B C] 3.3. 2382: The Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission (hereinafter referred to as the Commission) issued a notification dated June 21, 1963, notifying a list of backward classes in each State, and pursuant thereto the Government of Andhra Pradesh by G.O.M.S. 1786 dated July 29, 1966, notified a list of castes for the purpose of selecting candidates from the backward classes in the Medical Colleges in the State of Andhra Pradesh. In the said list the caste of the appellant was mentioned as "B" caste. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it violated his fundamental right under article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Government order constituted a violation of the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens of India by article 29(2) of the Constitution, notwithstanding the directive principles of State policy laid down in Part IV of the Constitution; that after considering the replies received from the Chief Secretaries of various States, the Government of A.P. issued an order which included the name of the appellant as a member of the Scheduled Castes. The appellant appealed to this Court with special leave. HELD: (i) The Government Order is not invalid because it does not provide for any reservation of seats for the backward classes. It merely provides for the inclusion of certain communities in the list of backward communities. [599 F] (ii) The Government order is not invalid on the ground of violation of article 14 because it does no more than make reservations for the backward class of citizens. [600 B C] (iii) The Government has power to issue orders providing for reservations of seats for any class or community. The Government order cannot be struck down on the ground either that it violates the fundamental rights of the citizens or that it offends against the provisions of article 14. [601 D E] (iv) The Government had the power to make rules providing for the reservation of seats in favour of certain categories of persons. The Government could not go into the question whether the appellant was entitled to be considered for selection. [604 H] (v) The Government did not act arbitrarily in making the impugned order. [605 D]
6607: The respondents filed a suit for the recovery of certain amounts due to them from the appellant. The appellant, who was the trustee of the trust, filed an application under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, seeking leave to institute a suit as required by section 92 of C.P.C. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the said application on the ground that the grant of leave was an administrative act of the court and no notice to the respondents was required before such leave was granted. On appeal, the High Court held that the grant was not an administrative act but was merely an administrative act and it could be enforced only in accordance with the provisions of section 92 of Code of Civil Proce dure. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The grant of leave is an administrative act. It also imposes a check on the institution of the suit. [975F] 1.2. The grant or refusal of leave is not an administrative action. It is a grant of judicial power which confers on the person concerned a right to institute a proceeding for the proper administration of the trust. It also gives a direction to the trustees to take appropriate steps in the matter. [976G H] 1.3. The grant is not an executive act of the Court. It is the grant of permission to institute a case of public charity. It also passes through the time it comes into effect. It is therefore, a grant of leave. [977A B] 1.4. The grant does not confer any title upon the person concerned. It is merely an administrative order. It is not a grant of a judicial power. [978B] 1.5. The grant can be made without any notice to the respondent. [979E F] 1.6. The grant may be conditional or subject to conditions. It is an administrative decision. It is one of the matters in the discretion of the court. [980D] 2.1. An order granting leave is not a mere formality. It is really an administrative act, though the grant of the leave may be conditional. It is essentially an administrative act; it is a grant or a licence to use the property in question. [981C D
1567: The appellant was in occupation of the premises since prior to 1950. He filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the ground that he was a licensee and that there had been default in payment of rent. The trial court dismissed the suit but the Appellate Court allowed the appeal holding that the relationship of landlord and tenant had not been established. On appeal, the High Court held that the relationship was not proved and that the order striking out his defence was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in dismissing the second appeal as well as the first appeal. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in its view that the relationship between the parties was not proved. [263 B] (ii) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the appellant was a licensee. The appellant was a servant of the Union and was not a licensee. It is true that the appellant did not make any payment to the Union but he made an application under section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which will be referred to in the course of the judgment as the Act. 208: The appellant company was incorporated in the United Kingdom under the Government of India Act, 1935. It had a share capital of Rs. 100 lakhs and its shares were held by the Government of the United Kingdom. The company was incorporated as a private limited company with a capital of Rs, 500 lakhs and its registered office is at Bombay. The company had a paid up share capital of about Rs. 100 crores. The company claimed that it was not liable to pay any dividend on its shares but that it was entitled to receive from the shareholders a sum of Rs. 1,000 per annum as dividend on the shares held by it. The company contended that the provisions of section 12(1) of the Act had been contravened by the Government and that it had not taken possession of the share. Held, that the provisions contained in section 12(2) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, were supplemental to the provisions of the Act and were not applicable to the company. The provisions of section 13(3)(a) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which provided for the effect of repeals, were also not applicable to a private limited Company. The provisions in section 13(4) of the Central Act were also not similar to those in section 12 of the Act. The provisions relating to the payment of dividend on shares did not apply to a private company. The language of section 12 (2) of Act No. I of 1956 was different from the language of section 13 (3) of the same Act. The words "any person" in section 12 (4) of Act 1 of 1956 were used in a wider sense to include all persons who are parties to the transaction. The words 'any person ' in section 12 were not intended to be confined only to persons who were parties to the contract. The words were not intended merely to give protection to the shareholders of the company or to other persons who may have interest in the company. In the present case, the company was not a shareholder of the company but was merely an agent of the company. It was not therefore a shareholder of a private limited companies.
6304: The petitioners are manufacturers of cement and other goods. They manufacture cement from the same cement industry in Uttar Pradesh. The petitioners contended that the impugned notification was discriminatory inasmuch as it did not take into account the fact that the manufacturers covered by the said notification were entitled to sell the articles manufactured by them without liability to pay sales tax while the manufacturers in other States and non manufacturers of the same article selling the same goods in the State were liable to pay sales lax. The petitioners also contended that the manufacturers were discriminated against because they were not similarly situated with the manufacturers in the matter of levy of sales tax on the articles manufactured and sold by them. The petitioners further contended that the provisions of the Act were violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners pointed out that the impugned notifications were discriminatory since the manufacturers were not discriminated against in any manner. The petitioners therefore prayed for quashing the impugned notifications. The State contested the petition contending inter alia that the manufacturers involved in the present case were not similarly placed as the manufacturers in respect of the goods manufactured by them. It was contended that the petitioners had no locus standi to file the writ petition. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners have been subjected to hostile discrimination by reason of the impugned notifications being discriminatory. [803C] 2.1 The petitioners are not similarly situated as the manufacturers covered in the notification. [804E] 3.1 The question whether a manufacturer is entitled to purchase goods from outside the State or from outside the state is essentially a question of fact which has to be decided on the basis of evidence adduced before it. [805F] 3.2 In the instant case, the petitioners have failed to establish that the impugned Notification was discriminatory. [884G] 3.3 The petitioners have not established that the impugned Notifications were discriminatory. [894B] 3.4 The petitioners have failed in proving that the impugned orders were discriminatory. The petitioners cannot succeed
5104: The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he required the premises bonafide and reasonably for his occupation. The respondent landlord contended that the appellant was in need of the premises for starting a school, that the appellant had no means to pay the rent and that the building was needed bona fide by the respondent landlord for the purpose of running a school. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the appellate court held that the appellant 's requirement was not bona fide and that the first option should be given to the respondents. The High Court in second appeal reversed this finding and dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the plan showed that the shops were intended to be reconstructed in the new plan. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The plan Ext. 4 clearly shows that the shops are meant to be let out to tenants. The High court was right in holding that the plan indicated that the shops could be reconstructed only after obtaining sanction from the Municipal Corporation. [875C] 2. The plan does not show that the shops have been constructed as per the sanctioned plan. It is not clear whether the plan has been approved or not. The plan indicates that the shops which are proposed to be reconstruct are intended to be used for the purposes of running the school. The plan also does not indicate that the shops in question are intended to serve the purpose of the school. [877D E] 3. The plan shows that the existing buildings are intended to cover the area of the old building. The plan further shows that the old building is intended to be demolished. The plan therefore clearly shows that there is no other purpose for the construction of the new building. [878F] 4. The plan, therefore, cannot be said to be a mere plan showing the intention of the society to reconstruct the building for the purpose for which they were intended to use. [879E] 5. The plan did not show that any other purpose would be served by reconstruction of the old premises. The plan merely shows that the new building is intended for the benefit of the public. [880G] 6. The plan clearly shows that it is intended to serve this purpose
3147: The appellant was charged with an offence under section 9 of the , and was convicted by the Magistrate. He filed a revision petition before the High Court which dismissed it on merits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 9 of the Act is not applicable to the present case because the speech made in the course of speech does not amount to an offence under the Act. It is only when the speech is made in pursuance of the authority conferred by law that the offence can be said to have been committed. [835C D] (2) The words "in the course of" are very significant and they do not refer to any particular individual or group of individuals. They do not refer either to the actual acts done or intended to be done by them. [836D] (3) The expression "actually" used in section 9 of Act means "actually". The word "actually", therefore, refers to something more than mere intentional action. [837E] (4) The words 'intentionally' and 'intentionly ' used in section 2(a) of the Act mean "or otherwise"; but these words do not include "actually"; and, therefore, the words "intentful" and "intended" must be read as "actually or otherwise". [838F] (5) The words used in section 3 of the Act are not limited to the words "actually done or intended" and, therefore they cannot be construed as meaning "actually taken for the purpose of doing anything" within the meaning of section 2(b).
