1186: The appellant, a partner of a firm, was carrying on business in hides and skins. He had migrated to Pakistan after the dissolution of the partnership. On receipt of information that Abdulla Dhala had migrated from Pakistan after the dissolved partnership, he applied for registration of his name as an evacuee under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and the Custodian General of India, by his order dated December 30, 1949, refused to interfere with the order of the Custodian. The appellant contended that the transfer of the properties mentioned in the sale deed of August 10, 1949, was not for adequate and valuable consideration but only for the purpose of securing proper discharge of the liabilities of the firm and that the property in question did not belong to him. Held, that the property which was transferred by the firm to Abdulla Bhai was not the property of the firm, and that the transfer was not bona fide. The transfer was not made for adequate and important consideration. It was not merely a part of the transaction which was intended to be acted upon. The transfer of the property was not for sufficient and valuable consideration. The transfer could not be said to have been made for adequate consideration.

3529: The respondent filed four nomination papers for being elected from this constituency. The appellant contested the election and contested the election. The respondent filed two objections in the High Court. The High Court held that the petition was liable to be dismissed for non compliance with sections 81, 83 and 83 of the Act. The High court also held that the nomination papers filed by the respondent were not in conformity with sections 33 and 34 of the Act and dismissed the election petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 9A of Act provides that every election petition shall be accompanied by as many copies thereof as there are respondents mentioned in the petition. The object of the provision is to enable the petitioner to see that the election petition does not suffer from any defect which renders it necessary to take proceedings referred to therein. [839 B] (2) The object of section 9A is to enable a person to file an election petition against a returned candidate who has been declared elected. It is only when the returned candidate files an election petition that he can challenge the election of the returned candidate. 653: The appellant was a private limited company carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. 7056: The Goa Legislative Assembly was constituted on 1.1.1966 under the Goa, Daman and Diu (Islamic States) Law, 1959. The Legislative Assembly of Goa was dissolved on 15.2.1991. The Goa Legislative Council passed a resolution to constitute the Goa Legislative Assembly for the State of Goa. On 16.3.1991, the Governor of Goa promulgated an order under Article 371(2) of the Constitution of India, appointing Shri Ravi Naik as the Speaker of Goa Legislative Assembly. The said order was challenged by the writ petitioners in the High Court by filing writ petitions challenging the orders of the Speaker. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Speaker had no such power of review. Aggrieved by the dismissal of the writ petitions, the appellants filed appeals before this Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power of review is not an inherent power but it can be exercised only when there is some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record. It cannot be exercised to correct an obvious error either of law or fact. [832C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Speaker has acted within his powers under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution and he has exercised the power validly. He has also exercised the power within the four corners of the provisions of the Act. [833D] 1.3 The power of the Speaker to disqualify a member of the House of the People is a judicial power which is vested in him under the Constitution. The power of disqualification is a matter of discretion of the Speaker and the same cannot be interfered with unless the decision of the Speaker suffers from any infirmity. [834E F] 1.4 The power of judicial review is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution. It is a plenary power. It is not a source of power. It must be limited by limits. It is circumscribed by limits. [835F] 1.5 The power of reviewing the order of disqualification made by the Speaker is a discretionary power. It does not confer any kind of right upon the Speaker. [836A] 1.6 The power of Review is a power which is conferred on the Speaker by the Constitution. [837B]

[166 B] (2) The purchase at the rent sales was made by availing themselves of their position as such. The mortgagee did not pay any rent to the mortgagor or to the mortgagee. It was only a usufructuary mortgagee who was entitled to redeem it. [161 G H] (8) The mortgagee in his possession was entitled to recover the rent from the mortgagor. The mortgagee in the possession was entitled only to get back the amount due to him.

The second proviso to Rule 7(1)(a) clearly indicates that an income received by a non resident person from all sources would be from all resources including lands. [800D
5159: The respondents were granted licences under the Madhya Pradesh Excise Act, 1915 for manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquor. 3068: The appellant was a workman who was employed by the respondent company. The Labour Court held that the order of dismissal was passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour Court directed reinstatement of the third respondent with all back wages. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending inter alia that the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under section 7 8 (1) D. The Labour court took the view that the order was passed by an employer acting or purporting to act under the standing orders and therefore the Labour Court could not issue any direction for reinstatement of the respondent. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the order of the employer was illegal or not. HELD:The Labour Court was right in holding that the order passed by the employer was legal and valid. [739 E] The Labour Court was competent to pass such an order as it thought fit. The Labour Appellate Tribunal has rightly held that the Labour court had no jurisdiction. [740 F] The Labour Appellate Tribunals are competent to give relief under section 7 7 8 (I) D. [912E F] (3) The fact that the accused had no motive whatsoever to falsely impeach the witness is not a ground to discard the testimony of the witness. [913A]

3943: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission (hereinafter referred to as the Commission) was constituted under section 133 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir. It is not required to consult the Public Service Com mission before making appointments to the posts or to making promotions to them. 4113: The appellant, who was the widow of a tenant in respect of land in village Bhanguri, Tehsil and District Ambala, applied under section 10 A(b) and 10B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 for allotment of land to her. She claimed that she had been in possession of the land as a widow and that she had not taken any steps to get the land allotted to her. The Collector (Surplus) declared the "surplus area" of the land to be 30 standard acres and 8 standard units of land as "surplus" and directed the appellant to allot the "sur surplus area". The appellant challenged the order by a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it holding that the "surallotment" could not be completed unless the "surface" was completed. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The expression "surplus Area" is defined in section 2(5a) of the Act to mean "the area of land held by a person on his own account and not on behalf of or for the benefit of any other person." The expression " Surplus Area" has not been defined in the Act but it must be understood in its ordinary meaning and must include all lands which are acquired by the State Government or the holder thereof. [306 D] The expression "Surplus Area" means the area of land which is actually used by the holder for the purpose of resettling tenants. It cannot be said that the "Surplus area" would be confined only to the area of the land which is being used by the tenant himself. [307 E]
4923: The appellants filed applications before the Collector in 1964 under section 5 of the M. Land Revenue Code, 1959 for a revision against the order of the Collector and the Board of Revenue in 1964. The application was rejected by the Commissioner on the ground that there was no provision in the Abolition Act or the Code to review or revise any orders passed by the Collector. The appellants then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the orders of the Commissioner as also the Board of revenue. The High Court held that the two authorities were not competent to entertain an appeal against the orders of one authority without filing an appeal before the Commissioner. It therefore set aside the orders of both the authorities and remanded the case back to the Commissioner for disposal according to law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the two powers were distinct and separate from each other and that the two provisions did not confer any power of revision on the Commissioner or the Board. HELD: (i) Under the Abolition Act as also the Code, both the Commissioner and the Board are appellate as also revisional authorities. [804 E] (ii) The distinction between a quasi judicial and administrative function is well established. A quasi judicial function consists in the determination or exclusion of some right or liability. The former does not however affect the latter. But the latter may be said to have taken away the right or obligation created by statute. The question whether the two functions are independent of each other has to be decided by the Legislature and not by the Courts. [805 B C] (iii) The distinction made between a quasi-judicial and administrative function cannot be ignored if the two functions being qualitatively different. [806 D]

The respondents filed a suit against the appellant and the appellant for possession of the premises on the ground that the appellant had permitted the buildings to be used for commercial purposes contrary to the terms of the lease deed and that as they had permitted the building to be used by the respondents for commercial purposes, contrary to the provisions of the lease, the lease was liable to be determined and called upon them to discontinue the use of land for commercial purpose, failing which they were asked not to use the land for any other purpose. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was entitled to recover possession of the land from the respondents. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents were aware of the use of their premises for commercial purposes; that the appellant did not have any right to take advantage of clause (k) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, because the letting of the premises is governed by the lease deed executed between the parties; that the respondents had no right to get possession of the property under the lease deed; that the lease granted by the Delhi Improvement Trust was void and inoperative as the respondents had not been put into possession of the building; that the provisions of clause (kk) of the Proviso to sub section(1) of section 14 of the Act were not applicable to the facts of the case; that the High Court erred in holding that the respondents could not take advantage of the proviso; that the letting of premises is governed only by the lease agreement entered into between the parties and the respondents had nothing to do with the building; and that the respondents are estopped from claiming possession. On January 26, 1950, the Government of India issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Institutions (Temple) Act, 1951, declaring that the temple was a private temple belonging exclusively to the Gowdavi Brahmins of the Gudalur village of Moolky Taluk in the State of Madras. The appellant in the other appeal was the owner and the third respondent in Civil Appeal 238 of 1960 was the purchaser of the goods supplied by the third respondent to the appellant. The appellant contended that the State legislature having authority to enact a law imposing a tax on the sale of goods was not competent to levy sales tax on the value of the materials used in the execution of works under the contract. Held, that the State Legislature having authority to legislate on the subject, the State legislature must be held to have competence to impose a tax on transactions which are not inter vivos or which are not in the course of import into India. 6110: The appellant was prosecuted for exporting fertilisers without a valid permit. The Trial Magistrate held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused were attempting to export the fertiliser bags from Madhya Pradesh to Maharashtra in contravention of the FM. The High Court acquitted the accused holding that the prosecution did not establish any mens rea on the part of the accused in exporting are fertilisers and that the materials on record would, at best, make out only a case of preparation by the accused to obtain their conviction and sentence. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the High Court is correct. [553C] 2. The expression "any person" occurring in Sec. 7(1) of the Act as it stood at the relevant time, namely, the contravention of an order made under Sec. 3 of the Act, as mens re aness, must be read in the context of the definition of the word "agent" in Sec. 2(c) of the FERA. The words "any person", which occur in Sec.7(1), must be given the same meaning as the word "person". [535D E] 3. The expression 'other person ' appearing in Sec.2(c) has been used in a wider sense so as to include persons who are not actually in the employ of the company but are merely its servants or agents. Therefore, the expression "any other person" appearing in Secs. 2(d) and 2(e) must be construed as including all persons who are generally employed by the company. [554F G] 4. The expression used in Sec.6(1)(b) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 means that wherever it occurs in this section, the context requires that the context requires the expression to be given a wider meaning. [555G] 5. In the instant case, the High Court was right in holding that the appellant was guilty of having committed an offence punishable under Sec. 7 of the Act. [556E]
2026: The respondent was a married woman. She left her husband 's service and joined the appellant company as a casual labourer. On the question whether she had to work in teams in the respondent concern, the Industrial Court held that she had worked in teams and that she could not be treated as an employee of the appellant company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rule requiring un married women to resign as soon as they marries is not mandatory and that there was no justification for such a rule being made. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) There is no reason why a woman who has left her husband service should be excluded from the benefit of the rule. [495C] (2) The rule does not provide for any other kind of leave but only provides for the termination of employment by giving one month's notice or pay in lieu thereof. It is not possible to accept the contention that the rule requires an unmarried woman to resign as early as possible. The rule does require an unmarried woman who has been employed in teams. But if the rule is intended to cover the situation where the woman is not employed, then the rule would have been different. [496E F] (3) The rule is not mandatory but directory. [497A]
3405: The appellant Bank was a banking company within the meaning of section 5 of the Banking Companies Act, 1949 and has its Head Office in London and branch offices in different parts of India. The Bank maintains its accounts according to the calender year and it brings out not only a consolidated balance sheet and profit and loss account for its Indian business but also a separate balance sheet and profits and loss account. The Bank is a banking company in India and carries on banking activities. The Bank has its head office in London and Branch Offices in different parts in India. The dispute between the Bank and its workmen related to bonus for the accounting year 1965. The Bank maintained its accounts according the calender Year and it brings into existence an industrial dispute between the bank and its workmen. The Bank claimed that the bonus payable by it should be calculated as per the provisions of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The Industrial Tribunal held that the bonus paid by the Bank was not deductible under section 7(2)(d) of the Act and that the amount of bonus payable by the Bank to the workmen was not dedu ctable under section 7 (2)(d). On appeal by the workmen, the Appellate Tribunal held that there were no deductions made from the gross profits of the Bank under section 7 of the Act. The Bank appealed to this Court with special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that: (1) the Tribunal had erred in holding that the available surplus had been arrived at after deducting therefrom the amounts already paid by way of depreciation allowance; (2) the Tribunal erred in holding the available surplus to be deductible; (3) the Tribunal fell into error in holding that there was no deduction under section 7; (4) the Tribunal committed an error in holding the amount of available surplus to have been deductible as deductible from the gross profit of the Bank. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that even though the available surplus was not deducible under section 7, the Tribunal could not go behind the calculation of the available surplus. [137 D] (ii) The Tribunal had correctly applied the principles laid down by this Court in the case of [Bharat Forge Co. Ltd. vs Union
4121: The appellant was the tenant of a house in Dehra Dun. He died during the pendency of proceedings in this Court and was substituted by his legal representatives, instituted a suit against the respondent for damages and for eviction from the house. The trial court held that the rent which was in arrears upto June 13, 1960, had not lost its character as arrears of rent and therefore, no ground for eviction had been made out under section 3(a) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act No. 6 of 1947. The trial Court also held that the amount of Rs. 75 towards the rent of 3 months prior to August 12, 1961, was due under the agreement dated June 12, 1960, and that amount could not be treated as arrears of the rent for three months prior to December 31, 1961. On appeal, the Additional Civil Judge, Dehradun, reversed the finding of the Munsif and held that the arrears of rent were due from the date of demand notice served upon the appellant. The High Court on reference, however, allowed the appeal of the respondent and directed eviction of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the amount due to the respondent from the date when he became the owner of the house was not recoverable from him. [639E] 2.1 It is true that the rent payable by the tenant at the time of the execution of the decree was not the same as the rent payable at the time when the decree was passed but it would be difficult to say that the rent paid by the tenant was more than the amount of rent which he was liable to pay under the decree. But the fact remains that the rent was in arrears for a period of three months prior thereto. [640F H] 2.2 The rent payable by a tenant at the date of the notice of demand must be regarded as having become due and payable immediately after the receipt thereof by the landlord. The question whether the rent was due or not has to be determined with reference to the date of service of the notice. [641A B]
6344: The appellant tenant was in arrears of rent for a period of more than one year. He filed an eviction petition before the Rent Controller, Delhi on grounds of non payment of rent as also on other grounds. The Rent Controller passed an order under section 15(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 directing the tenant to deposit arrears of rent within one month from the date of the order and further to pay month to month rent by the 15th of every calendar month. The tenant deposited Rs. 10,000 to cover arrears of rent as well as to cover future rent uptill September 15, 1973. Thereafter neither on October 15, 1973 nor on November 15, 1973 did the tenant deposit monthly rent as required by the aforesaid order of the Rent Controller. On June 1, 1974 the Rent Controller passed another order striking out the defence of the tenant on appeal by the tenant and remitted the case back to the Rent Controller for further proceedings. The Rent Appellate Tribunal, Delhi set aside the order of the Additional Rent Controller striking out the defen dant 's defence and remanded the case back for further proceedings to the Rent Control Court. The Rent Control Tribunal, Delhi dismissed the appeal of the tenant but allowed the appeal of respondent tenant holding that the tenant had not complied with the terms of the order made under section 15 (1) of Act in as much as depositing future rent late it was not impera tive in all events of the defence of default being struck off and a fair amount of discretion had been left with the Rent Controller under section 15 of the Act granting the tenant two months time to vacate the premises. The tenant preferred a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In the appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that even if the tenant had failed to file an appeal against the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller dismissing his application for striking out the defend ant 's defence, the Rent Controller had no power to pass any order striking out his defence and that the order of striking out the defendant 's defence was illegal and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Appellate Authority striking out the tenant 's defence is not open to challenge in this court. [839E] 2. The order striking out a defence
1056: The appellants were assessed to income tax for the year 1950 51 corresponding to the assessment year 1949 50 corresponding to the year of account 1949 50. The Income Tax Officer, on a finding that the appellants had not exercised their option under section 2(ii) of the Indian Income Tax Act in respect of the year of assessment 1949 50, rejected their return and directed the Income Tax Officer to assess the appellants for the year of its account 1949 50 after giving them an opportunity to explain the nature and source thereof. The appellants submitted their returns of income for the year ending June 30, 1950, but the Income Tax officer did not take any action against them. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellants having failed to exercise their option under s. 2(ii), they could not be said to have exercised their option. On appeal, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the assessees had not exercised the option under s 2(ii). The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 34(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act at the relevant time in so far as it is material provided: "(1) if (a) the Income Tax authority has reason to believe that income chargeable to income tax has escaped assessment for any period; or (b) the Income tax authority has reason 'to believe that such income has been concealed, by reason of the omission or failure on the part of the assessee to make a true and full disclosure of the particulars contained in his return or statement of his income for the same period, the Income tax Officer shall, whether or not there are sufficient grounds for making the requisite satisfaction, serve on the person liable to pay the tax a notice containing all or any of the requirements which may be included in a notice under sub section (2) a notice requiring him to furnish within such period not being less than thirty days from the date of service of the notice, a return in the prescribed form and verified in the prescribed manner and setting forth such other particulars as may be required in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder together with a notice of the estimated average total income of the assessee for the year for which the return is filed, the amount or the aggregate of the sums specified in the return
6991: The respondent was working as a Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax. He was served with a charge memorandum dated 2.5.1989 containing three charges, namely, (1) that he failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty and exhibited a conduct unbecoming of a Government servant thereby violating provisions of Rules 3(1)(i), 3(1) (ii) and 3(1). (iii) of the CCS (Conduct) Rules 1964; (2) that he had acted in a manner unbecomely and in an irresponsible manner, in an improper and in disregard of the relevant rules and orders governing the service conditions of the employees of the Company; (3) that he did not act in a proper and reasonable manner in the matter of promotion of the respondent to the post of Deputy Commissioner of income tax; (4) that he acted in a negligent manner in the discharge of his duties as a Deputy Director of Income Tax and thus violated Rule 3(1A) of the Central Civil Services (Conduct Rules); (5) that he has acted in a way which is prejudicial to the interest of the Company and adversely affecting the interests of the Company. The respondent filed O.A. No. 2540/89 before the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the validity of the said charge memo. The Tribunal allowed the application holding that the action taken by the officer was quasi judicial and should not have formed the basis of disciplinary action. The Union of India preferred an appeal against the order of the Tribunal. The Union contended that the charge sheet issued to the respondent was not sustainable because it was issued without any authority or sanction of law and therefore, it could not be sustained. The Tribunal held that the action of the officer was quasijudicial and should not be based on any legal principle. The Union also challenged the correctness of the decision of the Tribunal in the appeal. The Union further contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the decision of a statutory authority. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right in its conclusion that the action was mala fide. [307D] 2. The Tribunal has rightly held that the charge memo issued to the appellant was not sustainable. [308
2374: The appellant was the owner of a factory. He obtained an order for possession under section 3 of the Punjab Act XX of 1948 against the judgment debtors. The judgment debtors filed objections under the Act and obtained an order directing delivery of possession. The decree holder applied to the court for execution of the order for possession through court. The executing court rejected the application on the ground that the court had no jurisdiction to pass an order for delivery of possession without the requisite sanction from the State Government. The High Court dismissed the appeal by certificate. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order passed by the Subordinate Judge in execution proceedings is not final as it does not operate as res judicata between the parties. [708 B] (2) The decree holder could not be granted possession unless the requisite sanction was obtained. [709 D] (3) The decree was passed in favour of the judgment debtor 's representative. The judgment debtor ' could not be said to have been prosecuted with due diligence. [710 C] (4) The decree-holder could not be asked to pay the arrears of rent or deliver possession of the premises to him. [711 E] (5) The decree passed by the court in favour of a person who was not a party to the suit, cannot be treated as a nullity. [712 F]
4013: The appellant company was a Government Company. It had been granted a licence to set up a generating station at Renusagar, in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The appellant company made an application for grant of licence to set-up a generating station. The State Government granted the licence to the appellant company on September 26, 1959, for the manufacture of 20,000 metric tonnes of aluminum. The appellant 's case is that the High Court has not granted all the reliefs which it had claimed in its petition under article 226 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has interfered with the grant of relief by way of a writ of certiorari. The High Court should have given full effect to the consent order dated September 19, 1977, and the consent order should have been given by the Government of India. [425C] (2) The High court could not interfere with the grant only if it had acted arbitrarily or capriciously or had ignored relevant considerations or had ignored irrelevant considerations or had disregarded extraneous considerations. In the present case, the High Court did not act arbitrarily but merely applied the consent order as a whole. [426D E] (3) The High Courts were wrong in interfering with the grant without any basis whatsoever. [427F] (4) The High courts were wrong in granting relief to the appellant. [428G]
6979: The appellants filed an application under section 145 of the Code before the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Sadabad in which they claimed ownership of the suit property. The learned Magistrate passed a preliminary order under Section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code and thereafter on 22nd April 1977 made an order of attachment under section 146 directing that the attachment would continue till the competent civil court determined the rights of the parties with regard to the said property. Against this order, the appellants preferred revision before the Sessions Judge who by his interim order dated 23rd April 1977 stayed the order of attachment issued by the Magistrate. On 25th July 1978, the Magistrate ordered restoration of possession of the property to the appellants from whom allegedly the possession was taken. The appellants then moved the High Court for quashing the order of the Magistrate and the Sessions Judge. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of attachment. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The Magistrate has not committed any illegality or irregularity in passing the order of attaching the property in dispute. [550C] 2.1 In view of the fact that the Magistrate had already passed an order of stay against the attachment of the property in question, it is not necessary to pass any further order of stay. [552E] 3.1 It appears that none of the parties including the Sessions Judge realised this error on the part of the Magistrate. The Magistrate did not commit any illegality or irregularities in the order of attached property. [553F] 3.2 The Magistrate could have directed the attachment of property only if he found that there was no valid attachment. [554G]
472: The appellant was tried for the murder of one Sabir. He was acquitted by the trial court but convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted him under section 302 read with section 114 I.P, Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the evidence against the appellant was not reliable and that the High Court had erred in relying on the testimony of the eye witnesses as against the appellant. HELD: (i) There is no reason why the High Court should have accepted the testimony of a witness who has been believed by the trial judge. [474 F] (ii) The High Court was wrong in accepting the testimony of PW 1 as against the prosecution. The High 'Court was right in holding that the testimony of PWs 1 and 2 was not reliable. [475 G] (iii) The High ' Court was wrong when it held that the testimony was not reliable because the witnesses who had deposed against the appellant were interested and partisan witnesses. [476 A B] (iv) The High court was wrong in convicting the appellant under section 302 IPC. [477 D]
3452: The appellant brought a suit in the court of the Assistant Collector, Baran for possession of land comprised in khasra Nos. 513 and 678 situate in village Balakhera under sections 180 and 183 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The respondent pleaded that he was a trespasser and that he had been inducted as a tenant by the appellant without any authority or consent from him. The appellant contended that he was not a trespasser but a trespasser. The Revenue Appellate Authority held that Birdhi Lal being a trespasser was not liable to be ejected from the land. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Board of Revenue which allowed the same holding that Birdhis were not tenants within the meaning of section 5(43) of the Act and hence not liable to ejectment. The Board of Revenue reversed the decision of the Assistant collector and dismissed the appeal. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the correctness of the order of the Board of Revising Authority and the Board of revenue. The High Court allowed the petition and set aside the judgment of the Board. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The High court has rightly held that Birdar was a trespassee and there was no error apparent on the face of the record. [515B] 1.2. The High Courts' decisions are based on sound principles of law. It is well settled that the High Courts have power to interfere with findings of fact even if they are erroneous. [516C D] 1.3. In the instant case, the finding of the Revenue Authorities that Birdi Lal was a trespassers and that he was inducted as such by the appellant, is based on correct appreciation of evidence. The High courts ' findings are based on proper appreciation of evidence and do not call for interference. [517E F] 1.4. The High Courtily failed to consider the scope of section 180 of the Act. The High Com missioner had correctly applied the provisions of section 180 and recorded his conclusion. [518G H] 1.5. The High Commission had found that Birdari Lal was a tenant within the meaning section 5(44) of
1385: The appellants were accused of having committed offences under sections 467, read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. They filed a complaint in the Court of the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta, against the two appellants for offences under sections 120B and 34 of the Indian penal code alleging that they had entered into criminal conspiracy with one another to commit an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term of two years or upwards. The Magistrate dismissed the complaint on the ground that the complaint was not maintainable as it was barred by limitation. The High Court held that the complaint could be said to have been made within time only if the prosecution was instituted within three years from the date of commission of the offence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The complaint was not barred by limitation because the cognizance was taken on the basis of the complaint which was filed after the expiry of the period of limitation. [314 D] (2) The complaint did not disclose any offence under section 465 of the Indian Panel Code. It was merely stated that the accused persons had forged documents and used them as genuine. The fact that the accused had forged documents would not make the complaint itself a false complaint. [315 B C] (3) The complaint must be construed as being in continuation of the original complaint. [306 A] (4) The complaint is not barred by time. [307 E] (a) The complaint cannot be said to be barred by limitation unless the prosecution is launched within three years of the date on which the offence complained of is alleged to have been committed. [308 F] (b) The complaint can be said to contain all the necessary facts constituting the offence charged. [309 G H; 310 A] (c) The complaint does not disclose any cause of action. [317 B] (d) The complaint has been filed within three years. [318 C] (e) The complaint should be treated as one filed within three year of the date of the commission of the crime. [319 D]
3425: The respondent was appointed as a Gazetted Officer in the Punjab Education Service (Class I) on October 1, 1949. He received a copy of letter No. 5137 ED I 60/9269 dated May 2, 1960 addressed by the Secretary to Government, Punjab, Education Department to the Director of Public Instruction, Punjab, Chandigarh, conveying sanction of the Governor of Punjab to the grant of pension and death cum retirement gratuity under rule 6.4 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Vol. II read with para 9(1)(a) of the New Pension Rules, 1951. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the aforesaid order of the Government imposing the cut in his superannuation pension and deathcum retirement gratuity on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the said decision of the Government to apply the cut in the pension and gratuity admissible to him. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order imposing the cut was an administrative order and the case did not fall within the purview of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the order imposing a cut in the superannuation pension and gratuity is an administrative order; (ii) the order is an administrative act and the case does not fall within any of the three clauses of article 311(2); (iii) the order being an administrative order is not amenable to judicial review; (iv) the order has been passed in colourable exercise of power; (v) the order cannot be sustained on the grounds of mala fides or arbitrariness; (vi) the order was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice; (vii) the order having been passed after the conclusion of the enquiry, the order could not be sustained; and (viii) the order of the Governor imposing the cut of 10% in the pension of the respondent was arbitrary and violative of article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore liable to be quashed. HELD: (i) The order imposing the penalty of reduction of pension and gratuity in the present case was an administrative action and not a punishment. [560 F] (ii) The order of the State Government imposing the penalty was an administrative act. It was not a pun
87: The plaintiff, the first defendant, filed a suit for partition of his share in the joint family properties. The defendants pleaded that the parties were Sudras and belonged to the Nanak Shai sect of Fakirs, and that they had separate from Nandkishore. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff 's case was that Budparkash Das was separate from Nand kishore and that he was in possession of his share of the property as the daughter of Nandkishor. The High Court on appeal reversed the decision of the trial court and held that the plaintiff was entitled to a decree for partition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the plaintiff ' s claim was barred by limitation; (2) the suit was not maintainable because the parties were brothers and were joint in status; (3) the plaintiff had no cause of action against the defendants; and (4) the suit being one for partition was not maintainable. HELD: (1) The finding of the High Court that the plaintiff did not prove that he was the son of Nandkishto is correct. The finding that the plaintiff had not proved that he was a member of the joint family was based upon the evidence adduced by the parties. [880C] (2) The plaintiff 's contention that the parties are Sudras and that he should be treated as separate from Nandki shore could not be accepted because the plaintiff 'S' himself admitted that he was not a member of any of the branches of the family. The plaintiff 'S 's case that he was separate from the other branches was not established. [881D E] (3) The plaintiff has failed to establish that he was entitled to the share of the properties which were the subject matter of the suit. He has also failed to prove that he had been in joint possession of the properties. [882F] (4) The plaintiff had not led any evidence to show that he was ever in joint possession. The plaintiff had produced some documents to show that the properties were joint and that he had not been able to produce any document to show that his father was in joint possession with him. The plaintiff has also failed in proving that
2200: The appellants, who were dealers in iron and steel products manufactured by them, purchased iron from various dealers in Punjab and outside for making rolled steel section and selling the same. They filed petitions under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the orders of assessment and for a writ quashing the orders of the assessing authorities and for restraining them from levying purchase tax on the goods purchased and for refund of the tax illegally collected from them. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the amended provision, section 2(ff), was void as it conferred merely legislative power on the provincial Government and, therefore, the said section was stillborn and that, as the transaction defined therein was not a sale within the meaning of that expression in entry 52 of List 11 of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the entire Act was void; (ii) the amended provisions, section 2 (ff) was also void because they contravened sections 14 and 15 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, whereunder sales tax was prohibited to be imposed on the declared goods at more than one stage, whereas under the Act it could be imposed both at the purchase point and at the sale point of the transactions entered into by the manufacturer. HELD : (i) The amended provision, Section 2(ff) was void as the transaction covered by it was not a purchase but a sale. [701 F] (ii) The amended provisions, Section 2 (ff), were also void because it infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. [702 B C] (iii) The amended section 2(f) was also valid because it contravened sections 14 or 15 of the Act. [703 D] (iv) The amended Section 2(f), is also void because the transaction defined thereunder was not a contract of sale. [751 E] (v) The amended clause, section 2, introduced by Act 7 of 1958, provided that no tax shall be levied or collected except after consultation with the Collector of the district concerned. The words "subject to" in the amended clause are wide enough to include all taxes which may be levied or recovered before the amendment. [752 H] (vi) The amended sub section (1) of
1307: The appellant, a money lender, filed a suit for an order reopening the personal decree. The trial court decreed the suit and directed that a new decree be drawn up and that the amount due under the personal decree be paid in three annual instalments. Against this decree, an appeal was preferred to the District Court which allowed the cross objections of the appellant and set aside the decree of the trial court. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the provisions of 0. 34, r. 6 of the Civil Procedure Code were not applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The provisions of 0, 34, r., 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not applicable to a proceeding under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act. [890 B] (2) The provisions contained in 0. 34 of the Code are not applicable in proceedings under section 36. The provisions of rule 26 of Order XLI of the Code do not apply to proceedings under section 4 or 5 of the Bengal Act. [889 D] (3) The provisions relating to execution of decrees passed by courts in suits for recovery of money advanced before the commencement of the Act are not applicable. [894 C] (4) The provisions regarding execution of decrees are not applicable when the decree is passed by a court having no jurisdiction to execute it. [895 E] (5) The provisions in 0.34, r.6 of the Code cannot be applied to proceedings under the Act. [897 F] (6) The provisions under 0. 34 are not applicable where the decree is not fully satisfied by the first day of January, 1939. [898 G] (7) The provisions made in 0. 35, r. 3 of the Code would not apply to such proceedings. [899 A] (8) The provisions with regard to execution of orders passed by courts other than those mentioned in 0.35, r. 2(a), are not applicable because the decree is a final one and has not become final. [891 H] (9) The provisions about execution of decrees in the Act are also not applicable to proceedings under 0.35 r. 6. [892 D] (10)
2933: The respondent was a watches carrying on the business of woollen ts and watches. He carried on the same business in the name of Walton Watch Company, which was seized on March 19, 1963. The Collector under section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 extended the period for giving notice under section 124 (a) of the Act either after the initial period of six months or the extended period had already expired. The Collector 's order was confirmed by the Appellate Authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the liability to return the goods seized under section 110 (1) of Customs Act, 1961, could not be imposed on the respondent as he did not have a reasonable belief on the facts disclosed in the grounds of his application for extension of time. HELD : (i) The proviso to section 1 10(2) does not contemplate any notice to the respondent as the considerations which would weigh with the Collector or which would be relevant for granting extension would be of such a nature that they could not be disclosed. [808 F] (ii)The proviso to section I 10(2), therefore, cannot be construed as an exception to the general rule that where there is no question of any right being vested in the person who has to make a claim for refund, the proviso must be read subject to the exception that where there are special circumstances justifying the grant of extension of time, the proviso should be so interpreted as to exclude the applicability of the proviso to section 11(1). [808 A B] (iii)In the instant case, the Collector 's orders were made within the period prescribed under section 110 of the Customs act, 1962. The Collector had no power to extend the period of time. The proviso to Section 1 10(1) does not require any notice to be given to the respondent. [809 C D]
975: The appellant, a resident of Bombay City, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1955 56 and 1956 57. He filed returns in pursuance of the notice issued under section 34 read with section 22(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer served upon him notices under section 34 of the Act for assessment of tax in respect of those years. In response to the notices he received notices under section 22(2) of the Act from the Income Tax Officer on March 31, 1957. The appellant 's case was that the notices were not served within the period prescribed by cl. (a) of sub section (2) of section 22 but were served only after the expiry of eight years from the end of the year of assessment. The Income tax Officer did not accept this contention and held that the notices had been duly served. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the notice was properly served. The High Court dismissed the reference. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the provisions of section 22(3)(b) of the Indian Income Tax Act applied to residents only and that an obligation to make a return must be complied with before the time limit for making a return is reached; (ii) that the notice under section 22 was not served within eight years from when the assessee could have made a return and (iii) that the failure to submit a return within the prescribed period was not fatal to the proceedings initiated against the assessee. HELD : (i) The requirement of a notice under section22(1) is not mandatory but directory. It is open to the Income tax officer to issue a notice under s.22(2). If he does so, he has no power to issue such a notice. [398 F] (ii)The proviso to section 22(4) applies only where a notice under sub section (1) is served. 1488: The appellant was a registered association of jute mill companies which purchased raw jute and manufactured finished goods therefrom. The appellant filed an application under section 5 of the , for revocation of the authority of an arbitrator appointed under certain contracts, on the ground that the respondents had entered into a contract with the appellant for the sale or purchase of raw jute and that the appellant had no power to revoke the authority of the arbitrator appointed under the provisions of the . The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the appellant had not been given notice of the appointment of an arbitrator under the ,; (ii) the appellant was not entitled to invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court under section 5(4) of the , as the respondents were not members of a recognised association or through or with any such member; (iii) the appellant could not be said to have acted in contravention of the terms of the contract; (iv) the appellant 's case was that the respondents were placed in two different camps and the vast majority of the arbitrators in the panel of arbitration comprising of the appellant and the respondents had no opportunity to express their views on the question whether the respondents were members of a recognized association or through its members. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was entitled to exercise its powers under section 5. The agreement provides for the constitution of the tribunal consisting of three persons who are agreed upon by the parties. It is not necessary that the agreement should be signed by all the parties. If the agreement does not contain the names of the persons who are to be nominated, the agreement has to be deemed to be properly made and duly executed. [958 B C] (iii) The appellant did not act in breach of the conditions of the contract. The appellant was entitled only to damages. [959 E]

932: The appellant, a resident of the village in which an additional police force was stationed, was exempted from liability to bear any portion of the cost of the additional force. He challenged the validity of section 15 of the , on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 15(1) does not apply to the case of a person who is not a citizen of India but is a resident of a particular area and is entitled to be exempted from the obligation to bear the additional force if he has been convicted of offences under the Act. (ii)The exemption granted by the notification is only for those persons who are residents of the area where the additional force is being used. It is not necessary that the persons who are not residents of the locality should have been residing in the area where they were sought to be exempted. The notification merely exempts persons who are citizens of India from liability to pay the additional force and does not prohibit such persons from claiming exemption from liability to the additional force as they do not fall within the purview of article 15(1).

1225: The respondents entered into three contracts for the construction of a aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. After the work was completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and ultimately by an agreement dated February 6, 1948, they were referred to arbitration of one Col. Col. S. K. Das, an arbitrator appointed by the Government under section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The arbitrators made their award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. On July 5, 1948, the appellant filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The respondents contended that there was no valid agreement of reference to arbitration and that the award was not binding on them. The Subordinate Judge held that the award did not comply with the requirements of section 175(1) of the . He also held that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not complywith the provisions of section 175 (3). The High Court confirmed the decree of the Subordinate Judge but granted a certificate under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution. Held: (i) that the agreement was not a contract relating to the execution of works within the meaning of section 175 of the Government Of India Act, or the Constitution; (ii) that the award could be enforced only if it complied with the provisions of the Act and not otherwise. It is well settled that where a contract is governed by the provisions of a statute which are not specifically made applicable to a contract, the provisions of such statute would apply even though the contract may have been modified by subsequent legislation. A contract cannot be said to be void merely because it has been modified by a notification issued under section 19 of the Contract Act. The modification must be deemed to be a condition precedent to the validity of the contract itself. The modification can be proved to have been made either expressly or by necessary implication. In the present case, the modification was not made in accordance with the provisions contained in section 175(2) of the Act.

1518: The appellants purchased the properties in dispute from respondent No. 1 under section 128(f) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. 1785: The petitioner was selected by the Madras Public Service Commission as a Lower Division Clerk under the Madras Ministerial Service Rules, 1959. He was allotted to the Revenue Department and posted in South Kanara District. In 1956, the Government of India issued an order reducing the petitioner in rank from the post of Upper Division Clerk to that of Upper Division clerk. The petitioner challenged this order before the High Court. The High Court held that the proviso to section 115(7) of the Act was not applicable to him because he had been promoted as Upper Division Clerk with effect from April 2, 1956, but was not selected as he was not considered fit for inclusion in the eligibility list from 1955 onwards. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The proviso to section 5 of the Act is not intended to affect the operation of the provisions of Chapter of Part XIV of the Constitution in relation to determination of conditions of service of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union or any State. [551 G] (ii) The proviso does not apply to cases where the conditions of service are varied to his disadvantage after November 1, 1956. It only applies to cases where there is no such provision in the Act. The proviso does nothing more than make it obligatory that the conditions of services should be varied to his advantage after November 1. 1956. [552 D E] (iii) The proviso cannot be construed as giving any retrospective effect to the proviso. The proviso must be read subject to the object of the Act. If the object of a statute is to give retrospective effect to all matters within the purview of the enactment then the same would be contrary to the purpose and intent of the legislature. [553 F H]
351: The petitioners were tenants of certain villages in the State of Punjab. They had been paying rent to the State Government for the same land and had been paying the same rent to the Government. In the year 1949, the Government decided that the rates of rent should be fixed on the basis of the average of ten years preceding the settlement of the jagirs of the petitioners. The petitioners challenged the validity of this decision by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. The Act was a piece of legislation with respect to the regulation of the conditions of service of the tenants and the fixation of rents payable by them. The Act did not impose any restrictions on the right of the tenants to hold agricultural lands or to enjoy them as tenants. The Act imposed no restrictions on the rights of the tenants. The provisions of the Act were not applicable to the petitioners as they were not tenants of the State. The Act could not be said to have made any discrimination between the tenants who were holding agricultural lands and those who were holding such lands. The Act therefore violated articles 14 and 31(2) of the Constitution and was void.

In 1955, the appellant filed an application under section 10(1)(a) of the Indian Divorce Act, seeking a decree for divorce on the ground that the respondent had deserted him for a continuous period of not less than one year immediately preceding the date of the petition and that the appellant had no reasonable cause for not returning to the matrimonial home when she was there in connection with her passport, and that the respondent was guilty of desertion. The trial court dismissed the application but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellant was guilty of having deserted the respondent for a continuous time of not less one year immediately before the date of marriage and that the conduct of the respondent in not returning to her matrimonial house after permission had been obtained from her father in law and after she had herself taken her father 's place, amounted to "desertion" as contemplated by section 10(i)(a). The High Court held that the appellant could not be said to have deserted the husband for a continuous or partial period of not more than one year before the date on which the petition for judicial separation was filed. It further held that the respondent could not be deemed to have deserated the appellant for the purpose of section 10(2) (b) of the Act. 4189: The respondents were charged for violation of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 and the Imports & Exports (Control) Act, 1947. They were convicted under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5(2) of the Act and sentenced to two years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000 and in default, to suffer further six months ' rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence to one year 's 'punishment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The facts proved by the prosecution fell short of establishing that the accused had 'attempted ' to export silver in contravention of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, . 1947. [1162 B] 2. There was no evidence to show that the respondents attempted to smuggle out of India silver in contravention or that they made preparations and with the intention to commit the offence. The fact that the respondents did not make any attempt to bring the silver within the meaning of section 5(3) of the , does not mean that they intended to commit the offences. [1163 C D] 3. The High Courts' view is supported by the decision of this Court in State of Bombay vs Kusaldas Somayya, A.I.R. 1958 S.C. 702. In that case, the High Court held that the respondents ' attempt to smuggle gold into India was an act amounting to a direct movement towards the commission of the offence. It was also held that the acts of the respondents amounted to "an act done during the course of the employment" and that the respondents could not be said to have committed the offence of criminal conspiracy unless they actually knew that the gold would be smuggled out of India. [1164 E F]
5886: The petitioner and his wife filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the acquisition proceeding initiated by the State Government for acquiring the land. The Land Acquisition Officer passed an award on 19.1.1984 fixing the market value of the land at Rs.4,000 per acre. The petitioner challenged the acquisition proceeding in a petition under article 226 of the constitution before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice of the award was served on the petitioner only on 30.9.1986 and since more than two years had elapsed from the date of the publication of the notification under section 3(1) of the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, the acquisition proceedings should be declared as having lapsed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the notice of award having been served on him on 30.09.1986, the acquisition proceeding should be deemed to have lapsed; and (ii) that the land acquisition proceeding having been completed within two years from the date on which the notice of acquisition was served on him, the acquisition could not be said to have lapsed. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The period of limitation prescribed for making an application seeking reference to the Civil Court is one year from the date when the Collector takes possession of the land after he has made the award. [650C] 2. The proviso to section 11 A of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 provides that where the award is made on the date of expiry of the period specified in sub section (2), if any dispute arises as to the correctness of the amount of compensation awarded by the Collector or as to the person to whom the balance of the amount is payable. It also provides that the determination of the dispute shall be conclusive proof of the fact of the matter referred to the arbitrator. [653E F]
4732: The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling spares and materials. It supplied to the Indian Air Force aircrafts, instrument or accessory in which the spare parts were used in the execution of service contracts. The spare parts were sent to the appellant for servicing the air force. The spare part was then returned to the appellant on the ground that it was not sufficient to meet the requirements of the air force and that the spare parts had been replaced by another spare. The appellant claimed that the spare part was liable to be taxed as a sale under section 5(2) (a) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The Sales Tax authorities rejected the claim. The High Court held that the contract was a works contract only and not a contract for sale. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the contract in question was a works Contract only and not an agreement to sell the spare parts. The work done by the appellant was not a works contract but a contract for services and labour. The work was done on the basis of contracts or job orders issued from time to time. The spare items were supplied to the appellant as a result of their use in the process of repairing, servicing and overhauling of a specified aircraft. The spare item was not a work contract. The spare was not a "works contract" within the meaning of section 5(1)(b) of the Act.
252: The appellants were charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947 for receiving from Shankar Das Gupta a sum of Rs. 2,400 as premium or 160 pugree in respect of the grant of a lease. The appellants accepted the sum of Rs, 2,400 and paid it to the complainant. The complainant was not willing to accept the amount but the appellants refused to accept it. The appellants then instituted a suit against the complainant for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that they had received Rs. 2.400 as premium and Rs. 160 pugrees in respect of an agreement of lease executed by them with the complainant. It was contended that even if the receipt of Rs.2,400 could be held to be a payment within the mischief of section 18(I) of the Act, the receipt would not bring the case within the mischief. Held, that the appellants were entitled to recover possession of the property on the basis of the oral agreement of the complainant and the acceptance of Rs. 1,400 by the appellants. The word " payment" in section 18(l) means payment made voluntarily and without consideration. The word 'payment ' is used in the sense of making a contract between the parties. In the present case the payment was made by the complainant to the appellants in pursuance of an agreement which was entered into by them with their landlord. The appellants did not receive any money on the execution of the agreement. The appellants were not liable to pay the amount of Rs. 75 per month to the complainant because the complainant had no right to receive the amount.

The firm had obtained a lease for collection of tendu leaves from the forest units in the State and had also applied to the Divisional Forest Officer for permission to transport the leaves from the godowns of the forest units to the factories. The Divisional Forest Officer, Saugor seized two quantities of such leaves of 9007 bags imported from the State Government or its agent and seized two quantities each of 9007 bagats of tendu leaf grown in the State. The respondents ' grievance was that notwithstanding the communication and in spite of the fact that they had not moved the imported leaves from their godowns, the Sub Divisional Forest Officer Saugor took them out of the factory premises of the firm and seized two quantity of tendu liens from the godown of the firm. The High Court rejected the contention of the State. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Act does not prohibit the import of tendu Leaves into the State of M.P. by a person who is not an Indian citizen. Section 5(2) of the Act provides that no person shall transport any tendu leaves except under a permit granted by the Divisional Forest officer. [880C] (ii) The Act did not prohibit the transport of tendu bles whether grown in the state or outside the State. Section 3 of the Act empowered the State Government to fix prices at certain other places in the State where the tendu plants were to be grown. 4281: The appellant was the adopted son of a Hindu. He executed a deed of adoption in favour of his father on August 10, 1944. The deed recited that the appellant 's father had been appointed as a guardian of the adopted son and that he would be entitled to take care of the adopted child if he was not able to do so. The appellant presented the deed for registration on September 11, 1944, but the Registrar refused to register it on the ground that Mansaram was not in a fit state of mind at the relevant time. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that Mansram was in a fit condition of being adopted by him and that he was entitled to the benefit of the deed of adoption. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the deed of adopting was valid and that the deed did not confer on the appellant any right of an adopted son. On appeal the District Judge set aside the decree of the trial court and decreed the suit. In second appeal the High Court held that the deed dated August 10, 1946, which is impugned in the present suit was invalid because it did not mention the name of the person who was present at the time of adoption and that the fact that the adoption took place in the year 1944 was not proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the deed was void ab initio and that the High Court erred in setting aside the judgment of the courts below and dismissing the suit. HELD: (i) The deed of adoption dated August 10. 1944, which is challenged in the present case, does not contain the factum of adoption. [597 H] (ii) The deed dated August 4, 1944, which purports to appoint the appellant as the guardian of the minor children of the adoptive father, clearly shows that the appellant had taken the adoption. The deed of appointment of the appellant was not signed by the guardian. The deed merely stated that the appellant "was in sound health" and that he should take care of his children. 7035: The appellant, who was a resident of the village of the deceased, was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. for causing death of his wife and two minor children by assaulting them with sticks and daggers. He was also charged under section 323 I.P,.C. for having caused injuries to the deceased with a crowbar. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 304 Part II I.P.,C. on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the case because of enmity between the parties. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the evidence of PW3, PW4 and PW5 is not reliable; (ii) the evidence given by them is highly unreliable; and (iii) the possibility of the accused being falsely implicated cannot be ruled out. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that the courts have no difficulty in basing conviction on the testimony of a single witness provided it is trustworthy and cogent. [766A] 1.2 The mere fact that the witness has turned hostile does not necessarily mean that he has been disbelieved. The court has to scrutinise the evidence objectively and to see whether the version of the witnesses is credible or otherwise. If the court finds that the version of such witnesses is unacceptable then there is no reason why the court should not accept the evidence of such witness. [767B C] 1.3 There is no legal bar for convicting a person on the basis of the evidence of a single eye witness if his evidence suffers from some other infirmity. But it is necessary to remember that such a principle is based on the principle that evidence of an injured witness is not required for prosecution where the presence of the witness is doubtful. [768E F] 1.4 Where the evidence of the victim of the crime is found to be totally inconsistent with her statement made before the police, the one who claims to have seen the occurrence cannot be believed. [769F G] 1.5 The court has a duty to separate the chaff from the grain unless the truth is itself clear. [
2097: The appellant was a T.B. Hospital and its business was situated in the State of Rajasthan. The appellant purchased plots for various fixed amounts and paid the price thereof. The Government of Rajasthan issued notification dated May 18, 1955 offering the plots to the appellant on payment of the customs duty at the rate of Rs. 1 per plot. The appellant thereupon filed a suit against the State of Jodhpur and the Union of India for recovery of the amount due under the contract. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that item No. 3 of the Bharatpur notification was a term of sale between the parties and the Rajasthan State was bound by it and the succeeding States had recognised the concessions granted to the appellant and therefore the suit should be decreed. It merely provided that the goods were to be exported from the State of Bharatpur. [88 A B] (vi) The notification cannot be construed as a rule of construction. 6937: The appellant was a former Judge of the High Court who dismissed his writ petition in motion hearing without hearing him. He filed an application for review of the order dismissing the writ petition on the ground that there was error apparent on the face of the record because the writ petition was dismissed in motion hearing and thereafter the Review Petition on 23.4.79 and also impleaded Shri R.P. Singh, Advocate General who had been appointed as amicus curiae to assist the Court. The Division Bench of the High court after examining the matter held that the contempt petition was not maintainable under section 16 of the Act and dismissed the same. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court committed serious errors in entertaining the contempt petition and passing orders which were contrary to the rules framed by it; that the notice served upon the contemner did not show sufficient cause as to why he should not be punished for contempt of Court to which the appellant moved a Contempt Petition on 16.4.80 and thereafter the review petition on 23. 4.79 and again the respondent No. 2 was informed about the date of hearing fixed for hearing and the petitioner 's counsel was asked to appear before the Court on 24.5.80 and the petitioner was directed to file his reply within 10 days; that the petitioner ' s advocate appeared before the Court and made a statement that he would not press the petition and that he would be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The Division bench rejected the objections raised by the appellant/contemner holding that the cognizance of the criminal contempt was taken by it on suo moto action by the High Court, that the contemner was informed that the Court was invoking its jurisdiction under Article 215 of the Constitution of India to punish him for contempt, that the notice was not necessary, that the procedure followed by the High court was contrary to the Rules framed by it, and that the contemnor was informed that Court was exercising its jurisdiction under article 215 of the constitution of India to remove the name of the Advocate General from the roll of the High Courts. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Court has rightly exercised its jurisdiction under section 16(2) of the Act. [872C] 1.
1090: The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was granted leave to its workmen for a period of one month. The respondents claimed privilege leave with full salary and dearness allowance on completion of eleven months service in a year with a right to accumulate upto six months. The Tribunal held that the appellant had no jurisdiction to make such an award having regard to the provisions of section 79(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 79(2)(a) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, is not applicable to industrial adjudication and so the Tribunal had no jurisdiction under section 79(I) to make such a award. HELD : (i) Section 79(1), as it stood at the relevant time, provided that "no workman shall be entitled to receive from an employer any compensation or gratuity except - (a) an employee 's notice of discharge or dismissal; (b) a payment to him as compensation in lieu of notice;" [326 F] (ii) The words "no workman" in section 79(l) are used in a comprehensive sense to include all persons employed in any industry to do any work which is necessary for the working of such industry. But the words "any person" in section 78(1) are not intended to cover all classes of employees but only those who are employed in connection with the affairs of the undertaking. [327 B C] (iii) The words 'any person ' in section 79 have been used in a wider sense to include even those who are not covered by the said section. [328 D] (iv) The words used in section 79 are wide enough to include all categories of workmen including those who are members of the same class. [329 E] (v) The words `any person ' occurring in section 79 must be given their widest meaning and they should be construed in their popular sense. [330 A] (vi) The words employed in section 79 cannot be interpreted in a narrow and pedantic sense. They must be read in their ordinary sense. 7019: The respondent issued a notice on 10.7.1975 determining the lease in favour of the appellant with effect from 31.7.75. As the suit premises had not been let out for any manufacturing purpose, it was an admitted position that the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 was not applicable. On appeal being filed by the appellant, the Assistant Judge came to the conclusion that the premises in question had not been leased out for any industrial purpose but for a motor workshop and as such the notice under section 106 of the Act was valid and the respondent was entitled to the possession of the plot in dispute. The second appeal filed by the respondent was dismissed in limine by the High Court saying that no substantial question of law was involved. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even if it is held that bar under clause 13A is only on respect of passing of the decree as appeal before this Court, it shall be deemed that this Court has passed a decree for eviction which in view of the bar imposed by clause 13A would be barred and the said bar is applicable even on this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The bar imposed by Clause 13A is merely on the basis of the permission granted by the Controller under clause 13(2) of the Order. [866F] 1.2. The bar does not operate as a bar against passing of the order. It is only when the order is passed by the Controller after hearing the parties or their representatives, as the case may be, that the bar operates. [867G H] 1.3. The bar is not limited to the passing of the final decree. It applies to all proceedings pending before any court including this Court. [868B C] 1.4. The bar cannot operate as a stay of the execution proceedings pending before the Court. [886C D] 1.5. The bar will apply only where the final decree is passed by a competent court. [887D E] H.
