6740: The appellants were charged with the offence of rape under section 376(2)(g) I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for three years. The High Court, in appeal by special leave, reversed the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a case of rape, the evidence of the prosecutrix is required to be scrutinized carefully and not only that but also that of the prosecution witnesses. [811B C] 1.2 It is well settled that the court has to examine the broad probabilities of a case and weigh all the circumstances which are in favour of the accused. If on such examination and hearing the court comes to the conclusion that the case put up by the prosecution does not suffer from any infirmity then it is open to the court to reject the plea of the accused as being gospel truth. [812E F] 1.3 In the instant case, the victim girl was more than 16 years of age at the time of occurrence. She had been subjected to sexual intercourse by the appellants and they had tied her tutoring and she was raped by them. The evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 3 clearly shows that the victim girl had been forcibly taken away by the appellants. The evidence on record clearly establishes that the victim was more than 18 years of age. [813F G] 1.4 In the instant cases, the victim was less than 16 years at the time when she was ravished by the appellants, and therefore, the courts below rightly convicted the appellants under section 376 read with section 34 I.P,C. [814G H; 815A B] 1.5 In the instant appeals, the appellants have failed to make out any ground for interference with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the Courts below. [816D E]
1611: The respondent was convicted under section 323 and section 324 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code. He was released on bail by the High Court but he did not appear before the District Magistrate, Patna, when the petition for his release was taken up. On an application by the respondent, the High Court directed that the appellant State should appear on Monday following which was May 5, 1958, when the matter was to be taken up for preliminary hearing. The High Court ordered that the appellant 's application for release be heard on Mondays following which the respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High court allowed the petition and directed the appellant State to surrender to custody. The appellant State appealed against this order to this Court. Held: (i) The order of release by the District Magistrate of Patna on March 11, 1958, was an order for his unconditional release and therefore he could not be rearrested. The order of detention was an order made under section 3(1)(a) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, and it was open to the appellant State Government to move the High Court for cancellation of the order of detention. The order was an order of conditional release of the respondent from jail and the High Court had no jurisdiction to issue any direction for his release. (ii)The order of release passed by the District magistrate was an order directing him to be taken into custody and sent him to jail. The order merely required the respondent to appear before the court on Mondday and he was entitled to have his case considered by the High court. The order did not amount to an order for the release of the accused.

P.C. till he filed the petition for quashing. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1. The High court has quashed the First Information Reports on the ground of unexplained delay in the investigations of a criminal proceeding. [844D] 1.2. The High Courts power to quash an F.I.R. is circums tant with the powers conferred by section 482 Cr. P C. [845A] 1.3. The power of quashing is discretionary and can be exercised only when the ends of justice so demand. It is not possible to lay down any rigid rule as to what should be the standard of quashing in a criminal case. This is particularly true in cases where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused. [846E G] 1.4. The power to quash the FIR is discretionary and it cannot be exercised like a private interest. [847F] 1.5. The High courts power to quash criminal proceedings is an extraordinary power which is inherently unfettered but is limited to exceptional cases. [848G H; 849A B] 1.6. The High Powered Committee was justified in refusing to quash the First Information Re port on the ground, inter alia, that there was inordinate delay in the invocation of the First Informatio n Report. 5847: The appellant was allotted a flat on 6th floor of Nibhana Building by the disputant No.2, the respondent No. 2. The appellant filed a dispute before the Co operative Court for recovery of possession of the said flat alleging inter alia that the appellant was inducted in the flat without the written consent of the Society as a licencee and called upon the appellant to remove itself from the said flat. The appellant having failed to comply with the request, a dispute was filed by the member, that is, the respondent no.2 terminating the licence and calling upon the appellant for vacating the flat. The respondent No.2 also terminated the licence and called upon him to remove himself from the said premises. The appellant claimed to be hi m continuing in possession of the flat on the basis of a leave and licence agreement which was a renewed from time to time till some time in 1972 and on Ist October 1972, the member, the that is, respondent No.1 terminated the licence. The appellant 's claim was resisted by the respondent No 1 contending that they were inducted in th e flat as a trespasser after the licence in favour of the appellant was terminated. The appellant contended that he was occupying the flats in question as a trespassers after the licence was terminated. It was also contended that the appellant had not paid the licence fee uptill now and as such the dispute does not come within section 91 of the Co operative Societies Act as they have become tenants under section 15 of the Bombay Rent Act. The appellate authority held that the dispute fell within the jurisdicton of the Co operation Court as the appellant claimed to being hi m continued in possession of flat on the ground that the appellant claimed t o be hi s occupation as a trespassee after the licence, that is to say, the appellant was occupying the flat as a licensee and that the appellant could not transfer the flat in question in any manner whatsoever. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal. In the Writ Petition filed by the appellant, the High Court held that the appellant has been in possession of a flat since the date of his licence and that the dispute raised by the appellant falls within section 91(1) of the Co 'Act as it is not a dispute falling within the purview of section 91
468: The petitioner was a Sub Inspector of Police in the then State of Bhopal. He was prosecuted and convicted for offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Judicial Commissioner held that no sanction had been given by the Chief Minister to prosecute him and the Special Judge took cognizance of the case without a valid sanction. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed against the petitioner on the ground that the sanction had not been given by a competent authority. Held, that the order of the Chief Minister was illegal and void. The Chief Minister had no power to take cognizance of the offence without a legal sanction. The Chief Secretary had no power or jurisdiction to take cognizance without a valid legal sanction. It was not necessary that the Chief Minister should have obtained the sanction of the Governor before taking cognizance of the offences. The Chief Commissioner had no power of sanction at all. The Chief Engineer had no power whatsoever to grant sanction. The sanction had not become invalid merely because the Chief Engineer did not obtain the sanction.
2791: The appellants were charged with the offence of theft under section 379 I.P.C. and section 395 I.P,C. for having committed theft in a house belonging to the deceased. The prosecution case was that the appellants had stolen the buffalo and that they were keeping it in village Gunpara, police station Dankaur in Uttar Pradesh. The prosecution alleged that the appellants ' party had come to search for the buffle and that they had been beaten up by the police. The appellants pleaded that they had not taken the police station house officer to conduct the search under section 166(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court found that the appellants could not be convicted on the ground that the police party had not taken them to be dacoits. The High Court held that the action of the appellants was criminal because they knew that it was a police party. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The powers of the police station officer are not confined to this only because sub section 3 of section 166 of the Code gives the right and authority to the police station officers to conduct the searches under section 166 of Code of Criminal procedure. [1101 C] (ii) The power of the police officer to conduct search under section 165 of the Code is not limited to this only but he can do so if he has reason to believe that delay would be occasioned by requiring the officer in charge of the other police station to cause the search to be made and as a result evidence of the commission of the offence would be concealed or destroyed. [1100 B C] (iii) The police party at Dankaur was mixed up with the appellants and the police party was taken to the police post office where the appellants were kept. The police party was then taken to the Sub Inspector who was present there. The appellants were arrested and brought to the police lock up. The police force was also taken into custody. The appellants did not question the police party about their arrest. Therefore, the arrest and recovery of the articles from the appellants were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. [1102 E F]
1559: The appellants were dealers in sugar. They sold sugar to the State of Madras and the State of Tamil Nadu. The sale was not complete but was completed by the end of the year, and the sales were effected after the commencement of the Constitution. The State of Madras enacted the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, which provided for levy of tax on the sale or purchase of goods. The Act provided that the tax shall be levied at the point of last purchase in the series of sales by successive dealers. The Act also provided for the levy of a tax on the value of goods. In the course of assessment proceedings for the years 1946 45, 1947 47 and 1949 50, the appellants contended that the transactions in which they sold sugar were not sales within the meaning of the Act and therefore could not be taxed under Entry 48 of List II of the Seventh Schedule. The contention was rejected by the Sales Tax Officer who assessed them to tax under the Act. The appellants filed appeals before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The appeals were allowed. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the sales were not sales inside the State and that there was no transfer of property in the goods involved in the transaction. It further held that the sale was not a sale in the course of inter state trade between the parties. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The definition of sale in the two Acts at all material times was: "'sale" means, with all its grammatical variations and cognate expressions, a transfer of property from one person or thing to another in the ordinary course of law, whether by act of parties or by operation of law. A sale is a deemed sale. [801 G] (ii) The word 'sale ' has been defined in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, as meaning any contract in writing containing an offer or promise of anything. The word 'transfer ' has been used in the Act in the sense of transfer of property. [802 B C] (iii) The definition does not include a mortgage, hypothecation, charge or pledge; it only includes a mortgage by deposit of title deeds. [803 D] (iv) The definition is wide enough to cover every kind of transfer of right to use any goods.
3193: The appellant was the returned candidate for the Safidon Assembly Constituency No. 30, in which he had filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent on several grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of section 81(3) of the Act inasmuch as the requisite number of spare copies were not filed along with the petition within the period of limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court erred in dismissing the election petition on the ground that the appellant had failed to file the election petition within the time prescribed; and (ii) the delay in filing the election petition was due to the fact that the appellant was not aware of the defect in the election petition. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 80(1) are mandatory and non compliance thereof is a serious infirmity vitiating the election. [278C] 2. The provision of section 81 (3) is mandatory and noncompliance thereof would render the election void. [279E] 3. The provision is mandatory and not directory. It is only when the statute requires something to be done that it is said that something is to be done 'at the same time '. If the provision is merely directory but no other provisions are necessary for the performance of the thing required to be done, the non compliance with the provision will render the entire proceedings illegal. But if there is some other provision of law which is also mandatory and non non compliance therewith would render the entire proceeding illegal, the provision is mandatory. [280B C]
3421: The respondent company was a private limited company. It had its Head Office at Bombay. These workmen were laid off in accordance with law with effect from 5th February, 1968. The lay off of the workmen whose names were mentioned in the notice was recalled by the management on the 22nd April, 1968. This lay off was in operation and the workmen were not given their wages or compensation for the period of lay off. An industrial dispute raised by the workmen was referred to the Labour Court. The Labour Court held that the workmen were entitled to lay off compensation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the lay off was not illegal as the workmen were required to be paid compensation; (2) the layoff was not illegal because the workmen were prevented from working for more than two hours in a day; (3) the lay-off was not legal and justified; (4) the workmen were also entitled to full wages and dearness allowance for the period they remained out of employment; (5) the lay Off was not illegal since the workmen were denied work which would have been available to them if they had worked for one hour only; (6) the lay Ofter was bad because the workmen did not get any bonus for the whole day; (7) the lay ofter was bad inasmuch as it was not given to the workmen who were not paid bonus for the entire day; (8) the layof off was illegal because the lay off had been done without giving the workmen an opportunity of being heard; (9) the lay ' off was bad because it was not legally permissible to do so; (10) the lay Was bad because the lay Off had not been given to the employees; (11) the lay Out was bad because no notice was given to the workers before the lay off; (12) the layover was bad because there was no lay off; and (13) the layOfter was bad since the lay off itself was illegal because it was made without giving the workers an opportunity of hearing. HELD: (i) The lay off was illegal as the lay off gave the workmen sufficient notice of the intended lay off. [380 B] (ii) The lay Off was bad because notice
2297: The appellant, a former Judge of the High Court of Assam, was appointed as a Commission of Enquiry by the Chief Justice of the Gauhati High Court. He filed an application for stay of his order of stay granted by the Chief Jus tion on November 3, 1969 and also prayed that he should be allowed to function as a Judge of the Gauahti High Court. The petition was heard by a Bench consisting of the learned Chief Justice and Mr. Justice Dutta who had passed the order staying the operation of the order of stay. The appellant contended that the order of the Chief Justice could not be said to have been made without jurisdiction and that the order was bad in law because it was not made in accordance with the procedure laid down by the Code of Civil Procedure. Held: (i) A Judge of the Supreme Court is appointed under the Act to head Commissions for various purposes; he is appointed to discharge all or any of the functions assigned to him under the Act; he is not a Judge of a High Court within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Act. (ii) In any case as the seat of the High.Court was at Gauhati, Mr. Justice Das Gupta was working as a Commission 'of Enquiry ' and that appointment was in our opinion quite in order. (iii) The order of stay was not a stay order but only an interim order. It did not operate as res judicata against the appellant.
3390: The appellants were the subscribers to a telephone exchange. They had been using the telephones for their own purpose and were not in a position to pay the rent of the telephone exchange. On November 28, 1972, the appellants made an application to the Divisional Engineer stating that they would be taking temporary possession of the telephonecases and non exchange lines. The Divisional Engineer passed orders on November 28,1972 directing the appellants to restore the telephony. The appellants challenged the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was allowed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the impugned action was bad because: (a) no prior notice in regard to the same was given to the appellants; (b) the Divisional Engineer did not apply his mind and record his own satisfaction about the existence of any emergency; (c) the reason given in the impugned order, to the effect, that the appellants were making illegal and improper use of their telephones inasmuch as they were transmitting messages and information in regard to satta business which had been banned, was irrelevant and extraneous to Rule 422 under which the impugned action has been purportedly taken; (d) the reason for the impugned order was that the appellants could not have been asked to pay the amount of rent for the period of their stay in the telephoned post. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of notice under section 5(1) of the Telegraphs Act is not the same as a public emergency. It is a condition precedent for the exercise of power under section 5. [523C] 2. The expression 'public emergency ' in rule 422 means 'an emergency ' declared under section 5, but not 'any other emergency ' declared by the Central Government under section 5 of the Act. [524D] 3. The word 'public emergency' in rule 421 means 'an emergent situation ' declared under sec. 5 of the Telegraph Act. [552E] 4. The expression "public emergency" in rule 442 means "an emergency". [553F]
6645: The Government granted land to the Ziarat in lieu of his possessory right over about 400 kanals of land. The Ziarat was subsequently transferred by the Government in favour of their father in his personal capacity. The Zir was then transferred to the Zamindar. The Zamindar executed a deed of trust dated September 22, 1955 in respect of the land in dispute and the Zirat was registered as a public trust under section 5(1) (a) of the Jammu & Kashmir Public Trust Act, 1960. The Zikar was also registered as a private trust under section 6 of the Act. The Zidar died on November 30, 1956. The Zidars were succeeded by the defendants who claimed that they had acquired title to the land in question by adverse possession. The Z iddar contended that the Ziawar was not a public trust but a private trust and that the Zidar had no title to the property. The Zirmat filed a suit against the Ziardar for a declaration that the Zizardari was a public trust and that he was entitled to deal with the property in any manner he liked on the ground that the same belonged to him. The Zivas was held to be a public trust by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the zamindari was a public one and the Zamindar was not entitled to deal in the land in any manner whatsoever. HELD: The Zamindar was a public charitable trust and the Zidar was a trustee for the Zamindar and the Zamindars were entitled to deal only in the manner prescribed by the Act. [257 H] The Zamindar could not claim to have acquired title by adverse possession or adverse possession. He was merely a trustee for Zamindar. It was not a trust created for the benefit of the Zamindar or for the benefit or benefit of the public. [258 A] The Zidar was not a person interested within the meaning of section 4(2)(b) of the Act and therefore could not be regarded as a person interested in the trust. [259 B] The Zirman was a public Trust and the Zirdari was a private one. The Zuru was a public religious trust and the zamindar was
2618: The first respondent joined the State Service in 1937. He was absorbed as a Sales Tax Officer, Class III in the former State of Bombay after merger. In December 1962 he was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of attempt to obtain illegal gratification from certain cloth dealers. A departmental enquiry was held and on March 15, 1963, the Enquiry Officer submitted his report holding that the charges were proved against him. On March 15, 1964, the first respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of removal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that since the recommendations of the Enquiry Officer contained in the matter of punishment were wholly redundant and irrelevant, it could not be said that there was failure to comply with the requirements of article 311(2) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The first respondent was entitled to a copy of the report of the Enquiry officer containing his findings on the various charges which had been found to have been proved against him but the Enquiry Officer made some recommendations regarding the punishment which in his opinion should be inflicted on the first respondent. The first respondent did not make any recommendation about the punishment which would be imposed on him if he was called upon to show cause against the proposed penalty. [254 E F] (ii) The first question raised before the High Court was whether the failure to send a copy of his report of the enquiry to the first respondent vitiated the proceedings. The High court rightly observed that since the recommendation of the Enquiry Report contained in the report of enquiry was a part of the appropriate material for the consideration of the Government in the matter, the Enquiry officer was not required to make any such recommendation as to the punishment which may be imposed on the first Respondent on the charges against him. [255 G H; 256 A B]
2435: The petitioner, a Pakistani National Front of India (P) Ltd., was detained under section 3(1)(a) of the . The grounds of detention were that the petitioner "did not report to the Government any matter relating to the activities of the petitioner as a member of the State Legislature or any other party in the Assembly or in any other body". The detaining authority was satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the detention. The order of detention was confirmed by the State Government and the petitioner was arrested on December 12, 1968. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the order of detention. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the delay in sending the report could not have been avoided by the Commissioner and that when they were sent by him, they were sent 'forthwith ' within the meaning of section 3(3). HELD: The delay in sending report could not be avoided by the detaining authority because the report was not made on the 12th. The order was passed on the 13th. It is true that the District Magistrate was hard put to for time and the local Government had communicated his decision to the detenu. But the fact remains that the order of the District Magistrate did not contain any reference to the report of the Collector. The District Magistrate was very clear about the facts and circumstances of the case. [819 B] The order of the State Government was not an independent order but only a communication of the decision of the District Collector. The order merely stated that the report of Collector was considered and that the representation of the petitioner was rejected. The order also mentioned that the District Collector had given his opinion that the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to the interest of the State. The order further mentions that the District Superintendent of Police had informed the petitioner that he should make a representation to the State Government against the order of his detention. The District Superintendent of police was clearly aware of the fact that the petitioner was being prosecuted for offences punishable under the Indian Penal Code. He was therefore fully aware of the facts and the circumstances of the cases. [820 C D; 821 A B]
1748: The petitioners, who were members of a joint Hindu family governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law, filed a suit in the Court of the Chief Commissioner for the State of Tripura against the Ruler of the State of West Bengal and the Union of India praying that the said Act be declared ultra vires. The petitioners contended that the said section was ultra vires because it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution as it infringed their fundamental rights under article 14 and 19 (1)(f). The petitioners also alleged that the Ruler had no authority to sanction the expenditure on the allowances of the members of the Ruling Family without any regard to their status and their legitimacy. Held, that the provisions of section 87B(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are not applicable to the case of the petitioners. The provisions of section 86(4) of the Act are not applicable where the Ruler is a Ruler of an Indian State. Section 87B(2) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, which provides that the provisions Of section 85 and of sub sections (1) and (3) of section 86 shall apply in relation to the Rulers of former Indian States, does not contravene article 14 of the Constitution. The provisions contained in section 87B of the Code cannot be read into section 86(2) and section 86(5) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The provisions relating to the payment of allowances of the Ruler of an erstwhile Indian State are not applicable in the present case. The provisions regarding the payment of allowance of the Ruler are not applicable when the Ruler of a former Indian State is a Ruler. The provisions in section 87 B(1) are not applicable if the Ruler of one of the Indian States is a Ruler and the other is a Ruler or a Ruler of another State.
3489: The respondent, a displaced person from West Pakistan, applied to the Estate Officer for fixation of standard rent. The Estate Officer passed an order on September 28, 1960 under section 7(1) of the , directing the respondent to pay the amount demanded by him. The respondent 's appeal to the Additional District Judge was dismissed and the High Court allowed his writ petition in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 7 does not bar the remedy of recovery of arrears of rent due before the Estate Officer. [880C] (ii) The right to recover arrears of rent is a statutory right which can be enforced only by a creditor whose suit is barred by limitation. [881D] (iii) The expression "any person" in section 7 means a person who has been in arrears of rent payable in respect of any public premises. The word "payable" in section 3 includes all persons who are entitled to receive the rent in respect of the public premises. [882F] (iv) The right of recovery of rent in respect thereof is a statutory one. It is not a vested right. [883A] (v) The right conferred by section 7 is a statutory proceeding and cannot be taken away except by express enactment or necessary intendment. [884B]
4072: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain jewellery belonging to the Nizam 's Jewellery Trust. The appellant purchased the said jewellery from the Nizam ' 's Jewellers in the year 1957 and sold it to the respondent on March 9, 1978. The respondent, who had been the Managing Trustee of the Jewellery Trust, filed a suit for recovery of the jewellery and other articles mentioned in the Schedule to the plaint alleging that the sale of the jewellery was illegal and void as the respondent had not complied with the terms of the trust deed. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale was illegal and invalid and that the respondent was entitled to recover the jewellery and the other articles mentioned therein. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sale in question was not binding on them because the respondent had accepted their bids at the time when they were put up for sale and that the acceptance of the bid by the respondent would amount to frustration of contract. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondent was entitled under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure to recover the gold ornaments which he had received from the respondent during his lifetime. [817C] 2.1. The respondent having accepted the offer of the appellant and having accepted the same, the appellant cannot now be heard to say that the respondent has no right to recover the ornaments. [818B C] 3.2. The respondent is entitled to recover his share in the jewellery. [819D] 3.3. The respondent has not been able to show any valid contract between him and the appellant. The respondent had accepted the offer made by the appellant and the appellant had accepted the same. The respondent did not dispute the acceptance of his offer. He had accepted the said offer. The respondent could not therefore claim any benefit out of the acceptance of such offer. [820E F] 4.1. It is true that the respondent had agreed to sell the jewellery to the appellant but the appellant had not done so. The respondent never disputed the acceptance of offer. The appellant had accepted all the offerings.
5027: The appellant was granted a quarry lease for the period ending with 31st March, 1984. The first respondent, the State of Haryana and the second respondent the Director of Industries, Haryana, granted a quarry licence to M/s Pioneer Crushing Co., for the period commencing from 1st April, 1984. On the question whether the appellant could have been granted a quarry contract without giving him an opportunity of being heard, the High Court held that the appellant had not made out any case for interference. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant was entitled to a quarry contract and that the High court should have given reasons for granting the grant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the grant of quarry contract is not a matter of right but a matter of discretion. [546C] 1.2 The grant of quarry lease is governed by the provisions of the Haryana Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964 as applicable to the State of Punjab. The appellant did not participate in the auction nor did he make false allegations against the appellant whose bid was the highest. The appellant had no locus standi to challenge the action of the Chief Minister in issuing the quarry lease. [547E F] 1.3 The appellant had not challenged the action of Chief Minister in refusing to confirm the auction. The High Court was justified in quashing the order of the Chief Secretary. [548A B] 1.4 The appellant had participated in the auction and then made false allegations against him which were baseless. [549B] 1.5 The appellant had made false allegations in the writ petition. The High court was wrong in quashing the grant of the quarry lease in favour of the appellant. [550D]
1145: The appellant, a registered union of the Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh, Bombay, was awarded bonus for the years 1952 and 1953. The appellant challenged the validity of the award on the ground that it was not enforceable as an award by the Industrial Court against the appellant. The High Court held that the notification dated July 31, 1956, issued under section 114(2) of the Act was valid and did not contravene the provisions of article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The notification dated July 1, 1956, was in conformity with the industrial law laid down by the Full Bench of the Industrial Court and also by any decision of this Court. [110 D E] The appellant had been awarded bonus for certain years. The appellant had not signed the agreement or settlement but had written a letter to the Government of Bombay requesting that the award made by the Industrial Tribunal should be enforced against the appellant in exercise of the powers vested in the Government by section 114(3). The Government of Bombay had no power to issue such a direction. [110 F H] The appellant was entitled to enforce its rights under article 32 of the Constitution before the award could be enforced. [111 B C] The appellant cannot claim to be a workman within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution because the appellant is not a workman within that article. [111 D] The appellant has not been able to show that the award was invalid. [111 G] The appellant is not entitled to challenge the validity of an award on the grounds that it was invalid. It is only if the award is found to be invalid that the appellant can have recourse to the remedy available to it under article 226 of the Constitution for enforcement of its right. [111 E]
5346: The appellant landlord filed a petition under Section 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that the respondent was in occupation of a part of the building for his residence and had leased out the same to him to be used as a godown for storing his business ware. The Rent Controller held that the respondent had not been able to prove bona fide requirement of additional accommodation for his residential purpose and dismissed the petition for eviction. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Authority reversed the findings of the Rent Controller and also held that the Respondent was not entitled to recover possession of non residential premises for their residential requirements. The High Court allowed the revision petition and set aside the order of the Appellate Authority and restored the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in interfering with the finding of fact rendered by the Appellate Authority while exercising its revisional powers under section 25 of the Act. [847E] 2. The High Courts ' interference is permissible only when the finding is perverse or based on no evidence. [848F] 3. In any event the factors of relative hardship should be tween the parties weigh more in favour of the appellant than the respondent. [849G] 4. The High courts ' interference with the findings of fact is permissible only if they are perverse or based upon no evidence at all.[850A] 5. The High has rightly interfered with the findings. [851C]
1091: The respondent company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1952 53 under section 16(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 35 of the Act on January 25, 1954, and after giving an opportunity to the assessee to be heard in person or by agent, rectified the error and imposed additional tax at the rate of one anna in the rupee. The assessee filed a revision petition before the Commissioner of Income tax but the same was dismissed. Thereafter the respondent company filed a writ petition in the High Court of Kerala challenging the order of the Commissioner of Incometax. The High Court held that the orders made were without jurisdiction and therefore quashed the orders. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the order of rectification was not without jurisdiction; (ii) the Income tax Officer had no power to make the order which he did, and (iii) the order was without jurisdiction. HELD: (i) The order of rectification could not be said to be without jurisdiction because the proviso to section 18A(2) of the Act expressly provides that "any mistake apparent from the record" would mean any clerical or arithmetical mistake as defined in the Explanation to section 2 of the Finance Act, 1952. [866 C] (ii)The proviso to section 2(b) of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1956, is not applicable to the case of the respondent company. It is only a clarification of the provision that the proviso has been introduced into the Act with retrospective effect. [867 D E] (iii)The proviso does not apply to the facts of the present case. The proviso applies only where there is a mistake apparent on the face of the order. [868 F] (iv)In the instant case the order of assessment was passed on January 25th 1954, and the question of rectification arose only thereafter. The order of assessment having been passed on January 24th 1954, the proviso to Section 18A(5) was not attracted. [869 B]
6912: The plaintiffs filed a suit for possession of the suit premises on the ground that they were in arrears of rent and that the defendants had not paid the rent. The defendants contested the suit by filing written statement. The trial court held that the service of notice dated 7.8.1980 was not proved, as the defendants had made full payment as demanded in the notice and that the case did not fall under Section 12(3) (b) of the Act as the defendants failed to prove that the postal acknowledgment Exhibit 51 contained the correct address. The trial Court also held that the case does not fall under section 12(3)(b) of The Act as the defendant persistently committed default during the pendency of the suit and also the appeal in paying the rent. On appeal, the Additional District Judge reversed the finding of the trial court and held that the evidence of the plaintiff showed that the copy of the notice was sent to all the defendants by registered post. The appellate court confirmed the findings of the trial Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The presumption of service of notice in the facts of the present case is rebuttable. [10] 1.2. The burden of proof lies on the party who asserts that the notice was served on him. In the instant case, the defendants have admitted the receipt of the notice. They have denied the contents of the notice and have stated that it was sent by registered post to the addressee. The defendants have not led any other evidence to show that the postal acknowledgement was received by them. [11] 1.3. The defendants had made the payment of Rs. 55,800 on 16.1.1984 and thereafter made regular payment of Rs 600 every month. It is important to note that the defendants consistently maintained that the notice dated 7th August 1980 was duly served on the company and in the facts and circumstances of the present matter, the defence plea taken by the defendants that the notice could not be treated as valid notice was rejected. [12] 1.4. The defendants failed to rebut the presumption of service. The trial judge has rightly held that the presumption of good business was drawn under Section 114 of the Evidence Act. [13] 1.
7118: The appellant, a Lecturer in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology in Medical College Jabalpur applied for admission to the MBBS Course in the year 1989. He was selected by the State Government as a candidate belonging to the Scheduled Caste category. His application was rejected on the ground that he had not studied the subject of Anatomy, Physiology, Biochemistry, Preventive and Social Medicine including, Behavioural Science and Biostatistics, Medical Psychology and Developmental Studies and Medical Surgery. The first respondent challenged the rejection before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the migration could not be allowed because the ground was not sufficient for such migration. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The migration can not be allowed since the ground is not sufficient for it. However, the review petition was dismissed by the High Court on the ground of delay. [790C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant did not produce the required document. That led to the filing of Interlocutory Application No. 2805 of 1992 for grant of no objection to the transfer. The first Respondent claimed to have passed G.C.E. Biology, Physics and Chemistry and 'O ' level in six subjects i.e. It was also stated that he had studied the subjects in Anatomy and Physiology including, Behosisal Science and biochemistry and 'Nelastomonthly ' Physiology and 'Dental Psychology ' in the second year. Therefore, according to him, he possesses the eligibility criteria for admission to MBBS Degree Course at Jabalpur. [791B C] 1.3 The migration could have been allowed only if the ground was sufficient for such upgradation. But the review petition has been dismissed by the high court. [792F] 1.4 The migration cannot be allowed because of the fact that the ground was available to the candidates. [793G] 1.5 The migration should not be allowed unless the candidate produces the requisite documents. [795A] 1.6 The migration need not be permitted where the candidate does not possess
6184: The appellants were tenants of certain intermediary landlords known as Girasdars. They filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the ground that they had acquired title to the land by adverse possession and that they had become owners thereof by operation of law. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal reversed the decree holding that the Girasdar was entitled to separate allotment in respect of the land held by them jointly and the separate allotments made in their favour by the Girasdar were not binding on the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Girasdas are entitled to separate allotments in respect of land held by him jointly and the joint family consisting of the appellants and the respondents constituted a joint Hindu Family and (ii) the Girasidars were entitled to separate plots of land held jointly by them. HELD: (1) The Girasdari lands are not liable to be partitioned under section 4(2)(a) of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951. [560C] (2) The Girasadars have no interest in the result of these appeals. The Girasds are not entitled to separate allotments in respect of lands held by them separately. [540B] (3) The Girasidari lands were not liable to partition because they were joint family properties. [541A] (4) The Girasiadars were not entitled to any separate allotment in the Girasdiadars. [542E]
1946: The plaintiff, the first defendant and the second defendant are the legal representatives of the first defendant. The first defendant instituted a suit for a declaration that she was the owner of half share in the properties described in the schedule to the plaint and for partition and separate possession of her half share and for mesne profits. The plaintiff alleged that the property was the absolute property of her mother Puttananjamma and upon her death this property devolved on her and the first defendant as her mother 's heirs. Since,according to her, the first respondent did not want to join her as coplaintiff in the suit, she was joined as a defendant. The plaintiff claimed that she had a right to the suit properties and the first respondent had no right to the same. The trial court decreed the claim of the plaintiff but held that the first defendant was estopped from claiming possession of her share in the suit properties. The first appellate court dismissed the appeal filed by the first defendant but allowed the cross objection filed by the plaintiff. 1277: The respondent K. Rangachari was appointed as a Clerk in the scale of Rs. 260-400 by order dated March 31, 1956. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Superintendent in the scale Rs. 330-480 on February 1, 1957 and was confirmed in that post on April 30, 1958. On September 2, 1959, he applied for and obtained a certificate from the said High Court under article 132(1) of the Constitution as it involved a substantial question of law as to the scope of article 16(4). The respondent challenged the validity of the circular on the ground that it violated his fundamental right guaranteed under article 16(1) and (2) of the constitution. Held, that the Circular dated September 2,1959 could not be construed as giving effect to the provisions of article 16 (4) of the Indian Constitution. Article 335 of the Constitution provides that the President may with respect to any State or Union Territory make provision with respect to all matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the Government of India or any State Government. Article 336(a) gives power to the President to make any provision with respect thereto in accordance with the Constitution. Article 340(b) provides that the executive power of the Union shall extend to the matters with respect to which Parliament has power to make laws. Article 341(1) provides that Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule. The expression "any other matter" occurring in article 342(i) is used in connection with the matters mentioned in the said clause. The word "posts" in article 342 means posts, whether temporary or permanent, and includes such other conditions of service as are prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament. The word 'posts' in article 342 does not include appointments to public services. The word posts is used in the widest possible sense to cover all posts including promotions and termination of probationary rights. The word promotion and termination of service are not synonymous terms but are intended to convey different meanings. The word appointment is used in a wider sense to include both substantive and officiating promotions. In the case of appointment to a post, the appointment must take place either
2660: The appellant firm was assessed to income tax for the year 1946 47. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal filed by the firm. In proceedings for assessment to incometax for the year 1947 48, the firm contended that it had taken over the entire share capital of the firm and that the transaction was one to facilitate acquisition of a capital asset being a capital investment. The Tribunal rejected the contention holding that the transaction did not involve any business activity but was merely an adventure in the nature of trade. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the transaction involved a series of transactions which were purely commercial in character and could not be regarded as a casual receipt. The fact that the assessee had borrowed loans at interest to purchase shares was not decisive of the question whether the transaction was a business activity or not. The transaction was one for acquiring capital assets and not for carrying on business. The transaction did not amount to a trading venture. The transaction must be regarded as one for the purpose of profit. The Court observed that the circumstance that the tax payer had borrowed loans from the bank was not relevant because the transaction was not a business activity. The Court further held that the transaction fell within the definition of "business" under section 2(6) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922.
1910: The appellant was a local board of the Barpeta district in Assam. He had been granted licence under section 62 of the Assam Local Boards Act, 1923 for holding a market on his land. The local board imposed a tax on the Kharma market at Rs. 500/ per annum. The appellant challenged the validity of the impost on the K Sharma 's market by filing a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutionality of the impeached imposition on the ground that it was unconstitutional. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The rule is not applicable to the present case because the tax has been imposed by the local board in accordance with the rules framed by the State Government under section 62(3). The rule does not provide for any other method of collection of fees and taxes. It only provides that the tax shall be paid by the owner of any land used as a market which again shows that it is a tax on land. [556 H] (ii)The rule is not intended to give any special benefit to the local board but to enable them to collect fees from the persons who are actually carrying on the business. [557 D] (iii)The rule does not make any distinction between a market and a market. It merely lays down that the fee shall be levied by the local Board. The rule does nothing more than to fix the amount of fee payable by the owner. [558 B C] (iv)The rule also does not provide that the tax should be collected from the person who is carrying on the activity. [559 A B]

The word is used in the sense of income from property. The word has been used to denote the income from property which is received or is deemed to be received in the hands of the recipient. The word must be understood in its ordinary meaning. The word includes not merely the income from trade but also income from other sources. [982 B C] (3)The word 'incomes' is not defined either in the Income Tax Act or in the Companies Act. The word means income derived or receivable by an assessee. 5432: The respondent filed an application before the Competent Authority under section 19 of the Slum Act for permission to execute the order of eviction. The Competent Authority dismissed the application on the ground that the application was barred by limitation and it was further held that supplementary objections were not maintainable. The appellant filed a second appeal before the High Court which was dismissed in limine. In the meantime, the came into operation. On the 19th April, 1978, the respondent filed an execution application before the Rent Controller for execution of the decree. The appellant contended that the execution application was time barred as the decree holder did not take any steps for 12 years which expired before 20th March, 1975 to obtain permission from the Competent Authority. The executing court rejected the objection raised by the appellant. The High Court allowed the revision petition holding that the execution was barred by res judicata. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The question whether the decree passed by the competent authority is executable or not has to be considered in the light of the facts of each case. [847F] 1.2. The question that falls for consideration is whether the decree holder had taken steps for 12 year after the decree became executable. [848G] 1.3. The question of limitation does not arise when the decree is executed. It is only when the decree becomes executable that the execution can proceed. [849A] 1.4. The question about the period of limitation does no more than that when the decree holder takes steps for 12 or more years. [850B] 1.5. The question regarding the period of time during which the execution proceedings are pending is a mixed question of fact and law. [851C] 1.6. The question as to whether the execution application is barred by limitation or by principles of res judicata arises only when the execution application itself is barred by time because in the opinion of the said Rent Controller till such time the permission of the Competent Authority is obtained, no execution application could have been filed. [852D] 1.7. The question is whether the execution proceeding should be stayed until the permission of Competent Authority is sought. [853E] 1.8.
710: The Uttar Pradesh Transport Service (Development) Act, 1955, was passed by the U. P. Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 246(1) of the Constitution and section 68B of the Amending Act, which provided that the provisions of Part III of the Constitution shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any law other than the said Part. The U.P. Legislature passed a resolution on March 31, 1956, whereby it decided to enact a law for the regulation of transport of motor vehicles and for the control of their movement throughout the State and for the acquisition and disposal of property in the possession, custody, control or control of persons who may be found within the State. The U P. Legislature passed an Act, which was published in the U.P., Gazette on April 1, 1956, and was brought into force with retrospective effect from April 1, 1957. The appellants challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the provisions Of Part III of Constitution had been contravened by reason of the fact that the U.p. Legislature had no power to pass the Act. Held, that the U P. legislature had no power at all to pass the impugned Act. The U .P. Legislature had power to pass it as soon as the Act came into force but the Legislature did not think fit to pass it immediately after the Act came in force. The U Pradesh Legislature had power under article 254(2) of the Constitu tion to make laws with respect to matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The U p. Legislature had the power to legislate with respect to any matter not enumerated in List II of the Seventh Sche dule to the Constitution and therefore the U P Legislature had no authority to pass the U. p. Act. The provisions of the U P Act were valid and could not be challenged on the ground of violation of article 14 of the Constitution.

It cannot be said that the word is used in a particular sense and that it can only mean a piece of paper or a piece of glass. 6204: The respondents were recruited to the Indian Forest Service and were appointed to the IFS in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Forest Services (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1954. They joined the service on different dates between January 1, 1966 and June 22, 1966. In the year 1966, the Government of India issued a notification under section 3(2)(d) of the Act, which provided that the period of probation shall be one year. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court contending that they had been appointed to the Indian Police Service after the first or second attempt, namely, in the year 1966 and therefore, their seniority should have been fixed from the year of allotment assigned to them in the year of selection. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondents were entitled to be considered for promotion to the Indian Administrative Service from the date of their joining the service. The appellants contended that the respondents having joined the service after the first attempt, they are not entitled to be promoted to the Indian Civil Service even though they had completed the requisite number of years of service as required under the rules. The word 'year of allotment' is defined in clause (c) of sub regulation (3) of Regulation 2 of the Indian Administrative Services (Appointment by Promotion) Regulations, 1955 as meaning the period of time during which a member of the Indian Civil Services, who has been appointed to an All India Service or appointed to an ex cadre post in accordance with rule 7A of the Indian Forests Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1966, as the case may be. [8E F] (2) The expression "year of allotment" is defined in sub regulation (4) of regulation 2 of the IPS (Regulation of Senior Duty Posts) Rules, 1968 as meaning the year of appointment to the Indian Service. In the accounting years relevant to the assessment years 1943 44 and 1944 45, the Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs. 1188,000 on the ground that it relates to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company in Elphinstone Mills Ltd., Bombay. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the profit and loss account did not relate to the price of the shares purchased by the company in question but related to the price payable for the shares acquired by the company. On appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the reference made by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 23A(1) of the Act is not applicable to the facts of the case because the profits and gains distributed as dividends by any company within the twelve months immediately following the expiry of the previous year are less than the statutory percentage of the total income of the company of that previous year. [882E] (iv) The Income-tax Officer could not be said to have exercised his powers under section 23 A(1) in cancelling the orders of assessment made by him. [883F]

1892: The respondent was a licensee under the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951. The appellant Corporation fixed the scale of fees on the basis of annual valuation of cinema houses made by a method which does not appear on the record. The respondent moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the resolution. His main contention was that the levy was invalid as it did not comply with the provisions of section 548(2) of the Act and that the imposition was not authorised by the Act. Held, that the levy imposed by the Act was not ultra vires. Section 548(1) of the Calcutta Municipal act, 1951, provides that "no person shall carry on any trade or business in any place within the City except under and in accordance with the terms and conditions of a licence granted by the Commissioner". The respondent was carrying on the trade or business of running a cinema house in Calcutta. The Act was passed to provide for the regulation of the use of premises belonging to the Corporation and for the regulation thereof. Section 549 of the Act lays down that no person shall carry out any trade or carry on any occupation, trade or business without a licence from the Commissioner. The words "or otherwise" in section 548 (2) are wide enough to include all activities carried on by a person within the city. The word "business" has been defined in section 2(6) of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, to mean "any trade or business carried on by or under the authority of the Corporation." The word "trade" is defined in section 3(7) to mean "the doing of any of the following acts, namely, (a) the granting of a licence, (b) the granting, whether prospectively or retrospectively, of a licence or permission, authorizing the doing of any one or more of such acts; (c) the gambling, beating, exceptional rendering, performance of eggs, betting and gambling; (d) the Taking into consideration any other special circumstances; (e) the maintenance of public order; (f) the promotion of public health, safety or convenience of the public or any other matter relating to public streets or the public health, maintenance of supplies and services essential to
4851: The appellant company paid to its employees a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as incentive bonus for the period of employment. The question was whether the said amount should be included in the definition of 'wages ' and not in the wages payable under the contract of employment. Held: (1) that the expression 'and includes ' is an inclusive one and includes all payments made by the employer to the employee during the course of his employment; and the word 'awarded ' means 'paid or payable ' at intervals not exceeding two months '. [717 F] (2)that the word 'additional remuneration ' has been used in the definition clause in the Act and it must be given the widest possible meaning. It cannot include any payment which may have been made to an employee during the period of his employment but is not included in the term 'wages' within the meaning of section 2(22)(e) of the Act. (3)the word 'basic wage ' is defined in section 2(p) of the ,as "any allowance granted to meet necessities which are incidental to the purpose of employment."
2331: The appellants were tried for offences under sections 467/471, 420/465/471 read with section 120B I.P.C., and section 466/467/468/470 read with section 471/120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted them but convicted them under sections 467, 468 and 471 read with section 34 I.P,.C. The High Court confirmed their convictions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the charge of criminal conspiracy was not established by the prosecution; (ii) the sanction contemplated under section 196A(2) was a pre requisite to any Court taking cognizance of the offence; (iii) the trial was illegal because the necessary sanction under section 196 A(2) had not been obtained; and (iv) the trial having been held in violation of the provisions of section 196A (2), the trial was bad as no sanction was required under section 196(3). HELD: (i) The charge of criminal conspiracies is one of abetment of the crime. It is well settled that if an accused is charged with a conspiracy then all the conspirators need not be made parties to the conspiracy unless there are other circumstances which may reasonably lead to the conclusion that they were also parties to the agreement. [532 F] (ii) The trial of the appellants was illegal because they were prosecuted for non cognizable offences under sections 466, 467 and 471 I.P., Code. [533 C D] (iii) The trial was illegal since the necessary sanction for the prosecution of the appellants under section 196 (A)(2) was not obtained. [534 E] (iv) The trial is not vitiated merely because the sanction has not been obtained. [554 G H] (v) The trial must be held to have been vitiated on account of want of sanction. [535 D]

The Act also made provision for the payment of compensation and it is also provided that the provisions of the Act shall be deemed to have been validated from the date of publication of the Act. The Act was amended in 1955 and the Act was further amended in 1956. The Act came into force on January 26, 1957. The Act repealed the earlier Act and the new Act provided for the recovery of arrears of land revenue and other dues payable to the State Government. The Act provided for a machinery for collection of compensation and the procedure for recovery of the amount of compensation. The Act, however, did not provide for any appeal against the order of the Collector or the appellate authority. The Act therefore became void and inoperative. The Act then applied to certain areas which were included in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Act authorised the State Government by notification to declare areas which had already become subject to the jurisdiction of the Court of Wards and to direct that the provisions thereof would apply to those areas. The Act accordingly applied to those areas also. The Act thus made provision for payment of compensation to the persons who held or had interest in the land in which eradicating and other ancillary and subsidiary operations therein. The Act made provision for compensation to be determined in accordance with the principles laid down in section 7 of the Act for the recovery and distribution of the amount among the persons interested. The Act further provided that the amount of the compensation should be paid in cash or in bonds or partly in cash and partly in bonds. The Act again made provision for determination of the amount payable by the persons interested in the land. 2165: The respondents filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of possession of the plaint schedule land and mesne profits. They pleaded that their title to the property was declared by the Tahsildar in an application under the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932, and that the decision would be a bar to the maintainability of the suit in a civil court. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the Additional District Judge held that the suit had been filed within the period of limitation prescribed by section 90(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and that it was barred by limitation; but he held that the decree passed by the Tahsildar was a bar to a suit instituted by the respondents. In second appeal, the High Court held that the concurrent finding given by the courts below on the question of title to the suit land could not be challenged in a civil suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 90(2), which is a special provision, provides that no suit shall lie in any civil or revenue court against a person who is not a party to the suit. [623F] (a) Under section 91 of the Code, the jurisdiction of the civil court is barred in respect of matters specified therein. The words "any other matter" are used in section 90(3). Therefore, the word "any other matters" must be read as "other matters". [624G H] (b) The word "any" in section 90 does not mean "all other matters". It means all matters which are expressly mentioned in the said section. [625A] (c) The word 'any' in section 90 cannot be construed to mean only "every other matter". [626B] (d) The word, 'any other matter ' has been used in section 91(3) in the sense of all other matters. [627C] (e) The word is used in section 92(4) of the Act to give a wider meaning to the expression "any other case" than "any other kind of case". [628E]
435: The workmen of the appellant company were employed as clerks and depots cashiers in the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. They claimed that they should be paid dearness allowance at the same rate as the other employees of the Company, but the Industrial Tribunal rejected their claim on the ground that the recommendation made by the Bengal Chamber was not accepted in its entirety for the reason that it had no basis whatsoever for fixing the dearness allowance payable to the employees of the company. The Company 's appeal before the Labour Appellate Tribunal was also dismissed. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that (i) the Industrial Tribunal had erred in applying the principle laid down by the Bengal High Court in the case of Bengal Chamber of commerce; (ii) the Tribunal had ignored the fact that the recommendation of the Bengal Chamber had been accepted by the Bengal Chambers of Commerce; and (iii) the award of the Industrial Tribunal was contrary to the provisions of section 33(1)(b) of the Act. HELD: (i) The Tribunal has failed to apply the principle laid by the Bengal and Bombay High Courts in the case reported in [Bengal Chamber of Commerce vs The Workmen] ; and has wrongly applied the principle laid in the Bengal case. [778 F] (ii) The Tribunal had adopted a principle which was not accepted by the Calcutta High Court in its judgment in the case referred to above. It is true that the Tribunal had not considered the question whether the recommendation of Bengal Chamber or the Bengal Chamber Of Commerce should have been accepted in its fullest sense. But the Tribunal did not consider the question whether it had adopted any legal principle or acted in violation of any statute. [779 B C] (iii) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that the recommendation was made to the Bengal Chamber or to the Bengal Chamratary. The Tribunal had not taken into consideration the fact that it had adopted the principle which it had followed in the case. [772 D E] (iv) The Tribunal could not have relied upon the recommendation of a subordinate tribunal when it had not accepted it. [773 G H]
6500: The appellant was the second son of Raja Padam Singh, who died in 1942. He executed a lease deed dated 14th Maghar 1999 in favour of the respondent for a period of 20 years. The said lease deed provided that the land would be used by the respondent for the purpose of his own business and that he would not transfer any rights in the land to any third party without the previous sanction of the Government. The respondent made an application under section 27 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953 for grant of occupancy right in respect of the land in question. The appellant objected to the grant on the ground that the land had been granted to him for the purpose mentioned in the lease deed. The respondent contended that the land was not a forest land but was a part of the land which was reserved for the purpose. The respondent also contended that the grant was in respect of revenue yielding lands only admeasuring about 263.4 bighas and not in respect of forest lands. The respondent further contended that the lands were not forest lands but were held by the State as private forests. The respondent filed a suit for declaration of title and possession against the State. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the land could not be treated as forest land because the grant was not in respect to the forest lands. It was further contended that in view of the fact that the land in dispute was a forest land, the grant was invalid. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. 5488: The appellant was the owner of a building in which he had leased out a room to one M. 150: The petitioner was detained under section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code on a charge of having committed an offence punishable under section 193 of the Indian Penal Code. He challenged his detention in the High Court by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition but granted a certificate to appeal to this Court. It is contended for the State that the order of remand made by the trial Magistrate on the 9th March, 1953, was not a valid one and that it could be set aside only if he had applied for bail before the expiry of the period of remand. Held, that the order passed by the trial magistrate on the 9 th March, 1953 was not a lawful one and was liable to be set aside. The order of remand dated the 6th March, was not merely an order of remand but was directed to be produced in court on the 11th March itself. The order did not contain any direction for remand nor did it mention anything about the production of the accused at the time of the return of the case. The order dated the 12th March, therefore, was not an order of release of the accused on bail.
1018: The respondent was appointed a constable in the U.P. Police Force and on December 1, 1945, he was posted as officer incharge of Police Station, Intiathok, District Gonda. On November 17, 1952, the District Magistrate sent an endorsement to the Superintendent of Police that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent, that he had also received such complaints and that his general reputation for integrity was not good but that his general public reputation for integrity would be not good. The Superintendent of Police then issued a notice to the respondent under section 7 of the Police Act directing him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the respondent was charged with committing cognizable offences and therefore sub paragraph (1) of para 486 of the Police Regulations did not apply to the case and dismissed the petition. It further held that the order of discharge could only be made by a police officer senior in rank to a Superintendent and that the order was bad because it was passed without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph (I) of para. 486 of Police Regulations. Held:(i) that the respondent could not be said to have committed any offence or irregularity which may affect his reputation for integrity. The order of dismissal was not passed by a police Officer below the rank of a Superintendent of Police. The order was not passed in the manner prescribed by the Regulation. (ii)that the respondent was not entitled to hold the post of a Sub Inspector of Police at the time when the departmental inquiry was started. 2643: The respondent, a firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Seth Brothers, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1962 63 under section 13(3) of the Income Tax Act 1961. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 13 (1) (c) of the Act calling upon the respondent to produce certain documents which he had seized during the search. The respondent filed an application before the Commissioner of Income tax requesting that the documents seized be released to him. The Commissioner rejected the application. He held that the documents were not relevant for the purpose of proceeding under the Act. The Commissioner also held that the respondent 's statement that the documents are not relevant for purposes of proceedings under the Act was false. The Commissioner however directed the respondent to appear before the Income tax Officer on September 30, 1963. On September 30, 1964 the respondent appeared before the Income Tax Officer and produced certain documents. The Income Tax Officer passed an order directing the respondent to pay Rs. 1,00,000 as penalty. The respondent appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal. The High Court held that the Commissioner 's order was illegal because the respondent did not comply with the requirements of section 132A of the Income tax Act, 1961. The appellant contended that the Commissioner had no power to issue a direction under section 132(2)(b) of the Indian Income tax Act. HELD: (i) The Commissioner had no authority to direct the respondent to furnish any documents which he could have done if he had been asked to do so. [547 C] (ii) The Commissioner was not competent to pass an order under section 132A. The Commissioner had jurisdiction to pass such an order. [549 E] (iv) The Commissioner is not entitled to ask the assessee to give evidence or to produce documents. [550 F]

927: The appellant was appointed as Inspector General of Police in the State of Pepsu. He was dismissed from service by an order dated August 16, 1950. The order stated that he would be put to heavy loss and that his pension would be affected. The respondent State contended that the order of compulsory retirement did not amount to removal from service within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution and that it was void in law. Held, that the order was not by way of punishment but only a penalty for misconduct. The order was not one of dismissal or removal within the meaning Of article 311 of Constitution. The order merely mentioned that the officer had been removed from service. The order therefore did not amount either to removal or dismissal within the meaningof article 311 of constitution. The order did not amount, to removal from public service within the terms of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The word "dismiss" used in article 311 of 'the Constitution has reference to the conduct or character of the officer concerned which means that he is guilty of some act or omission which causes or is likely to cause pecuniary embarrassment to the Government servant. The word 'removal' in article 311 includes removal from service.

2950: The appellant, a firm of which the respondent was a partner, was prosecuted for cheating and breach of trust.
