3805: The 5th respondent, who was the decree holder in O.S. 19 of 1953, purchased the properties situated in village Devanoor and the appellant/auction purchaser in another suit being O.S No. 15 of 1949, which fetched an amount which was sufficient to satisfy the decretal amount mentioned in the sale proclamation but a few days after the sale had already taken place. The appellant/au thority purchased the properties in village Devana and the appellant obtained another money decree against the 5th respondent/decreeholder in O.A. No. 19 of 1954. In other words, the appellant/judgment debtor purchased the properties from the 5th respond ent in O.P. No. 18 of 1954. The appellant filed execution proceedings for selling the properties in the village Devana. The Executing Court held that the sale of the properties in villages Devana and Gudipadu were sufficient to satisfy all the decretals due under the decree in O.C. No. 15/1949 and ordered the sale of those properties in the other two suits. The High Court allowed the appeal of the judgment debtor and set aside the order of the Executing Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The sale of the property in village Devganoor was sufficient to meet the requirements of 0.21 r. 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [639 E] (2) The sale was not complete till the sale certificate was issued. It was only after the sale was completed that the entire decretal amounts could be mentioned in the first sale proclamation. [640 F] (3) The appellant/judgement debtor did not have any reason to believe that the sale was not proper or that he should be put up for sale. He merely wanted to get the sale set aside as it was not possible to do so. The appellant did not have the means to pay the decrettal amount. The appellant was therefore entitled to the benefit of the decree. [641 B C] (4) The appellant was entitled to the protection of the provisions of 0. 21 r. 64, Civil Procedure Code. [642 D]
1187: The petitioners, who were the legal representatives of their father, and their six children, were declared evacuee properties. They filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the order dated August 14, 1952, made by the Custodian under section 11 of the Act vesting the entire property in the Custodian. The contention was that the order was not a nullity as it did not contain any particulars about the persons who had become entitled to hold the property in question or any interest therein. Held, that the order of August 14, 1951, was a nullity as the notice under section 7 of the Act on which it was based, was issued to Abdul Aziz who was admittedly not an evacuee. The order was therefore bad for the reason that it was issued to the petitioners who were not co sharers or partners in the properties covered by the orders. The order did not affect the rights of the petitioners. The order merely stated that the petitioners ' shares in the properties were held by them as evacuee property and that they would be entitled to retain the same. The order does not purport to determine the nature of the property. The order is only a direction to the Custodian to take possession of the property and do the needful. The order cannot be construed as giving effect to the order of the Custodian.
862: The respondents were the Apollo Mills, Ltd., and other companies owning cotton textile mills specified in the annexure to the Special Leave Petition. They were owned by the appellant Mill Owners Association, Bombay. The dispute related to the compensation which the workers claimed for loss of wages and dearness allowances due to the short working or closure of the Textile Mills on certain days during the period between November 1, 1951, and July 13, 1952. The Labour Court held that the Standing Orders and 17 were determinative of the relations between the workmen and their employers under section 40(1) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, and that the decision of the Bombay High Court in Digambar Ramachandra 's case (1), was not applicable. The appellant contended that the Industrial Court had jurisdiction to decide the dispute as it was within its jurisdiction. Held, that the decision in Digamber Ramachandra vs Khandesh Mills (2) was a correct one and that the Industrial Tribunal had jurisdiction to determine the question whether the Standing Orders were determinative or not. The decision in Digamber Ramachandra v Khandesh Mills, (3) was given in view of the provisions of section 40(2) of the Act and the addition of Sch. 111 item 7 in the Bombay Industrial Disputes Act, 1938, under which the decision in the Bombay High court was given, did not affect the validity of the award made by the Labour Court.

The Port Trusts Act, 1879, was enacted to provide for the regulation of the import and export of goods and for the control of their prices. Under section 3(1) of the Act, the Port Trust is empowered to levy demurrage on the value of the goods at such rate as it thinks fit. Section 4 provides that the rates of demurrages shall be such as may be determined by rules made under the Act. Section 5 provides that the provisions of the Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any law other than this Act. The Port of Bombay had been established by the Government of India for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this Act. Section 6 provides that the Port Trust shall be entitled to charge demurrage for the period during which the goods are detained by the Port Trust. Section 7 provides that the port Trust shall pay to the Central Government demurrage at the following rates: (a) where the goods are landed at the port of destination, the demurrai shall be paid at the port where the goods arrived; (b) where the property in the goods has passed to the consignee, the demoorer shall be paid by the Port trust at the port in which the goods have passed.
